breaths.text: I mean to set down, as honestly and as frankly as I can, the plain facts of the married life I share with my wife—a relationship that, I suspect, has few parallels anywhere.
For me it is a record I shall never forget, and precious; for my readers, I dare say, it will serve as a kind of reference.
Japan these days is growing more international by the hour.
Japanese and foreigners mix freely; every sort of doctrine and idea comes pouring in; men, of course, and women too, are turning Western at a clip.
In a climate like this, couples of our peculiar kind, once so rare, will surely start turning up all over.
Looking back, we were already odd from the start.
I first met the woman who is now my wife some eight years ago.
I no longer remember the month or the day, but at the time she was a waitress at a place called Café Diamond, near Kaminarimon in Asakusa.
She was barely fifteen by the old count.
When I came to know her she had only just entered service there, a complete novice—not a full waitress at all, only an apprentice: an egg of a waitress, if you like.
Why a man of twenty-eight should have fixed his eye on a child like that I cannot say even now, not clearly.
Probably, at first, it was the name that pleased me.
Everyone called her Nao-chan, but when I asked, her real name turned out to be Naomi.
That “Naomi” struck my curiosity hard.
Naomi—splendid, I thought.
Write it NAOMI in Roman letters and she might as well be a Westerner.
That was how it began, and from there I started watching her more closely.

Strange how it works: once the name is Western, the face itself starts looking a little foreign, and clever besides, and you find yourself thinking it is a waste to leave a girl like that serving in a place of that sort.

In fact Naomi’s face (I shall write her name in katakana from here on; otherwise the flavor is lost) had something of the motion-picture actress Mary Pickford about it, and was certainly Western-looking.
This is no mere fondness of mine.
Even now, as my wife, a great many people say the same, so it must be true.
And not the face alone: strip her bare and the body is still more Western—though of course I learned that later, and at the time I knew nothing of the kind.
I only guessed, vaguely, from the way she wore her clothes, that with a figure like that the arms and legs could not be badly made.
A girl of fifteen or sixteen is hard to read unless you are her own parent or sister.
Asked what Naomi’s nature was like in the café days, I cannot give a clear answer.
Naomi herself, I expect, would say she simply passed those months in a kind of daze.
From the outside she seemed, if anything, a gloomy, taciturn child.
Her complexion had a bluish cast, like pane after pane of colorless plate glass stacked together, a deep, sunken tint, and she did not look healthy.

Partly this was because she had only just come into service: she wore no powder, as the other waitresses did, and was still a stranger to customers and companions alike, so she kept small in a corner and worked in silence, fussing at this and that.
That may be why she struck me as clever, too.
I ought to say something of myself.
At the time I was an engineer at an electric company, drawing a salary of a hundred and fifty yen a month.
I was born near Utsunomiya in Tochigi, finished the local middle school, came up to Tokyo and entered the Higher Technical School at Kuramae, and became an engineer not long after graduating.
Except on Sundays I commuted every day from a lodging-house in Shibaguchi to the company in Ōimachi.
Living alone in lodgings on a hundred and fifty yen a month, I was fairly comfortable.
I was the eldest son, but I had no duty to send money home to my mother or brothers and sisters.
The family farm was a sizable concern; my father was already gone, but my aged mother and a loyal uncle and aunt ran everything, so I was entirely free.
That did not mean I dissipated myself.
I was, if anything, a model salaried man—frugal, earnest, so ordinary as to be almost without character, going through the day’s work with neither complaint nor discontent.
That, more or less, was how I was then.
At the company, “Kawai Jōji” had a reputation as a “gentleman. ”
My amusements, such as they were, amounted to going to the motion pictures of an evening, strolling Ginza-dōri, or, on a rare splurge, the Imperial Theatre.
I was a young man not yet married, of course, and I did not dislike the company of young women.

Raised in the country, I was clumsy with people and had no dealings with the other sex at all, which is probably how I got myself made into a “gentleman”; but if the surface was gentlemanly, the inside was anything but off its guard.
Walking the streets, riding the streetcar every morning, I kept a constant eye on women.
It was at just such a period that this person called Naomi happened to appear before me.
I had not, even then, decided that no one was more beautiful than Naomi.
Among the young ladies one passed in the streetcars, in the corridors of the Imperial Theatre, on Ginza-dōri, there were, needless to say, any number more beautiful than she.
Whether Naomi’s looks would improve was a question for the future; a slip of a girl of fifteen was both a pleasure and a worry to look ahead upon.
So my first plan was simply this: take the child in and look after her, and if she seemed promising, educate her thoroughly, and I might even take her as my wife.
That was about the extent of it.
Partly this was sympathy; partly I wanted a little change in a life too ordinary, too monotonous, a day-to-day existence.
Honestly, I had grown tired of years of lodging-house living, and I wanted somehow to add a point of color, a little warmth, to that bleak life.
Even a small house of my own—furnish a room, plant flowers, hang a birdcage on a sunny veranda—and keep a maid for the kitchen work and the dusting: how would that be?
And if Naomi came, she would serve as maid and as the bird as well.
That, more or less, was the idea.
If that was all, why not take a proper wife from a respectable family and make a formal household?
The truth is I had not yet the courage to marry.
I must go into this a little.
I am a common-sense sort of man, I dislike the eccentric, and I could not have managed it anyway; and yet, oddly, my views on marriage were quite advanced, quite Western.
“Marriage,” to most people, is a stiff, ceremonial affair.
First there is a go-between, sounding out both sides.
Then a miai.
If neither party objects, a formal matchmaker is appointed, betrothal gifts are exchanged, and the bride’s luggage—five loads, seven, thirteen—is carted to the groom’s house.
Then the procession, the honeymoon, the bride’s first visit home... a great deal of troublesome procedure, and I disliked all of it.
If I married, I wanted something simpler, freer.
At that time, had I wanted to marry, there would have been plenty of candidates.

I was a country fellow, but I was sturdy, my conduct was correct, and—funny to say it—my looks were ordinary enough, and I had the company’s confidence, so anyone would have been glad to arrange a match.
But the truth is I hated being “arranged.
” No matter how beautiful the woman, one or two meetings could never tell you a person’s spirit or nature.
To settle a companion for life on a passing feeling—“well, she’ll do,” “she’s rather pretty”—is a piece of folly no one should be capable of.
From that point of view, taking in a girl like Naomi, watching her grow at leisure, and then, if she pleased me, making her my wife, was the best method.
I did not want a rich man’s daughter or a woman of great education; this would do.

Besides, to make a friend of a young girl, to watch her develop morning and evening, and to live in a house together in a bright, easy, almost playful spirit, seemed to me a different interest from founding a proper household, and a special one.
In short, Naomi and I would play at house, innocently.
Not “setting up a household” in that bothersome sense, but an easy simple life.
That was what I wanted.

The Japanese “home” of today insists that a chest of drawers, a long brazier, floor cushions, and so on, must stand in their appointed places; the work of master, wife, and maid is divided with a nasty neatness; neighbors and relatives are a nuisance; extra expense piles up; what might be simple becomes complicated and cramped; and for a young salaried man it is neither pleasant nor good.
In that respect I believed my plan was, in its way, an idea.
I spoke of this to Naomi about two months after I first knew her.
In the interval I went to Café Diamond whenever I had time, making as many chances as I could to grow close to her.
Naomi was very fond of motion pictures, so on my days off we would look in at the theatre in the park, and on the way back stop at some little Western restaurant or a soba shop.
Even then she was a girl of few words, and you could never tell whether she was pleased or bored; she sat mostly in a sulk.
And yet when I invited her she never said no.
“Yes, I don’t mind going,” she would answer meekly, and follow me anywhere.
What she took me for, what she meant by coming along, I did not know; but she was still a real child, and she had not yet learned to turn a suspicious eye on “a man.
” This “uncle” took her to the pictures she liked and treated her now and then, so she went out to play with him: that, I imagined, was the whole of her simple, innocent feeling.
As for me, I asked of her then nothing more than to be a child’s companion, a kind and gentle “uncle,” and I showed nothing more in my manner.
When I think of those pale, dreamlike days, it is as if we had lived in a fairy tale, and even now I cannot help wishing we might be that innocent pair again.
“How is it, Naomi-chan?
Can you see? ”
When the picture-house was packed and there were no seats, we would stand in a row at the back, and I would often speak to her like that. Then Naomi would say, “No, I can’t see a thing,”
and stretch on tiptoe for all she was worth, trying to peek between the necks of the people in front.
“You won’t see that way.
Climb up on this wood here and hold on to my shoulder. ”
I would boost her from below and set her on the high rail of the barrier.
She would dangle both feet, one hand on my shoulder, and at last, satisfied, hold her breath and stare at the picture.
“Is it interesting? ” I would ask, and she would say only,
“It’s interesting. ”
She never clapped her hands or jumped for joy; but her face, silent, with clever eyes opened wide, like a wise dog listening to a far-off sound, told you she was very fond of pictures indeed.
“Naomi-chan, aren’t you hungry? ” Even then she would sometimes say,
“No, I don’t want anything to eat. ”
But when she was hungry she would say “Yes” without reserve.
And if you asked—Western food, or soba—she would answer clearly what she wanted.
“Naomi-chan, your face looks like Mary Pickford’s. ”
I forget when it was—one evening after we had seen a picture of that actress, we stopped at a Western restaurant on the way back, and the subject came up. “Oh,”
she said, with no particular look of pleasure, only staring at me in a puzzled way for having come out with such a thing so suddenly. When I asked again,
“Don’t you think so? ” she answered, quite composed,
“I don’t know whether I look like her or not, but everyone says I look like a Eurasian. ”
“Well they would.
First of all your name is odd.
Who gave you a Western name like Naomi? ”
“I don’t know who gave it to me. ”
“Your father? Your mother?— ” “Someone or other— ”
“Then what does Naomi-chan’s father do? ”
“Father isn’t here anymore. ”
“And your mother? ” “Mother is here, but— ”
“Then brothers and sisters? ”
“There are lots of brothers and sisters—an older brother, an older sister, a younger sister— ”
The subject came up often after that, but whenever she was asked about her family she would put on a slightly displeased look and blur her words.
When we went out together we generally arranged it the day before, and met at a park bench or in front of the Kannon hall at a set time; she never missed the hour, never broke a promise.
If I was late for some reason and went along thinking, “I’ve kept her waiting too long, she’s gone home by now,” she would still be sitting there, exactly as arranged.
The moment she caught sight of me she would rise abruptly and walk straight toward me.
“Sorry, Naomi-chan.
You’ve been waiting a long time, haven’t you. ”
When I said that, she would answer only, “Yes, I waited,”
with no look of complaint, no sign of anger.

Once we had agreed to wait on a bench, and rain came on suddenly; I went out wondering how she was managing, and found her squatting under the eaves of that little shrine by the pond, still waiting, which struck me as painfully touching.
On such days her clothes were a faded meisen kimono, probably a hand-me-down from her sister, with a merino yūzen obi, her hair in the Japanese peach-split style, and a thin dusting of powder.
And always, though they were patched, she wore well-shaped white tabi that fitted her small feet snugly.
When I asked why she did her hair Japanese-style only on her days off, she would say, as usual without any real explanation, “They tell me to at home. ”
“It’s late tonight; I’ll see you to your door. ”
I said that more than once, but she would answer,
“It’s all right.
It’s right nearby; I can go home alone,”
and at the corner of Hanayashiki she would toss off a “goodbye” and patter away down a side street toward Senzoku-chō.
Yes—there is no need to dwell too long on those days, but once, when we had grown a little easier with each other, I had a long talk with her.
It was a warm evening toward the end of April, with a fine spring rain falling, I think.
The café was quiet that night, very still, and I sat a long while at a table, sipping at my drink.
That makes me sound like a drinker, but in fact I am a very poor one; I was only killing time, having a sweet cocktail of the sort women drink mixed for me, and licking at it a sip at a time.
She brought some food to the table, and I said, a little flushed with drink,
“Naomi-chan, sit down here a minute. ”
“What for? ”
she said, and sat down quietly beside me.
When I took a Shikishima from my pocket she struck a match at once.
“It’s all right, isn’t it, if we talk a little here.
It doesn’t look very busy tonight. ”
“No, this almost never happens. ”
“Are you always so busy? ”
“I am, from morning to night—there isn’t even time to read a book. ”
“So Naomi-chan likes to read, then. ”
“Yes, I do. ”
“What sort of things do you read? ”
“All kinds of magazines.
Anything to read is fine. ”
“That’s admirable.
If you want to read so much, you ought to go to a girls’ school. ”
I said it on purpose and looked into her face.
She seemed stung; she sat up stiffly and stared off in some other direction, but in her eyes there was clearly a sad, helpless color.
“Well, Naomi-chan, do you really want to study?
If you do, I could have you taught. ”
She still said nothing, so this time I spoke in a coaxing tone.
“Eh?
Naomi-chan, don’t sit there silent; say something.
What do you want to do?
What would you like to learn? ”
“I want to learn English. ”
“Hm, English—and that’s all? ”
“And I want to try music, too. ”
“Then I’ll pay the fees; why don’t you go and take lessons? ”
“But it’s too late to enter a girls’ school.
I’m already fifteen. ”
“What of it?
Unlike a boy, a girl isn’t too late at fifteen.
Or if it’s only English and music, you needn’t go to school at all; we can hire a teacher separately.
Well?
Are you in earnest? ”
“I am, in a way—then you’ll really let me do it? ”
And Naomi suddenly looked me full in the eyes.
“Yes, really.
But Naomi-chan, if we do that you can’t go on working here.
Is that all right on your side?
If you can leave this place, I wouldn’t mind taking you in and looking after you... and I’d take the responsibility, all the way, of making a proper woman of you. ”
“Yes, that’s all right, if you’ll do that. ”
The crisp, immediate answer, without a shadow of hesitation, surprised me a little.
“Then you’ll leave the café? ”
“Yes, I’ll leave. ”
“But Naomi-chan, even if that’s all right with you, we’ll have to hear what your mother and brother say, and how things stand at home. ”
“You don’t need to hear about home.
Nobody will say anything. ”
That is what she said, but in fact she was more anxious about it than she let on.
It was her usual habit: she hated me knowing the inside of her family, and put on an air that it was nothing.
I had no wish to force out of her what she so disliked telling, but to make her wish real I would still have to visit the family and talk it over thoroughly with her mother or brother.
As the matter advanced between us I said more than once, “Introduce me to someone of your family,” but oddly she was not pleased, and her stock answer was,
“It’s all right; you needn’t meet them.
I’ll talk to them myself. ”
I need not, for the sake of the woman who is now my wife, for the honor of “Mrs.
Kawai,” go raking up Naomi’s origins of those days at the cost of her displeasure, so I shall touch on that as little as I can.

It will come out of itself later, perhaps; and even if it does not, anyone can imagine what sort of household it was, considering that her home was in Senzoku-chō, that at fifteen she had been sent out as a café waitress, and that she never wanted anyone to know where she lived.
And that is not all.
I did in the end talk her round and meet her mother and brother, and they took almost no interest in their daughter’s or sister’s virtue.

The proposal I put to them was this: the girl herself was fond of study, and it seemed a pity to leave her long in a place of that sort, so if they had no objection, would they not place her in my charge?

I could not do a great deal, but I had been wanting a maid anyway, and she could do the kitchen work and the dusting, and in the intervals I would give her a decent education—I told them everything, my circumstances, that I was still unmarried—and they answered, in a way that took all the fight out of it, “If you would do that, she would be very fortunate indeed...
” Exactly as Naomi had said: there had been no need to meet them.
There are, in this world, remarkably irresponsible parents and brothers, I felt keenly then; and for that very reason Naomi seemed all the more touching, all the more pitiable.

From the mother’s words they seemed to have found Naomi a handful: “The truth is we meant her to be a geisha, but she herself had no taste for it, and we could not keep her idle forever, so we had no choice but to send her to the café.
” If someone would take her in and bring her up, they would, in short, be able to breathe easy.
Ah, so that was it: she hated being at home, and that was why on her days off she always went out, to the pictures and so on.
Hearing the circumstances, I at last solved the riddle.
That her family was of that sort was, for Naomi and for me both, a great piece of luck.
Once the matter was settled she at once took her leave of the café, and every day the two of us walked about looking for a suitable house to rent.

My work was in Ōimachi, so we wanted somewhere convenient for that; on Sundays we met early at Shimbashi Station, and on other days we met in Ōimachi just as I left the company, and we went round Kamata, Ōmori, Shinagawa, Meguro, mainly those suburbs, and in the city around Takanawa, Tamachi, Mita; then on the way back we would have supper together somewhere, and if there was time look in at the pictures as usual, or stroll Ginza-dōri, and she would go back to Senzoku-chō and I to my lodgings in Shibaguchi.
Houses to rent were scarce just then, and a suitable one was not to be found in a hurry; we lived like that for a little over two weeks.

If anyone, on a fine May Sunday morning, had noticed a man who looked like a company employee and a shabby little girl with her hair in the peach-split style, walking side by side along a leafy suburban road around Ōmori, what would they have made of it?

The man called the girl “Naomi-chan,” the girl called the man “Kawai-san,” and they were neither master and servant, nor brother and sister, nor yet husband and wife, nor quite friends, a little shy of each other as they talked, asked for house-numbers, looked at the scenery, and turned to catch the color and scent of flowers on hedges, in garden plots, along the roadside, walking here and there through a long late-spring day, looking happy: an odd pair they must have seemed.
Speaking of flowers, she was very fond of Western flowers, and knew a great many names I did not know at all—difficult English names, too.

She had learned them, it seemed, from always handling the flowers in the vases at the café; and if there happened to be a greenhouse inside a gate we were passing, she would stop at once, sharp-eyed, and cry,
“Oh, what pretty flowers! ”
with a look of real pleasure.
“Then which flower does Naomi-chan like best? ” I asked her once, and she said,
“I like tulips best. ”
Raised in a cramped alley like Senzoku-chō in Asakusa, Naomi had, perhaps by reaction, come to long for open country and to love flowers.
Violets, dandelions, milk vetch, primroses—if such things were growing on a field-path or a country lane she would trot off at once to pick them.
And in the course of a whole day’s walking her hands would fill with picked flowers, she would make I don’t know how many bunches, and she would carry them carefully all the way home.
“Those flowers are all wilted already; throw them away, that’s enough. ”
Even then she would not agree.
“It’s all right.
If you give them water they’ll come right back to life.
You should put them on Kawai-san’s desk. ”
And when we parted she would always give me the bunches.

We searched everywhere and still could not easily find a good house; after much wandering, the place we finally rented was a very shabby Western-style house near the government railway line, some twelve or thirteen chō from Ōmori Station.
What they call a “culture house”—they were not yet so fashionable then, but in today’s language that is what it would have been.
A steep roof of red slate that seemed more than half the height of the whole building.
An outside wrapped in white walls like a matchbox.
Rectangular glass windows cut here and there.
And in front of the porch, rather a patch of vacant ground than a garden.
That was the look of it: more interesting as a picture than as a place to live.
And no wonder: the house had been built by some painter, they said, who had lived there with a model-girl as his wife.
The arrangement of rooms was accordingly quite inconvenient.

A ridiculously vast atelier, a tiny entry, a kitchen, and that was all downstairs; upstairs there were a three-mat room and a four-and-a-half-mat room, but those were like storerooms in the attic, not rooms you could use.
To reach the attic there was a staircase inside the atelier, and at the top a railed gallery from which, like a theatre box, you could look down into the atelier.
When Naomi first saw the “scenery” of this house she said,
“My, how Western! I like a house like this,”
and seemed very pleased.
And I, because she was so delighted, agreed at once to take it.
Probably Naomi, in her childish way, felt a curiosity about the odd, fairy-tale style of it, even if the plan was not practical.
It was certainly a good house for a carefree young man and a girl who meant to live as little like a household as they could, in a spirit of play.
The painter and the model-girl before us had no doubt meant the same; and if there were only two of you, that one atelier room was enough to sleep in, get up in, and eat in.
It was toward the end of May, I think, that I finally took Naomi in and we moved into that “fairy-tale house.

” Once we were in, it was not so inconvenient as I had feared: from the sunny attic rooms you could see the sea; the vacant ground in front, facing south, was well suited to a flower bed; the government-line trains that passed now and then near the house were a flaw, but there was a little rice-field in between, so they were not so noisy, and all in all it was a dwelling without complaint.
Moreover, because it was so unsuitable for ordinary people, the rent was unexpectedly cheap: twenty yen a month, no deposit, in those days when prices generally were low, and that pleased me too.
“Naomi-chan, from now on don’t call me ‘Kawai-san’; call me ‘Jōji-san.’ And let’s live really like friends. ”
That is what I told her on the day we moved.

Of course I wrote home as well, that I had left my lodgings and taken a house of my own, that I had hired a fifteen-year-old girl in place of a maid, and so on; but I did not write that I meant to live with her “like friends.
” Relatives from the country almost never came to visit, and if a need to tell them arose, I would tell them then, I thought.
For a while we spent busy, happy days buying all sorts of furniture to suit this unusual new home, arranging it, decorating.

I tried as far as I could to cultivate her taste: even for a small purchase I would not decide alone, but let her give her opinion, and adopted as many of her ideas as I could; and since it was a house with no place for the usual household goods—chests, long braziers, and so on—the choice was free, and we could design things as we liked.

We found some cheap Indian chintz, which Naomi sewed with precarious stitches into window curtains; from a Western furniture shop in Shibaguchi we hunted up old rattan chairs and a sofa, an easy chair, a table, and set them in the atelier; on the walls we hung two or three photographs of American picture actresses, Mary Pickford among them.

I would have liked the bedding Western-style too, if it could be managed, but buying two beds would have cost money, and quilts could be sent from the country house, so in the end I had to give that up.
But what they sent from the country for Naomi was a maid’s bedding: the regulation arabesque-patterned, stiff cotton pancake of a futon. I felt somehow sorry for her, and said,
“This is a bit too hard on you.
Shall I swap one of my quilts with you? ” But she said,
“No, it’s all right. This is plenty for me,”
and pulled it over herself, and slept alone in the lonely three-mat attic room.
I slept in the next room—the four-and-a-half-mat one, also in the attic—and every morning, when we woke, we would call to each other from this room and that, still burrowed in our quilts.
“Naomi-chan, are you up yet? ”
I would say.
“Yes, I’m up.
What time is it now? ”
she would answer.
“Half past six—shall I cook the rice this morning? ”
“Shall you?
I cooked it yesterday, so today Jōji-san can cook it. ”
“Well, then I suppose I must.
Or shall we just have bread, to save the trouble? ”
“Yes, that’s all right.
But Jōji-san is quite a cheat. ”
And if we wanted rice we would wash it in a little earthen pot, and without even transferring it to a rice-tub bring it to the table and poke at some tinned stuff or other as we ate.

If even that was a nuisance we would make do with bread and milk and jam, or nibble Western cakes, or for supper get by with soba or udon; when we wanted a bit of a feast the two of us would go out to a Western restaurant nearby. “Jōji-san, give me beefsteak today,”
she would often say.
After breakfast I would leave Naomi alone and go to the company.
In the morning she would fuss with the flowers in the bed, and in the afternoon lock up the empty house and go to her English and music lessons.

For English it seemed better to start with a Westerner, so she went every other day to a Miss Harrison, an elderly American lady living in Meguro, for conversation and a reader, and what was lacking I would drill her in at home now and then.

Music I had no idea how to arrange, but I heard that a woman who had graduated from the Ueno music school two or three years before taught piano and voice in her own house, and for that Naomi went every day to Isarago in Shiba for an hour’s lesson.

In her meisen kimono with a navy cashmere hakama over it, black stockings and pretty little half-shoes, she made herself over completely into a schoolgirl, her heart beating with the joy that her ideal had at last come true, and went back and forth diligently.
Sometimes I would meet her on the street on her way home, and you would never have thought she was a girl raised in Senzoku-chō who had been a café waitress.
She never again did her hair in the peach-split style; she tied it with a ribbon, braided the ends, and wore it in pigtails.
I said earlier “the feeling of keeping a bird”; after I took her in, her color grew healthier, her nature gradually changed, and she became in truth a lively, sunny little bird.
And that vast atelier room was, for her, a great cage.
May ended and the bright climate of early summer came.
The flowers in the bed grew day by day and gained in color.
When I came home from the company and she from her lessons, of an evening, the sun leaking through the Indian-chintz curtains still lit the four white-painted walls of the room as sharply as day.

She would put on a flannel unlined kimono, slip her bare feet into slippers, and stamp about the floor singing the songs she had learned, or play blindman’s buff or tag with me; at such times she would run round and round the atelier, leap over the table, wriggle under the sofa, overturn chairs, and still not have enough, race up the stairs and scurry back and forth along that box-like attic gallery like a mouse.
Once I became a horse and crawled about the room with her on my back.
“Hai, hai, dō, dō! ”
Naomi would say, making a towel into reins and putting them in my mouth.
It was on a day of such play, I think—Naomi, laughing kya-kya, went up and down the stairs too vigorously, missed her footing at last, tumbled from the top, and suddenly began to whimper.
“Here, what’s the matter—show me where you hit yourself. ”

I said, and lifted her up; she still sniffled, and rolled back her sleeve to show me: in falling she must have caught on a nail or something, for the skin at the elbow of her right arm was broken and blood was oozing.
“What, crying over a little thing like this!
Come here, I’ll put a plaster on it. ”
And while I put on the plaster and tore a towel for a bandage, Naomi’s face, full of tears, with drops of snot falling as she hiccupped, was like a mere infant’s.
The wound, unluckily, festered after that and did not heal for five or six days, and every time I changed the bandage she never failed to cry.
But whether I was already in love with Naomi then, I do not well know myself.
Yes, I must have been in love; but in my own mind I thought the pleasure was in bringing her up, training her into a fine woman, and that that alone would satisfy me.

Then that summer the company gave me two weeks’ leave, and as I did every year I went home; I left Naomi at her family in Asakusa, locked up the Ōmori house, and when I got to the country those two weeks felt unbearably monotonous and lonely.
Is it so dull without that child?
Is this the beginning of love?
I thought then, for the first time.
And making some excuse to my mother, I cut the stay short and arrived in Tokyo after ten at night, but I had a taxi run at once from Ueno Station to Naomi’s house.
“Naomi-chan, I’m back.
There’s a car waiting at the corner; let’s go to Ōmori right away. ”
“Oh. Then I’ll come at once,”
she said, and kept me waiting outside the lattice, then came out with a small furoshiki bundle.
It was a very muggy night, and Naomi had on a pale, fluffy muslin kimono with a pattern of pale-purple grapes, her hair tied with a wide, showy rose-pink ribbon.
I had bought her the muslin at the Obon just past, and while I was away she had had it made up at home and was wearing it.
“Naomi-chan, what have you been doing every day? ”
As the car started toward the lively Hirokōji, I sat beside her and spoke, drawing my face a little toward hers.
“I went to the pictures every day. ”
“Then you weren’t lonely, I suppose. ”
“No, I wasn’t particularly lonely, but... ” She thought a moment, then said,
“But Jōji-san came back sooner than I expected. ”
“The country is dull, so I cut the plan short and came.
Tokyo is still the best, after all. ”
I said it with a sigh of relief, and looked at the glittering night-flowers of the city lights outside the window with a feeling of inexpressible homesickness.
“But I think the country is nice in summer, too. ”
“That depends on the country.
My house is a deep-grass farmhouse, the scenery nearby is ordinary, there are no famous places, mosquitoes and flies drone from broad daylight, and it’s so hot you can’t stand it. ”
“My, a place like that? ”
“A place like that. ”
“I want to go somewhere, to the seaside. ”
The sudden tone of Naomi’s voice had the sweetness of a spoiled child.
“Then shall I take you somewhere cool soon?
Would you like Kamakura, or Hakone? ”
“The sea is better than hot springs—I want to go, I really do. ”

Hearing only that innocent voice, she was still the old Naomi; and yet in the mere ten days I had not seen her she seemed suddenly to have grown, stretched out, and I could not help stealing a glance at the rounded shape of her shoulders and the region of her breasts breathing under the muslin kimono.
“That kimono suits you well.
Who sewed it for you? ”
I said after a while.
“Mother sewed it. ”
“What did they say at home?
Didn’t they say the choice was good? ”
“Yes, they did—not bad, but the pattern is too Western, they said—”
“Your mother said that? ”
“Yes—the people at home don’t understand anything. ”
And she, with a look as if she were staring into the distance, said,
“Everyone said I had completely changed. ”
“Changed how? ”
“That I’d become terribly Western. ”
“Well they would.
Even I can see that. ”
“Do you think so?—They told me to try Japanese hair once, but I didn’t want to, so I didn’t. ”
“Then that ribbon? ”
“This?
I went to Nakamise and bought it myself.
How is it? ”
And she twisted her neck, letting her dry, unscented hair blow in the wind, and showed me the rose-pink cloth fluttering there.
“Yes, it sets you off well.
This is so much better than Japanese hair, you can’t imagine. ” “Hm,”
she said, and gave a little toss of that snub nose, smiling as if she had got her way.
That slightly impertinent way of smiling with the tip of her nose was a habit of hers, but to my eyes it looked, on the contrary, very clever.
Naomi kept begging, “Take me to Kamakura!
” so we went, intending only two or three days, at the beginning of August.
“Why does it have to be two or three days?
If we’re going, it’s no fun unless we stay ten days or a week. ”
She made a slightly sulky face as we set out; but I had come back from the country on the pretext that the company was busy, and if that came out it would be a little awkward vis-à-vis my mother.
To say so, though, would only make Naomi feel small, I judged, so I said,
“Well, put up with two or three days this year; next year I’ll take you somewhere unusual and we’ll stay as long as we like.
There, isn’t that all right? ” “But only two or three days—”
“That’s true, but if you want to swim you can swim at the Ōmori shore after we come back. ”
“I can’t swim in a dirty sea like that. ”
“Don’t say such unreasonable things.
Be a good girl and do as I say; in return I’ll buy you some clothes.
That’s right, you said you wanted a Western dress, didn’t you?
I’ll have a dress made for you. ”
Caught by that bait of a “Western dress,” she at last consented.
In Kamakura we stayed at an unimpressive seaside inn called Kinparō in Hase.
There is a funny story about that, looking back.
I still had most of the bonus I had received that half-year, so there was really no need to economize for a stay of two or three days.

And I was so pleased to be going on an overnight trip with her for the first time that I wanted, if possible, to make the impression a beautiful one, not to pinch, and at first I thought of going to a first-class inn.
But on the day itself, from the moment we boarded a second-class car of the Yokosuka line, we were seized by a kind of shrinking.
The train was full of wives and young ladies going to Zushi and Kamakura, making a glittering row of them, and when we squeezed in among them Naomi’s appearance struck me as terribly shabby.

It was summer, of course, so those wives and young ladies were not loaded with ornaments; but comparing them with Naomi, I felt there was an undeniable difference of quality between those born in the upper ranks of society and those who were not.
Naomi had become a different person from her café days, and yet I thought—and she herself must have felt it still more strongly—that those of poor birth and breeding are, after all, hopeless.
And that muslin kimono with the grape pattern, which usually made her look so Western—how pitiful it looked then.

Among the ladies sitting in a row there were some in simple yukata, but a jewel glittered on a finger, or some luxury showed in what they carried, something that spoke of their wealth; in Naomi’s hands, besides that smooth skin, nothing shone that was worth boasting of.
I still remember how she hid her parasol, looking embarrassed, in the shadow of her sleeve.
And no wonder: the parasol was new, but anyone could see it was a cheap article of seven or eight yen.

So although we had been dreaming of Mitsuhashi, or even of putting up at the Kaihin Hotel, when we went as far as the gate we were cowed by the imposing entrance, walked the Hase road two or three times, and in the end went to Kinparō, a second- or third-class place by local standards.
The inn was full of noisy young students and we could not settle, so we spent every day on the beach.
Tomboy Naomi was in good spirits the moment she saw the sea, forgot how she had drooped in the train, and clinging to my arm said,
“I simply must learn to swim this summer,”
and splashed about vigorously in the shallows.

I would hold her body in both hands and float her on her stomach, or have her grip a post firmly and take her legs and teach her the kick, or suddenly let go on purpose and make her drink bitter seawater; when we tired of that we practiced riding the waves, or lay about on the beach playing in the sand, and from evening we would hire a boat and row out toward the offing—and at such times she would always wrap a large towel over her bathing suit, sit in the stern or pillow her head on the gunwale looking up at the blue sky, without a thought of anyone, and in a high voice sing her favorite Neapolitan boat-song, “Santa Lucia. ” O dolce Napoli, O soul beato,
I would listen, enchanted, to her soprano singing in Italian, ringing over the evening-calm sea, and row quietly on.
“Farther, farther,” she wanted to run on endlessly over the waves.
Before we knew it the sun had set, stars twinkled down on our boat from the sky, the surroundings grew dim, and her figure was only a faintly white towel, the outline blurring.

But the bright singing voice would not stop: “Santa Lucia” was repeated again and again, then became “Lorelei,” then “The Wandering People,” then a passage from Mignon, and with the slow progress of the boat she went on through various songs...
Experiences of this kind everyone has once in youth, I suppose, but for me that was the first time.
I am an electrical engineer, remote from literature and art; I rarely pick up a novel; but what I remembered then was Natsume Sōseki’s Kusamakura, which I had once read.

Yes, there is a place in it, I think, “Venice is sinking, Venice is sinking”; and rocking in the boat with Naomi, looking through the curtain of evening mist from the offing at the lights on shore, that phrase rose strangely in my breast, and I felt somehow tearful, dreamily drunk, as if I wanted to be carried with her just as we were into some boundless far world.
That a rough fellow like me could taste such a mood at all meant those three days in Kamakura were not wasted.
And that is not all: those three days gave me another important discovery.
Until then, though I had been living with Naomi, I had had no chance to know what sort of figure she had—to put it bluntly, the look of her naked body; and this time I came to know it truly well.

When she first went out to the bathing beach at Yuigahama, wearing next to her skin the dark-green bathing cap and bathing suit we had gone to Ginza the night before to buy, I cannot tell you how glad I was, honestly, at the regularity of her limbs.
Yes, I was simply glad.
Because from the way she wore her clothes and so on I had already thought Naomi’s curves must be thus and so, and the imagination had been right.
“Naomi, Naomi, my Mary Pickford, what a well-proportioned, fine figure you have.
Those supple arms of yours.
Those straight legs, as clean as a boy’s. ”
I cried it out, unbidden, in my heart.
And I could not help remembering the lively bathing girls of Mack Sennett, familiar from the pictures.

No one likes to write too particularly of his own wife’s body, I suppose, and I too take no pleasure in talking grandly of such things, years later, about the woman who became my wife, or letting many people know.

But if I do not say it the story will not hang together, and if I hold back even that much there is no point in keeping this record at all; so I must set down here, in outline, what sort of physique Naomi had when she stood on the Kamakura shore in August of her fifteenth year.

Naomi then, standing beside me, was perhaps an inch or so shorter than I.—I should note that though I was of a robust, rock-like build, I was only about five feet two, on the small side for a man.—But a striking feature of her bone-structure was that the torso was short and the legs long, so that seen from a little distance she looked much taller than she was.
And that short torso was very deeply nipped, like an S, and at the lowest part of the nip there was already a quite womanly round swell of the hips.
Around that time we had seen a mermaid picture called, I think, Daughter of the Sea-God, with the famous swimming champion Miss Kellerman in the lead, so I said,
“Naomi-chan, do Kellerman for a moment,”

and she would stand on the sand, both hands raised to the sky, and show me a diving pose; and when she put her thighs tightly together there was not a hair’s breadth between the legs, and from the hips down they drew one long, slender triangle with the ankles at the apex.
She seemed proud of that, and would say,
“How is it, Jōji-san?
My legs aren’t crooked, are they? ”
and walk, and stand still, and stretch them out hard on the sand, looking with pleasure herself at the shape.
Another feature of Naomi’s body was the line from neck to shoulder.
The shoulders...
I often had occasion to touch her shoulders.
Because whenever Naomi put on her bathing suit she would come to my side and say, “Jōji-san, just fasten this for me,” and have me do the buttons at the shoulder.

Girls with sloping shoulders and a long neck like Naomi’s are usually thin when they undress, but she was the opposite: she had unexpectedly thick, ample, splendid shoulders, and a chest that looked as if the breath in it were strong.

When I fastened the buttons, if she drew a deep breath or moved her arms and set the flesh of her back rolling in waves, the bathing suit, already fit to burst, would stretch full at the hill-like swell of the shoulders and look ready to snap.
In a word it was a shoulder charged with force, overflowing with the feeling of “youth” and “beauty.
” I compared her privately with the many girls around, and it seemed to me there was no one else who combined such healthy shoulders with so graceful a neck.
“Naomi-chan, keep still a little; if you move like that the buttons are too tight to fasten. ”
And I would pinch the edge of the bathing suit and force those shoulders in, as one stuffs a large thing into a bag.
That a girl of this physique should have been fond of sport and a tomboy was only natural.
In fact Naomi was clever at anything that used the hands and feet.

Swimming, beginning with those three days in Kamakura, she practiced hard every day afterward at the Ōmori shore, and by the end of that summer she had mastered it, and could row a boat, handle a yacht, all sorts of things.
And after playing the whole day, when the sun went down she would come home exhausted, saying “Ah, I’m worn out,” carrying the soaking bathing suit. “Aah, I’m hungry,”
she would say, throwing herself into a chair.
Sometimes cooking supper was too much trouble, so we would stop at a Western restaurant on the way back and stuff ourselves as if the two of us were in a contest.
After beefsteak, beefsteak again: she was fond of it, and would easily put away three plates.

If I wrote down all the happy memories of that summer there would be no end, so I will leave it at this; but one thing I must not omit is that from that time I formed the habit of putting her in the bath and washing her hands and feet and back with a rubber sponge.
Naomi was sleepy and found going to the public bath a bother, so it began with rinsing off the seawater in the kitchen, or taking a hip-bath.
“Come, Naomi-chan, if you go to sleep like that your body will be sticky and unpleasant.
Get into this basin; I’ll wash you. ”
When I said that, she would do as she was told and let me wash her quietly.

It became a habit, and even when the cool autumn season came the hip-baths did not stop; in the end we set a Western bath and a bath-mat in a corner of the atelier, screened it with a folding screen, and I washed her all through the winter.
Some of my quicker readers will already have imagined, from the last chapter, that Naomi and I had formed a relation beyond friendship.
In fact it was not so.
As the months went by, it is true, a kind of “understanding” had formed in both our breasts.

But one of us was still a girl of fifteen, and I, as I have said, was a strict “gentleman” with no experience of women; besides, I felt a responsibility for her virtue, so I rarely let a passing impulse carry me beyond the bounds of that “understanding.

” In my own mind, of course, the thought had taken firmer and firmer root that there was no woman I would make my wife but Naomi, and that even if there were, I could not now, as a matter of feeling, abandon her.
And for that very reason I did not want our first contact with that matter to be in a way that would soil her, or in an attitude of toying with her.

Yes: Naomi and I first entered that relation the following year, in the spring of her sixteenth year, on the twenty-sixth of April.—I remember the date so clearly because at that time, and indeed much earlier, from around the time the hip-baths began, I had been keeping a diary of various things about Naomi that interested me each day.

In those days Naomi’s figure was growing more womanly, strikingly so, day by day; and just as a parent who has had a baby notes down how the child grows—“first smile,” “first words”—I recorded one by one the things that caught my attention.
I still turn those pages now and then.
Under Taishō such-and-such, September 21st—that is, the autumn of Naomi’s fifteenth year—it says:
“Gave her a hip-bath at eight in the evening.
The sunburn from sea-bathing has not yet gone.

Only the parts that were in the bathing suit are white, the rest quite black; I am the same, but Naomi’s natural skin is white, so it shows all the more sharply, and even naked she looks as if she were still in a bathing suit.
When I said her body was like a zebra, Naomi laughed, finding it funny. ... ”
Then about a month later, under October 17th:
“I thought the sunburn and peeling had gradually healed, but on the contrary the skin became glossier and far more beautiful than before.
When I washed her arm, Naomi was silent, watching the soap-bubbles melt and run over the skin.
‘It’s pretty, isn’t it,’ I said, and she said, ‘It really is pretty,’ and added, ‘the soap-bubbles.’ ... ” Then November 5th—
“Tried the Western bath for the first time tonight.
Unused to it, Naomi slipped and slid in the water and laughed kya-kya.
When I said ‘big baby,’ she called me ‘Papa.’ ... ”
Yes: this “Baby” and “Papa” came up often afterward.
When Naomi begged for something or threw a tantrum she would always, in play, call me “Papa. ”
“Naomi’s Growth”—that was the title on the diary.

It was, needless to say, a record of matters concerning Naomi only; presently I bought a camera and photographed her face, which was coming more and more to resemble Mary Pickford, in various lights and angles, and pasted the pictures here and there among the entries.
I have wandered off on the diary, but according to it, at any rate, the date on which she and I became bound beyond cutting was the twenty-sixth of April in our second year at Ōmori.
There was already, of course, an unspoken “understanding” between us, so it came about quite naturally, neither of us seducing the other, almost without a word exchanged, in tacit agreement.
Then she put her mouth to my ear and said,
“Jōji-san, you won’t abandon me, will you. ”
“Abandon you?—Never, so set your mind at rest.
Naomi-chan knows my heart well enough, but... ”
“Yes, I know, but... ”
“Then from when did you know? ”
“Well, from when... ”
“When I said I would take you in and look after you, what did Naomi-chan take me for?—Didn’t you think I meant to make a proper person of you, and in time marry you? ”
“I did wonder if that was the idea, but... ”
“Then Naomi-chan came to me ready to be my wife, too. ”
And without waiting for her answer I went on, holding her as tightly as I could.—
“Thank you, Naomi-chan, truly thank you, for understanding so well. ...
I’ll tell you the honest truth now: I never thought you would become so... so completely the woman of my ideal.
I have been lucky.
I will cherish you all my life. ...
You only. ...
I will never treat you cheaply, as ordinary couples do.
Please think that I am really living for you.
I will grant whatever you wish, so study more and become a fine person. ... ”
“Yes, I’ll study with all my might, and I’ll become a woman Jōji-san really likes, I will, surely... ”
Tears were running from Naomi’s eyes, and before I knew it I was crying too.
And that whole night the two of us talked, without tiring, of what was to come.
Soon after that, from Saturday afternoon into Sunday, I went home to the country and for the first time told my mother about Naomi.

Partly Naomi seemed anxious about what they would think at home, and I wanted to set her mind at rest; and I myself wanted to carry the matter openly and fairly, so I hurried the report to my mother as much as I could.
I stated my views on “marriage” honestly, and explained the reasons why I wanted Naomi for a wife, so that even an old person could understand.
My mother had always understood my character and trusted me, so she only said,
“If that’s what you mean to do you may take the child as a wife, but a family like hers is apt to make trouble, so be careful there is no bother later. ”

I wanted, even if the public wedding were two or three years off, to have her entered in the family register soon, so I approached Senzoku-chō at once; but they were easygoing, mother and brothers, and it was settled without trouble.
Easygoing they were, but they did not seem black-hearted people: they said not one thing that smacked of greed.
After that, needless to say, the intimacy between Naomi and me developed at a sudden speed.
No one in the world knew yet, and on the surface we still lived like friends, but we were already, in law, a married couple with nothing to hide from anyone. “Naomi-chan,”
I said to her once.
“Let’s go on living like friends from now on too, no matter how long.— ”
“Then will you go on calling me ‘Naomi-chan’ no matter how long? ”
“Of course.
Or shall I call you ‘Okusan’? ” “I don’t want that—”
“Otherwise shall we make it ‘Naomi-san’? ”
“I don’t want ‘san.’ ‘Chan’ is still better, until I ask you to make it ‘san.’”
“Then I’ll be ‘Jōji-san’ forever too. ”
“Of course; there’s no other way to call you. ”
Naomi was lying on her back on the sofa, holding a rose, pressing it to her lips and fussing with it, when she suddenly said, “Jōji-san?
” and spread both arms and clasped my neck instead of the flower.
“My dear Naomi-chan,” I said, held so tightly I could hardly breathe, speaking from the dark of her sleeve,
“My dear Naomi-chan, I don’t only love you; to tell the truth I worship you.
You are my treasure, a diamond I found myself and polished.
So to make you a beautiful woman I’ll buy you anything.
I could give you my whole salary. ”
“It’s all right; you needn’t do that.
Rather than that, I’ll really study English and music more. ”
“Yes, study, study; I’ll buy you a piano soon.
And become a lady who needn’t be ashamed even before Westerners; you can, I’m sure you can. ”
—“Even before Westerners,” “like a Westerner”: I used such phrases often.
She of course was pleased, and would say,
“How is it?
If I do this, doesn’t my face look like a Westerner’s? ”
and make various expressions in front of the mirror.

When we saw pictures she seemed to watch the actresses’ movements very closely: Pickford laughs this way, Pina Menichelli uses her eyes like this, Geraldine Farrar always does her hair in this style; in the end she would get so absorbed she would undo her hair entirely and imitate them in various shapes; and she was truly clever at catching, in an instant, those actresses’ habits and feeling.
“You’re good at it.
Even an actor couldn’t imitate like that; your face looks Western. ”
“Does it?
Where, exactly, do I look like them? ”
“That nose, and the set of the teeth. ”
“Ah, these teeth? ”
And she would spread her lips as if to say “ee” and look at the row of teeth in the mirror.
It was a truly even, very glossy, beautiful set of teeth.
“Anyway you’re un-Japanese, so ordinary Japanese clothes aren’t interesting.
Shall we go over to Western dress entirely, or even in Japanese clothes make the style a little unusual? ”
“Then what style? ”
“Women from now on will grow more and more lively, so I think those heavy, cramped things of the past won’t do. ”
“Couldn’t I wear a tube kimono and a heko obi? ”
“A tube isn’t bad.
Anything, so long as we try as novel a look as we can: something neither Japanese nor Chinese nor Western—isn’t there a getup like that—”
“If there is, will you have it made for me? ”
“Of course I will.
I want to have all sorts of shapes of clothes made for Naomi-chan, and try them on you, changing them every day.
They needn’t be expensive things like omeshi or chirimen.
Merino and meisen are plenty; the thing is to make the design startling. ”
After talks like this we would often go together to drapers’ shops and department stores hunting for cloth.
In those days, especially, we hardly let a Sunday pass without going to Mitsukoshi or Shirokiya.

Ordinary women’s goods satisfied neither Naomi nor me, so finding a pattern we liked was not easy; we decided ordinary drapers were no good, and went as far as Yokohama on purpose, to chintz shops, carpet shops, shops selling shirt and suit cloth, and the cloth shops for foreigners in Chinatown and the Settlement, spending a whole day going round; and both of us, dead tired, our feet like pestles, would go on and on hunting goods.
Even walking the street we kept our eyes open for Westerners’ figures and clothes, and watched every show-window.
If something unusual turned up we would cry,
“Ah, how about that cloth? ”

and go straight into the shop, have the bolt taken from the window, hold it against her body, dangle it from under her chin, wrap it round and round her waist.—Just walking about teasing like that was, for the two of us, an ample and amusing game.
Only lately have Japanese women in general begun, here and there, to have organdy and georgette and cotton voile made up as unlined kimono; but were we not the first to notice those things?
Oddly, such fabrics suited Naomi.

And they would not do as serious kimono: we made them into tubes, or pajama-shapes, or like nightgowns, or wrapped the bolt as it was around the body and pinned it here and there with brooches; and in such getups she would only walk back and forth in the house, stand before the mirror, or have various poses photographed.

Her figure, wrapped in those clothes of white or rose or pale purple, sheer as gauze, was beautiful as a living great blossom, and I would say “Do this, do that,” lift her, lay her down, sit her, walk her, and look at her for hours.
So her wardrobe multiplied by I don’t know how many sets in a year.
She could not begin to put them away in her own room, so she hung them anywhere that came to hand, or left them in rolls.
We should have bought a chest, but if we had that much money we wanted a little more clothes; and as a matter of taste there was no need to preserve them so carefully.

There were many, but all cheap, and we would wear them to death anyway, so it was more convenient to leave them scattered where they could be seen and change them as often as the mood took us, and first of all they decorated the room.

The atelier was like a theatre wardrobe: on chairs, on the sofa, in corners of the floor, even halfway up the stairs and on the railing of the attic gallery, there was nowhere they were not slovenly left.
And they were rarely washed; besides, she had the habit of wrapping them next to the skin, so most of them were soiled.
Many of these many clothes were cut in eccentric ways, so not more than half, I suppose, could be worn out of doors.
Among them Naomi was very fond of a satin lined kimono and matching haori, which she sometimes wore outside.

Satin, but cotton-wadded satin; both haori and kimono were plain shrimp-color throughout, shrimp-color even on the sandal thongs and the haori cords, and everything else—half-collar, obi, obi-clasp, the lining of the under-kimono, the cuffs—was set off uniformly in pale blue.

The obi too was made of cotton satin, thinly padded, narrowly made, and tied as high and as tight on the chest as possible; for the half-collar she wanted something like satin, so we bought ribbon and put it on.

Naomi generally wore this to the theatre at night; and walking the corridors of the Yūrakuza or the Imperial Theatre, glittering in that dazzling, glaring fabric, there was no one who did not turn to look at her.
“What is that woman? ”
“An actress, perhaps? ”
“A Eurasian, perhaps? ”
We would hear such whispers, and both she and I would loaf about there on purpose, looking proud.
But even that kimono made people wonder so, still more eccentric things, however much Naomi liked the unusual, could not be worn out of doors.
They were, in fact, only vessels in which to look at her, in various containers, inside the room.
The feeling, perhaps, was the same as putting a single beautiful flower into various vases.
For me Naomi was a wife and at the same time a doll rare in the world, and an ornament; so there is nothing to be surprised at.
Accordingly she almost never wore a serious getup at home.
A three-piece velvet suit we had made, taking a hint from some American picture-play of a woman in men’s clothes, was perhaps the costliest, most luxurious indoor dress.

In that, with her hair rolled up and a hunting-cap on, she had a catlike, languorous feeling; but in summer, of course, and in winter too, with the stove warming the room, she often played in a loose gown or in nothing but a bathing suit.
How many pairs of slippers she wore, beginning with embroidered Chinese shoes, I cannot say.
And in most cases she put on neither tabi nor stockings, but always wore those things straight on her bare feet.

At that time, while I was buying her favor to that extent and letting her do every last thing she liked, I had not, on the other side, given up my first hope of educating her thoroughly and making a great woman, a fine woman of her.

If I examine what I meant by “fine” and “great,” I am not clear even now; in short, in a very simple idea of my own, I had in my head something extremely vague, like “a modern, Western lady one need not be ashamed to take anywhere.
” To “make Naomi great” and to “treasure her like a doll”—could these two things coexist?
Looking back it is a foolish story; but I, blinded by drowning in her love, could not see even so obvious a truth.
“Naomi-chan, play is play, study is study.
If you become great I’ll still buy you all sorts of things. ”
I said it as a catchphrase.
“Yes, I’ll study, and I’ll certainly become great. ”
Naomi always answered so when I told her.
And every day after supper, for about thirty minutes, I would drill her in conversation and the reader.

But on such occasions she would be wearing that velvet suit or a gown, leaning in a chair, playing with her slippers on the tips of her toes; so however much I scolded with my mouth, in the end “play” and “study” got mixed together.
“Naomi-chan, what are you doing, behaving like that!
When you study you must sit more properly. ”
When I said that, Naomi would twitch her shoulders in and, in a spoiled voice like a primary-school pupil, say, “Teacher, I’m sorry,” or, “Kawai sensei, please forgive me,”
and peep secretly at my face, or sometimes give my cheek a little poke.
“Kawai-sensei” had not the courage to be strict with this charming pupil, and the scolding would end in silly horseplay.

Naomi’s music I do not well know, but in English she had been taking lessons from Miss Harrison for some two years already, since she was fifteen, so she ought by rights to have been quite able: she had started the reader from Book One and was now more than halfway through Book Two; for conversation she was studying English Echo, and for grammar she used Kanda Naibu’s Intermediate Grammar, which should have corresponded to about a third-year middle-school level.
But even looking with a fond eye, Naomi seemed inferior even to a second-year student.
It was strange; it ought not to be so; I once visited Miss Harrison, but she said,
“No, not at all; that child is a very clever child. She does very well,”
and the stout, kindly old maid only smiled and smiled.
“Yes, she is a clever child, but I don’t think her English is as good as that would suggest.
She can read, but translating into Japanese, explaining the grammar... ”
“No, that is you who are wrong; your idea is mistaken,”
the old maid still said, smiling, cutting me off.
“Japanese people all think of grammar and translation.
But that is the worst.
When you learn English, never, never think of grammar in your head, never translate.
Read many, many times in English as it is; that is best.
Naomi-san’s pronunciation is very beautiful.
And her reading is good, so she will certainly become skillful presently. ”
There was reason in what the old maid said, to be sure.
But I did not mean she should memorize the rules of grammar systematically.

She had been learning English for two years and could read Reader Three, so she ought at least, in practice, to have a grasp of the use of the past participle, the construction of the passive voice, the application of the subjunctive mood; and yet if you had her do Japanese-into-English, it was a complete failure.
She was hardly up to a poor middle-school student.
However fluent the reading, there was no reason this should form real ability.
What on earth had been taught, and learned, in two years, I could not make out.
But the old maid, unconcerned by my dissatisfied look, nodded with a vastly reassured, lordly air, and only went on repeating “That child is very clever. ”
This is my imagination, but Western teachers seem to have a kind of favoritism toward Japanese pupils.
Favoritism—or if that is too strong, a prejudice?
In short, when they see a boy or girl with a Western-looking, fashionable, pretty face, they feel at once, without a second thought, that the child is clever.
The tendency is still stronger in an old maid.
That was why Miss Harrison praised Naomi so extravagantly: she had decided from the start that she was a “clever child.
” And besides, as Miss Harrison said, the pronunciation alone was extremely fluent.
With those even teeth and a grounding in voice, the voice alone was truly beautiful, and she seemed wonderfully good at English; I felt I could not come near her.
So Miss Harrison had no doubt been taken in by that voice and fallen for her completely.
How much the lady loved Naomi you could tell, amazingly, from the many photographs of Naomi decorating the mirror of the dressing-table when you went into her room.

Inwardly I was very dissatisfied with the lady’s opinions and teaching methods, but at the same time, that a Westerner should favor Naomi so, should call her a clever child, was just what I wanted, and I could not help a joy as if I myself had been praised.

Moreover I am—no, not I alone; most Japanese are the same—quite spiritless before a Westerner, and have not the courage to state my own views clearly; so when I was lectured at, grandly, in the lady’s Japanese with its odd accent, I ended by not saying what I should have said.
Well, if that is their opinion, I will make up what is lacking at home, I decided in my belly, and said,
“Yes, that is really so, just as you say. Now I understand, so I am reassured,”
or something of the kind, and with a vague, grinning flattering smile I came home in that uncomprehending way, dragging my feet. “Jōji-san, what did Harrison-san say?—”
Naomi asked that evening, and her tone sounded as if she were relying on the old maid’s favor and had quite got above herself.
“She said you do well, but Westerners don’t understand the psychology of Japanese pupils.
To say that if the pronunciation is clever and you can just read smoothly, that’s enough—that’s a great mistake.
You certainly have a good memory, so you’re good at learning by heart, but if I have you translate you don’t understand the meaning of a single thing.
That’s the same as a parrot.
However much you study it won’t help at all. ”
That was the first time I had given Naomi anything like a scolding.

I was stung not only by her taking Miss Harrison as an ally and wrinkling that proud nose as if to say “There, you see,” but first of all I felt very uneasy whether she could become a “great woman” at this rate.
Even setting English aside, a head that cannot understand the rules of grammar makes one anxious for the future.
Why do boys learn geometry and algebra in middle school?
Not mainly for practical use, but to make the working of the mind precise, to train it.
Girls too: until now they have got by without an analytical head.
But women from now on cannot.
Still more, one who means to become a “fine” woman “not inferior even to Westerners,” if she has no talent for organization, no power of analysis, it is a thin prospect.

I grew a little stubborn, too: before I had only drilled her for some thirty minutes, but from then on I made it a rule to teach Japanese-into-English and grammar every day for an hour or an hour and a half at least.
And in that time I would not allow a half-playful mood, and scolded her sharply.
What Naomi most lacked was understanding, so I would, on purpose, meanly, not teach the small points, give her only a slight hint, and lead her to invent the rest herself.
For instance, if we had studied the passive voice, I would at once show her an application problem and say,
“Now, try translating this into English. ”
“If you understand what we just read, there’s no reason you can’t do this. ”
And having said that I would wait in silence, patiently, until she made her answer.
Even if the answer was wrong I would never say where it was wrong, but
“What is this?
You don’t understand, do you? Read the grammar over again,”
and throw it back as many times as it took. And if even then she could not do it,
“Naomi-chan, what will you do if you can’t do a thing as easy as this?
How old are you, anyway. ...
Corrected in the same place again and again, and you still don’t understand this—where do you keep your head?
Harrison-san said you were clever, but I don’t think so at all.
If you can’t do this you’d be a poor student at school. ”
I would get too absorbed and raise my voice.
Then Naomi would puff out her face in a sulk, and often in the end begin to whimper.

Ordinarily we were truly close, if she laughed I laughed, we had never once quarreled, a pair of whom one would say there were no more affectionate man and woman—and the moment it was English-time we were both put into a heavy, choking feeling.

Not a day passed that I did not get angry, that she did not sulk; what had been in such good humor a moment before would suddenly stiffen on both sides, and we would glare at each other with looks that almost held hostility.—In fact at those times I would forget my first motive of making her great, and, irritated beyond measure by her lack of guts, come to hate her from the heart.
If the other had been a boy I might well, in a fit of temper, have given her a clout.
Even as it was I was always shouting “Fool!
” in a passion.
Once I even tapped her on the forehead with my fist.
But when I did that Naomi would grow oddly perverse, and refuse to answer even things she knew, and swallowing the tears running down her cheeks would keep a stone-like silence to the end.
Once Naomi had gone crooked in that way she was amazingly stubborn, an unmanageable type, so in the end I would lose heart and it would fizzle out.
Once it was like this.
A present participle like “doing” or “going” must always have in front of it the verb “to be,” but no matter how many times I taught her she could not understand it.

And she still made mistakes like “I going,” “He making,” so I got thoroughly angry, firing off the usual “fool,” and after explaining in such detail my mouth went sour, I had her conjugate “going” through various tenses—past, future, future perfect, past perfect—and to my amazement she still did not understand.
She still did “He will going,” or wrote “I had going. ” I flared up unbidden:
“Fool!
What a fool you are!
Didn’t someone tell you as clearly as that you can never say ‘will going’ or ‘have going’?
If you don’t understand, do it until you do.
I won’t let you off tonight until you can, even if it takes all night. ”
And I slammed the pencil down hard and shoved the notebook back in front of Naomi.
Naomi shut her lips tight, went quite pale, and with upturned eyes stared sharply, steadily, at the space between my brows.
Then, I don’t know what she thought, she suddenly snatched the notebook, tore it to shreds, flung it on the floor, and again fixed those dreadful pupils on my face, staring as if to bore a hole.
“What are you doing! ”
For an instant I was taken aback, cowed by that beast-like force, and said it after a moment.
“Do you mean to defy me?
Do you think study doesn’t matter?
All that about studying with all your might, becoming a great woman—what happened to that?
What did you mean by tearing the notebook?
Now, apologize; if you don’t I won’t stand for it!
Leave this house today, this minute! ”
But Naomi still stubbornly kept silent, only a kind of tearful thin smile at the mouth of that dead-pale face.
“All right!
If you won’t apologize that’s fine, so get out of here at once!
Come, I said get out! ”

I thought I could not possibly cow her without showing at least that much, so I stood up abruptly, quickly rolled two or three of her discarded changes of clothes into a furoshiki, brought my wallet from the upstairs room, took out two ten-yen notes, and thrusting them at her said,
“Here, Naomi-chan, your things are in this furoshiki, so take it and go back to Asakusa tonight.
Here is twenty yen.
It isn’t much, but keep it for pocket-money for the time being.
I’ll settle the matter cleanly later, and send the luggage tomorrow or so.—Eh?
Naomi-chan, what’s the matter, why are you silent. ... ”
When I said that, however willful she seemed, she was after all a child.
Cowed a little by my unusual fury, she hung her head, as if she had come to regret it, looking virtuous, and made herself small.
“You’re quite stubborn, but I too, once I’ve said a thing, will never let it rest.
If you think you were wrong, apologize; if you don’t like that, go home. ...
Come, which is it, you’d better decide quickly.
Will you apologize?
Or will you go back to Asakusa? ”
Then she shook her head, no, no.
“Then you don’t want to go home? ”
“Unh,” she nodded with her chin.
“Then you’ll apologize? ” “Unh,”
and she nodded in the same way again.
“Then I’ll forgive you, so put your hands down properly and apologize. ”
So Naomi, having no choice, put both hands on the desk—and still with a look somewhere of making a fool of one, lazily, turning her face aside, she bowed.
Whether this arrogant, self-willed nature had been in her from the first, or was the result of my spoiling her too much, in any case it was clear that as the days passed it was rising more and more.
Or rather, it was not that it had risen: at fifteen or sixteen I had overlooked it as childish charm, and it had not stopped as she grew, and so had gradually got beyond my hands.
Before, however she threw a tantrum, if I scolded she would listen meekly; but by now, if there was something a little not to her taste, she would puff up at once.

If she whimpered there was still something touching in it; but sometimes, however severely I scolded, she would not shed a single tear, and put on a hateful blankness, or use those sharp upturned eyes and look at me in a straight line, as if taking aim.—If there really is such a thing as animal electricity, Naomi’s eyes surely contained a great deal of it, I always felt.

For those eyes were so glittering, strong, and fierce they did not seem a woman’s, and besides they held a kind of unfathomable deep charm; and when she glared at you in one gulp, there were times I felt a chill.
At that time two contradictory things, disappointment and attachment, were struggling by turns in my breast.

That I had chosen wrongly, that Naomi was not so clever a woman as I had expected—this fact even my fondest eye could no longer deny, and I came to see that the hope she would one day become a fine lady was now nothing but a dream.
Breeding will out: a girl from Senzoku-chō is fit to be a café waitress, and giving her an education beyond her station comes to nothing.—I came to hold that resignation, deeply.
And yet at the same time, while I resigned myself on one side, on the other I was drawn more and more strongly to her flesh.
Yes, I say “flesh” especially, because it was the beauty of her skin, her teeth, her lips, her hair, her pupils, and every other aspect of her form, and there was nothing spiritual in it at all.
In short, while she betrayed my hopes in the head, in the body she grew more and more beautiful, just as I had imagined, no, more than that.
The more I thought “stupid woman,” “hopeless creature,” the more spitefully that beauty tempted me.
This was truly an unlucky thing for me.

I gradually forgot the pure feeling of “making her into something,” and rather was dragged along, slipping; and by the time I noticed that this would not do, I myself could already do nothing about it.
“Nothing in the world goes just as one thinks.
I meant to make Naomi beautiful in both spirit and flesh.
And I failed in the spirit, but in the flesh I succeeded splendidly, didn’t I?
I had not expected her to become so beautiful in this direction.
Looked at that way, the success more than makes up for the other failure. ”
—I forced myself to think so, and steered my feelings toward being satisfied with that.
“Jōji-san doesn’t call me a fool so much in English-time lately, does he. ”
Naomi saw the change in my heart already, and said so.
Dull as she was at study, she was truly sharp at reading my face.
“Yes, I thought if I said it too much you’d only get stubborn and the result wouldn’t be good, so I decided to change my method. ” “Hm,”
she laughed with the tip of her nose, and said,
“Well of course.
If I’m called a fool so wildly I certainly won’t listen to a thing.
The truth is, you know, I could think out most of the problems, but I pretended I couldn’t, on purpose, to trouble Jōji-san.
Didn’t you see that? ”
“Oh?
Really? ”
I knew what Naomi said was empty bluster, sour grapes, but I pretended to be surprised on purpose.
“Of course.
There’s no one who couldn’t do problems like that.
And you thought I really couldn’t, so Jōji-san is the bigger fool.
Every time you got angry I was so amused I couldn’t stand it. ”
“Well I’m dashed.
You had me completely taken in. ”
“How is it?
I’m a little cleverer, aren’t I? ”
“Yes, clever.
I can’t compete with Naomi-chan. ”
Then she grew proud and laughed holding her belly.
Readers, please listen without laughing when I suddenly start a strange story here.
Once, when I was in middle school, in history class we were taught the passage on Antony and Cleopatra.

You know it, I suppose: Antony meets Octavianus’s forces and fights a naval battle on the Nile, and Cleopatra, who has come with Antony, seeing her side’s situation is bad, at once turns her ship midway and flees.
Yet Antony, seeing this heartless queen’s ship leave him, even at a moment of life and death, puts the war aside and at once runs after the woman.—
“Gentlemen,” the history teacher said to us then.

“This man Antony ran after a woman’s backside and lost his life, and there is no one in history who has exposed such a fool of himself; he is truly, one must say, an unparalleled laughingstock of all ages.
Even a hero, when it comes to this... ”
The way he said it was funny, and the students looked at the teacher’s face and burst out laughing all at once.
And I, needless to say, was one of those who laughed.
But the important part is here.
At that time I could not understand how a man like Antony could have been so lost over such a heartless woman.
And not Antony only: just before, a hero like Julius Caesar had been caught by Cleopatra and lowered his dignity.
There are any number of other such examples.

If you look into the house-quarrels of the Tokugawa age, or the traces of a country’s order and disorder, rise and fall, there is never a case without the arts of some dreadful enchantress in the background.
Then are those arts so sinister, so cleverly laid, that once caught anyone is completely taken in?
I somehow felt it was not so.
However clever a woman Cleopatra was, one cannot think she had more wisdom than Caesar or Antony.
Even if one is not a hero, whether the woman has a true heart, whether her words are lies or truth, one ought to be able to see if one is careful.

And yet to be taken in, knowing it will destroy you, is too lacking in guts; if it was really so, perhaps heroes are not so great after all, I thought privately, and accepted as it stood the teacher’s criticism that Mark Antony was “an unparalleled laughingstock of all ages” and that “there is no one in history who has exposed such a fool of himself. ”
Even now I sometimes recall the teacher’s words of that time, and the figure of myself guffawing with the others.
And every time I recall it I feel keenly that today I have no right to laugh.
Because I now not only clearly understand how a Roman hero became a fool, why a man called Antony was so easily wound into an enchantress’s arts, but I cannot even help sympathizing with him.
People often say “a woman deceives a man.
” But in my experience it is never “deceiving” from the first.
At first the man himself is glad to go forward and “be deceived”; once he has a woman he is infatuated with, whether what she says is a lie or the truth, it is all dear to his ear.
If by chance she comes leaning on him with false tears,
“Aha, this creature is trying to deceive me with this trick.
