But you’re an odd one, a dear one; I see through your belly perfectly well, but since you’ve gone to the trouble I’ll let myself be deceived.
Come, deceive me all you like... ”
—in that way the man stands large-hearted, and, as if pleasing a child, lets himself be taken in on purpose.
So the man does not mean to be deceived by the woman.
On the contrary, he thinks he is deceiving her, and laughs in his heart.
The proof is that Naomi and I were just the same. “I’m cleverer than Jōji-san, aren’t I.”
Saying that, Naomi feels she has finished deceiving me.
I make a fool of myself and pretend to have been deceived.
For me, rather than exposing her shallow lies, it is far more pleasant to make her proud, and to look at her pleased face.
And besides I even had an excuse that satisfied my own conscience.
Even if Naomi is not a clever woman, it is not a bad thing to give her the confidence that she is clever.
The first shortcoming of Japanese women is that they have no firm confidence.
That is why they look cowed compared with Western women.
The qualification of a modern beauty is not so much the face as a sparkling expression and manner.

Even if it is not confidence, even mere conceit will do: to believe “I am clever,” “I am a beauty,” in the end makes that woman a beauty.—That was my idea, so I not only did not check Naomi’s habit of putting on cleverness, I greatly fanned it.
I let myself be pleasantly deceived by her always, and steered things so that her confidence grew stronger and stronger.

For example, Naomi and I often played soldier-chess and cards in those days; if we played in earnest I should have won, but I arranged as far as I could to let her win, so she gradually grew puffed up thinking “I’m much the stronger at games,” and would challenge me with an attitude of completely looking down on me:
“Come, Jōji-san, I’ll twist you once; come on. ”
“Hm, then shall I have a revenge match.—Why, if I took it seriously I wouldn’t lose to the likes of you, but I think of you as a child, so I let my guard down—”
“Never mind; put on a fine mouth after you’ve won. ”
“All right, come on!
This time I’ll really win! ”
And saying so I would play especially poor moves and lose as usual.
“How is it, Jōji-san?
Doesn’t it rankle to lose to a child?—It’s no use now, whatever you say you can’t stand up to me.
Well, just think, thirty-one years old, a grown man losing at such a thing to an eighteen-year-old child; Jōji-san simply doesn’t know how to play. ”
And she would say “After all it’s the head, not the years,” or “You’re the fool, so it’s no use being sore,” getting more and more above herself, and “Hm,”
she would sneer impertinently with the tip of that nose.
But the fearful thing is the result that comes from this.
At first I am buying Naomi’s favor; at least I myself think so.
But as it gradually becomes a habit, Naomi comes truly to have a strong confidence, and now, however much I strain in earnest, I cannot in fact beat her.
Winning and losing between people is not decided by reason alone; there is something called “spirit.
” In other words, animal electricity.
Still more in gambling: when Naomi fights it out with me she comes from the start swallowing my spirit, driving in with a wonderful force, so that I am pressed down, irritated, and lose my nerve.
“It’s dull to do it for nothing, so let’s bet a little. ”
In the end Naomi had quite got the taste, and would not play unless we bet money.
And the more we bet, the more my losses piled up.
Naomi, who had not a sen, would set the unit herself at ten sen or twenty, and squeeze pocket-money out of me to her heart’s content.
“Ah, if I had thirty yen I could buy that kimono. ...
Shall I take it from you at cards again? ”
she would say, challenging.
Sometimes she lost, but at such times she knew another trick, and if she really wanted that money she would not rest without winning, whatever she had to do.
Naomi, so that she could always use that “trick,” generally wore something like a loose gown at games, wrapped on purpose in a slovenly mess.

And when the situation grew bad she would collapse her posture lasciviously, open her collar, stick out her legs, and if that still would not do, lean on my knees and stroke my cheek, pinch the corner of my mouth and shake it, trying every last temptation.
I was truly weak when this “trick” was used on me.

Especially the last means—I cannot quite write it here—when that was taken, something cloudy would haze in my head, the scene before my eyes would suddenly go dark, and I would no longer know what was what about the game.
“That’s cheating, Naomi-chan, doing a thing like that... ”
“It’s not cheating; this is a trick too. ”
In my eyes, growing distant, everything seeming to mist away, I could see only Naomi’s face, full of coquetry, dimly, with that voice.
Only that face, with a grinning, odd smile floating on it...
“Cheating, cheating, there’s no such trick in cards... ”
“Hm, of course there is; when a woman and a man play a game they do all sorts of charms.
I’ve seen it elsewhere.
When I was a child, when my sister played hana with a man at home, I watched from the side and she did all sorts of charms.
Cards are the same as hana. ... ”
I think Antony was conquered by Cleopatra in just this way, his power of resistance gradually taken, wound in.
It is well to give the woman you love confidence, but as a result you yourself come to lose confidence.
Once it has come to that, you can no longer easily defeat the woman’s sense of superiority.
And unforeseen calamity arises from there.
It was one evening in early September of the year Naomi was eighteen, in the severe leftover heat.

That day I had finished at the company about an hour early, it being slack, and when I came back to the Ōmori house I unexpectedly saw, in the garden just inside the gate, a boy I had never seen, talking with Naomi about something.
The boy’s age was about the same as Naomi’s; even if older he could not have been more than nineteen.

He wore a white kasuri unlined kimono, a straw hat with a showy Yankee-style ribbon, and was talking while tapping the tip of his geta with a stick: a ruddy-faced fellow with thick eyebrows, features not bad, but pimples all over his face.
Naomi was squatting at the man’s feet, hidden in the shadow of the flower bed, so I could not see clearly how she looked.
Only her profile and hair flickered a little among the zinnias, cockscombs, and cannas in bloom.
When the man noticed me he took off his hat and bowed, and saying, “Well, then, again,”
looking back at Naomi, he at once walked briskly toward the gate. “Well, goodbye,”
Naomi said, rising after him, but “goodbye” the man tossed off still facing away, and as he passed in front of me he put a hand to the brim of his hat, hiding his face, and went out.
“Who is that man? ”
I asked, not so much from jealousy as from a light curiosity, as if to say “That was a curious scene just now. ”
“Him?
He’s a friend of mine, named Hamada... ”
“When did you become friends? ”
“Some time ago—he goes to Isarago for voice lessons too.
His face is dirty with pimples like that, but when you have him sing it’s really splendid.
A fine baritone.
At the concert the other day he did a quartet with me. ”
She had spoken ill of his face when she needn’t have, so I suddenly grew suspicious and looked into her eyes; but Naomi’s manner was composed, not at all different from usual.
“Does he come to play now and then? ”
“No, today is the first time; he said he’d come by because he was in the neighborhood.—They’re forming a social-dance club, and he came to ask me to join for certain. ”
I was a little displeased, it is true, but as I went on listening it seemed no lie that the boy had come only to say that much.
First of all, that he and Naomi had been talking in the garden at an hour when I was likely to come home was enough to clear my suspicion.
“So did you say you would dance? ”
“I said I’d think about it, but... ”
and she suddenly put on a spoiled, cat-stroking voice:
“Please, mayn’t I?
Come on!
Let me!
Jōji-san can join the club too and we can learn together. ”
“Can I join the club too? ”
“Yes, anyone can join.
A Russian that Sugisaki-sensei at Isarago knows will teach.
He escaped from Siberia, they say, and is hard up for money, so they formed the club to help him.
So the more pupils the better.—Please, let me! ”
“You’re all right, but I wonder if I can learn. ”
“It’s all right, you’ll learn at once. ”
“But I have no grounding in music. ”
“Music you’ll come to understand naturally as you go. ...
Please, Jōji-san must do it too.
I can’t go dancing if I do it alone.
Come on, let’s go dancing now and then, the two of us.
It’s no use playing in the house every single day. ”
—That Naomi of late seemed a little bored with the life so far, I had dimly seen.
Come to think of it, it was already some four years since we had nested in Ōmori.

And in that time, except for the summer holidays, we had shut ourselves in this “fairy-tale house” and cut off intercourse with the wide world, always always just the two of us face to face; so however many “games” we tried, it was no wonder we came in the end to feel bored.
Besides, Naomi was a very easily bored type: whatever the play, at first she would be ridiculously absorbed, but it never lasted.

And yet if she was not doing something she could not sit still even an hour; when cards were no, soldier-chess no, imitating picture-actors no, she would, having no choice, fuss with the flower-bed she had neglected, digging earth, sowing seed, watering, but that too was only a passing whim.
“Aaah, it’s dull.
Isn’t there something interesting? ”

Seeing her throw down a novel she had started, stretching back on the sofa, and give a great yawn, I too had been privately wondering if there was no way to give a turn to this monotonous life of two.
And it was just such a moment, so yes, learning to dance might not be bad.
Naomi was no longer the Naomi of three years ago.

It was a different matter from the Kamakura days, so if I dressed her splendidly and sent her out into society, she would probably not take second place even before many ladies.—That imagination made me feel an inexpressible pride.
As I have said, I had no particularly intimate friends from school days, and had lived avoiding useless associations as far as I could; but I by no means disliked going into society.

A country fellow, bad at compliments, clumsy in dealing with people even to my own eyes, I had grown retiring for that reason, and yet for that very reason I had all the more a heart that longed for a brilliant world.
Originally, in taking Naomi as a wife, a great ambition had been at work: to make her a thoroughly beautiful lady, to take her about everywhere every day, and have the world say this and that.
To be praised in society: “Your wife is wonderfully Western.
” So I had no intention of keeping her forever in a “birdcage. ”
According to Naomi, the Russian dancing teacher was named Alexandra Shlemskaya, the wife of a certain count.

The count-husband had gone missing in the revolutionary trouble, and there had been two children, it seemed, but their whereabouts too were now unknown; she had barely escaped with her own person to Japan and was hard pressed to live, so she had at last decided to begin teaching dance.
Sugisaki Harue, Naomi’s music teacher, had organized a club for the lady and become secretary; that Hamada, a student at Keiō, had become the manager.
The practice-place was the second floor of a Western instrument shop called Yoshimura on Hijirizaka in Mita; the lady went there twice a week, Mondays and Fridays.
Members would go at a convenient time between four and seven in the afternoon, be taught an hour at a time, the monthly fee twenty yen a person, paid in advance each month.

If Naomi and I both went it would come to forty yen a month, and even if the other party was a Westerner it seemed ridiculous; but according to Naomi, dance was the same as Japanese dancing, a luxury anyway, so taking that much was only natural.
And you needn’t practice so much: a clever person could learn in about a month, a clumsy one in three, so even if it was dear it was limited.
“First of all, it would be a pity not to help this person called Shlemskaya.
To think a count’s wife has fallen so low—isn’t it really sad?
I heard from Hamada-san that she’s very good at dance, and not only social dance; if there are people who want it she’ll teach stage dance too.
Dance by professionals is vulgar, no good; learning from a person like that is best. ”
She took the side of this lady she had never even seen, and talked as if she were quite a dance connoisseur.

So Naomi and I, at any rate, decided to join, and every Monday and Friday, when Naomi had finished her music lesson and I left the company, we would go straight to the instrument shop on Hijirizaka by six in the afternoon.
The first day Naomi waited for me at Tamachi Station at five, and we went together from there; the shop was a modest, narrow-fronted place halfway up the slope.
Inside, pianos, organs, gramophones, various instruments were lined in a cramped space, and already upstairs the dancing seemed to have begun: noisy footfalls and the sound of a gramophone.
At the foot of the stairs five or six fellows who looked like Keiō students were crowding, and their staring at Naomi and me was not a pleasant feeling, but “Naomi-san,”
someone called her then in a familiar loud voice.

It was one of those students, holding under his arm a flat mandolin—is that what it is called?—a flat instrument a little like a Japanese gekkin, and twanging the wire strings as he tuned it. “Hello there,”
Naomi answered too in an unwomanly, student-like tone:
“What’s Ma-chan doing?
Aren’t you dancing? ” “Not me,”
the man called Ma-chan said, grinning, putting the mandolin on a shelf:
“That sort of thing, not on your life.
First of all, taking twenty yen a month—it’s just too dear. ”
“But if you’re learning for the first time it can’t be helped. ”
“Nah, presently everyone will learn, and then I’ll grab those fellows and learn from them.
That’s plenty for dance.
How’s that, pretty sharp, eh? ”
“You’re sly, Ma-chan!
Too sharp by half.—By the way, is ‘Hama-san’ upstairs? ”
“Unh, he is; go and see. ”
This instrument shop seemed to be a “haunt” for the students of the neighborhood, and Naomi seemed to come now and then; the shop-clerks too were all familiar with her face.
“Naomi-chan, those students downstairs just now, what are they? ”
I asked as she led me up the stairs.
“They’re people from the Keiō mandolin club.
Their mouths are rough, but they’re not such bad people. ”
“Are they all friends of yours? ”
“Not exactly friends, but when I come here now and then to buy things I meet them, so I’ve got to know them. ”
“Is it mainly that sort who dance? ”
“Well, I don’t know—I shouldn’t think so; aren’t there more older people than students?—We’ll see when we go now. ”
When we went upstairs, the practice-room was at the end of the corridor, and five or six figures stamping “one, two, three” came at once into my eyes.

Two Japanese rooms had been thrown together and floored with boards you could enter in shoes; perhaps to make it slippery, that fellow Hamada was trotting here and there scattering fine powder on the floor.

It was still the long-dayed hot season, so the west windows were thrown wide, and the evening sun was glaring in; standing in that faintly red light at her back, in a white georgette blouse and a navy serge skirt, at the partition between the rooms, was of course Madame Shlemskaya.
Inferring from her having two children, her actual age might be thirty-five or six?

To the eye she was barely around thirty, a woman of a tightly drawn face with a dignity that indeed seemed of aristocratic birth,—that dignity, I thought, came from a complexion of a clear, somewhat ghastly pallor; but looking at the stern expression, the smart clothes, the jewels glittering on breast and fingers, you could not possibly take her for a person hard up to live.
The lady held a whip in one hand, her brows a little frowning, looking at the feet of the people practicing, “One, two, tree”—a Russian’s English, so she pronounced “three” as “tree.
”—repeating it in a quiet but commanding manner.

Following that, the pupils in a line, taking uncertain steps, going back and forth, it was like a woman officer drilling soldiers, and I recalled “The Women’s Army Goes to War,” which I had once seen at the Kinryūkan in Asakusa.

Three of the pupils were young men in lounge suits who at any rate did not look like students; the other two were young ladies just out of girls’ school, I suppose, in modest dress, wearing hakama, practicing hard together with the men, looking indeed like serious young ladies, not a bad impression.
If even one person missed a step the lady would at once
“No! ”
scold sharply, come beside them and walk it for them.
If they were slow to learn and missed too often she would cry
“No good! ”
and crack the whip on the floor, or strike the person’s feet, man or woman, without mercy.
“The teaching is truly enthusiastic, isn’t it; it has to be like that. ”
“Truly, Shlemskaya-sensei is so enthusiastic.
Japanese teachers simply cannot do it like that, but Western people, even ladies, are precise there, and it is really a pleasant feeling.

And as you see, during the lesson, even an hour or two, she never rests at all but goes on practicing, so in this heat it cannot be ordinary, and I think of offering her ice cream, but she says she wants nothing during the hours, and never takes anything. ”
“My, how she doesn’t tire. ”

“Western people have the physique, they are different from us.—But when one thinks of it she is a pitiable person; she was a count’s wife and lived without want, and because of the revolution she has come to do even this.—”
Sitting on a sofa in the next room used as a waiting-room, watching the practice, two women were talking like this, looking much impressed.

One was twenty-five or six, with thin large lips, a round-faced, protruding-eyed woman with the feeling of a Chinese goldfish; she had not parted her hair but puffed it gradually higher from the hairline of the forehead to the crown like a hedgehog’s rump, stuck a very large white-tortoiseshell hairpin in the mage, and wore a maru-obi of shioze with an Egyptian pattern and a jade clasp; it was this woman who sympathized with Madame Shlemskaya’s circumstances and praised her extravagantly.
The other woman, chiming in, had her thick makeup blotched with sweat, and from the small wrinkles and rough skin showing here and there she was probably near forty.
Whether on purpose or by nature, her reddish hair in a Western bun was wildly curled; a thin, lanky figure, gaudily dressed, but with a face a little like a former nurse.

Around these women there were people waiting modestly for their turn, and some who seemed already to have practiced a round, dancing about a corner of the practice-room with arms linked as they pleased.
Hamada the manager, whether as the lady’s deputy or putting on that air, was dancing as a partner for such people, changing gramophone records, busy by himself in a dizzying way.

Setting women aside, what sort of society were the men who came to learn dance, I wondered, looking; oddly, the only one in smart clothes was Hamada, and the rest were mostly in rustic navy three-piece suits like poorly paid clerks, not looking clever.
Their ages all seemed younger than I; there was only one gentleman who looked in his thirties.

That man wore morning dress, gold-rimmed thick glasses, and a strangely long, out-of-date mustache, and seemed the slowest to grasp; he was shouted at “No good” any number of times by the lady and given a crack of the whip.
And each time, with a grinning, vacant thin smile, he would start “one, two, three” over from the beginning.
What did a man like that, of a decent age, mean by taking it into his head to dance?
No—when I thought of it, was I not of the same company as that man?

Even without that, I who had never gone out into a brilliant place, thinking of the instant of being shouted at by that Westerner in front of these women’s eyes, even as Naomi’s companion, somehow as I watched a cold sweat seemed to well up, and I came to dread my turn coming round. “Ah, welcome,”
Hamada said, having danced two or three numbers running, wiping the sweat from his pimpled forehead with a handkerchief, and came over then. “Ah, sorry about the other day,”
he greeted me anew today, looking a little proud, and turning to Naomi,
“Good of you to come in this heat,—I say, sorry, if you have a fan would you lend it?
After all, being assistant isn’t such easy work. ”
Naomi took a fan from her obi and gave it to him.
“But Hama-san is quite good; you have the qualifications of an assistant.
When did you start practicing? ”
“Me?
I’ve been doing it half a year already.
But you’re clever, you’ll learn at once; in dance the man leads, and the woman only has to stick to him. ”
“Those men here, what sort of people are most of them? ” When I asked that,
“Ah, these? ” Hamada became polite:
“These people are mostly employees of the Tōyō Petroleum Company.
A relative of Sugisaki-sensei’s is a director of the company, and they were introduced by that person, it seems. ”
Tōyō Petroleum employees and social dance!—a rather odd combination, I thought, and asked again,
“Then, that gentleman with the mustache over there, is he an employee too? ”
“No, that one is different; that gentleman is a doctor. ”
“A doctor? ”
“Yes, a doctor who is also the company’s hygiene adviser.
He says nothing is such exercise for the body as dance, and he is doing it rather for that. ”
“Is that so, Hama-san? ”
Naomi put in.
“Does it really exercise you so much? ”
“Ah, it does indeed.
If you dance you sweat even in winter, enough to soak your shirt, so as exercise it’s certainly good.
And Madame Shlemskaya’s practice is fierce, as you see. ”
“Does that lady understand Japanese? ”
I asked because, in fact, I had been worrying about that from a while before.
“No, she understands almost no Japanese; we do it mostly in English. ”
“English is, well... when it comes to speaking, I’m not good at it... ”
“Nah, we’re all the same.
Madame Shlemskaya herself is in very broken English, worse than we are, so there’s nothing to worry about.
And for dance practice you don’t need words at all.
One, two, three, and the rest you understand by gesture. ... ”
“Oh, Naomi-san, when did you arrive? ”
The one who spoke to her then was that Chinese-goldfish woman with the white-tortoiseshell hairpin.
“Ah, Sensei,—look, it’s Sugisaki-sensei. ”
Naomi said, took my hand, and pulled me toward the sofa where that woman was.
“Sensei, let me introduce you,—Kawai Jōji—” “Ah, yes,—”
Sugisaki, seeing Naomi blush, seemed to understand the meaning without hearing it to the end; she stood and bowed:
“—I am delighted to meet you; I am Sugisaki.
How good of you to come.—Naomi-san, bring that chair here. ” And turning back to me again,
“Please sit down.
It will be soon, but if you wait standing like that you will tire. ”
I do not clearly remember what I answered; probably I only mumbled in my mouth.
Women who come at one with such cut-and-dried phrases as “watakushi” were the ones I was worst at.
Not only that: how the lady interpreted the relation between Naomi and me, how far Naomi had hinted it, I had carelessly forgotten to ask, so I was all the more flustered. “Let me introduce you,”
the lady said, unconcerned at my fidgeting, pointing at the curly-haired woman:
“This lady is the wife of Mr. James Brown of Yokohama.—This gentleman is Kawai Jōji, who works at the electric company in Ōimachi,—”
So this woman was a foreigner’s wife; told that, I thought she was more the type of a foreigner’s mistress than a nurse, and I grew still stiffer and could only bow.
“Excuse me, but is this your foist time practicing dance? ”
The curly hair at once caught hold of me and began talking like this; the “foist time” was in a nastily affected pronunciation, said so fast that I said
“Ha? ” and was floundering, when “Yes, it is the first time,”
Sugisaki took it over from the side.
“Well, is that so; but you know, gentlemen are moh moh difficult than ladies, but once you begin it will be at once, you know. ... ”
This “moh moh” I did not understand either, but listening well it meant “more more.
” “Gentleman” became “jenruman,” “little” “riruru”; she mixed English into the talk with all such pronunciations.
And there was a kind of odd accent in the Japanese too; once in three times she would fire off “what it is, you know,” and talk without end, like oil-paper catching fire.
Then again talk of Madame Shlemskaya, of dance, of languages, of music...

Beethoven’s sonata this, the Third Symphony that, such-and-such company’s records better or worse than so-and-so’s; I had quite drooped and gone silent, so now she began rattling at the lady, and from the way of it this Mrs. Brown was perhaps Sugisaki’s piano pupil.

And I, in such a case, cannot do the clever trick of saying “Excuse me a moment” and leaving at a good tide, so I had to sit sighing at my misfortune of being caught between these talkative women, and listen whether I would or no.

Presently, when the practice of the petroleum-company group, beginning with the mustached doctor, was over, the lady took Naomi and me before Madame Shlemskaya and introduced us, Naomi first, then me,—probably following the Western custom of ladies first,—in extremely fluent English.
At that time the lady seemed to call Naomi “Miss Kawai.

” I was privately waiting with interest to see what attitude Naomi would take in dealing with a Westerner; but even she, ordinarily so conceited, was a little flustered before the madame; when the madame said a word or two, smiling at the dignified corners of her eyes, and held out her hand, Naomi went quite red and, saying nothing, furtively shook it.
As for me, still more so: honestly I could not look up at that pale, sculpture-like outline.
And in silence, head down, I only softly returned the grip of the madame’s hand, in which countless fine grains of diamond were glittering.
That I, though a rustic man, liked the Western as a taste and imitated Western ways in everything, my readers already know.

If I had had enough money and could have done as I pleased, I might perhaps have gone to live in the West and taken a Western woman as a wife; but circumstances did not allow it, so among Japanese I took as a wife, at any rate, Naomi, who looked Western.
And another thing: even if I had had money, I have no confidence in my looks as a man.
After all I am a small man of five feet two, dark-skinned, with bad teeth; to think of taking a Westerner of that imposing physique as a wife would be not to know my place.
Japanese with Japanese is still best, and one like Naomi fits my requirements best, I thought, and in the end I was satisfied.
But even so, to be able to approach a woman of the white race was, for me, a joy—no, more than a joy, an honor.

To tell the truth, I had grown sick of my own clumsiness at association and my poverty of linguistic talent, and had resigned myself that such a chance would never come in my life; occasionally I would see an opera of a foreign troupe, or grow familiar with the faces of picture-actresses, and so, faintly, long for their beauty as for a dream.
And then unexpectedly the dance lessons made a chance to approach a Western woman—and a count’s wife at that.
Setting aside an old woman like Miss Harrison, it was the first time in my life I had been granted the “honor” of shaking hands with a Western lady.
When Madame Shlemskaya held out that “white hand” to me, I unbidden felt my heart thud, and even hesitated a moment whether I might take it.
Naomi’s hand too is supple and glossy, the fingers long and slender, and of course not without elegance.

But that “white hand” was not too fragile like Naomi’s: the palm was thick and well-fleshed, the fingers too stretching softly, yet without a weak, thin feeling: a hand at once “thick” and “beautiful.
”—That was the impression I received.
The great ring set there, glittering like an eyeball, would surely have been in bad taste on a Japanese, but on the contrary it made the fingers look delicate, and added a high, luxurious flavor.
And what differed from Naomi more than anything was the extraordinary whiteness of that skin.
A ghastly beauty, the thin purple veins faintly showing through the white, like the mottling of marble.
Until now, playing with Naomi’s hand, I had often praised her:
“Your hand is truly pretty, as white as a Westerner’s. ”
But looking at this, unfortunately, it is still different.
White as it seems, Naomi’s white is not clear; no, after once seeing this hand it even looks dusky.
And another thing that caught my notice was the nails.

All ten fingertips, like a collection of the same shells, had the little nails evenly, vividly, shining cherry-color; and, perhaps this being the Western fashion, the tips of the nails were cut in a triangle, standing sharply.

Naomi, as I have written, was an inch or so shorter standing beside me; the madame, though she looked small for a Westerner, still had more height than I, and because of her high-heeled shoes, when we danced together her bare breast was just level with my head. When the madame first said
“Walk with me! ”
and put her arm around my back to teach me the walk of the one-step, how I held back so that this pitch-black face of mine should not touch her skin.
That smooth, clean skin was, for me, enough merely to look at from afar.

Even shaking hands had seemed more than I should do; to be held to her breast through that soft gauze, I felt I had done something I must not, and I worried only whether my breath smelled, whether these greasy, sticky hands would give her displeasure; even if a single hair of hers fell, I could not help a chill.
And besides there was a kind of sweet smell about the madame’s body.
“That woman has a terrible underarm smell, it stinks! ”

I heard the students of that mandolin club saying such ill later, and Westerners are said to have much underarm smell, so the madame was probably the same, and always careful to put on perfume to hide it; but to me that faint, sweet-sour smell of perfume mixed with underarm was not only not unpleasant, it was always an inexpressible enchantment.
It made me think of countries beyond the sea I had never seen, of wondrous gardens of foreign lands.
“Ah, so this is the fragrance given off by the madame’s white body,”
I would think, in a trance, always sniffing that smell greedily.

How did a clumsy man like me, who ought to be most unsuited to the brilliant air of dance, come, even for Naomi’s sake, not to tire of going to practice for a month, two months afterward?—I will confess it: it was certainly because there was this Madame Shlemskaya.
Monday and Friday afternoons, dancing held to the madame’s breast.
That mere hour had, before I knew it, become my greatest pleasure.
Before the madame I quite forgot Naomi’s existence.
That hour, like a fragrant wine, could not but make me drunk.
“Jōji-san is unexpectedly keen; I thought you’d soon get tired of it.— ”
“Why? ”
“Because you said, I wonder if I can dance. ”
So whenever such talk came up I felt somehow sorry toward Naomi.
“I didn’t think I could, but when you try it’s pleasant.
And as the doctor says, it’s great exercise for the body. ”
“There, you see; so one should try things without thinking. ”
Naomi, not noticing the secret of my heart, would say that and laugh.
Well, we had practiced quite a bit and it was about time, so the first time we went out to Café Eldorado on Ginza was that winter.
At that time there were not so many dance halls in Tokyo; besides the Imperial Hotel and Kagetsuen, that café had just begun it, I suppose.
Hotels and Kagetsuen were mainly for foreigners, and dress and manners were said to be strict, so for a first try Eldorado would do, we decided.
It was Naomi who had heard a rumor somewhere and proposed “Let’s go and see for certain”; I had not yet the nerve to dance in an open place, but
“You’re no good, Jōji-san! ” Naomi glared at me:
“You’re no good because you say such timid things.
Dance, however much you only practice, you’ll never get good.
You get good while you’re dancing shamelessly among people. ”
“That’s certainly so, but I haven’t that shamelessness... ”
“Then all right, I’ll go out alone. ...
I’ll take Hama-san or Ma-chan and dance. ”
“Ma-chan is that mandolin-club fellow the other day? ”
“Yes.
That person, without practicing once, goes everywhere and dances with anyone, so by now he’s quite good.
Much better than Jōji-san.
So if you’re not shameless you lose. ...
Come on, I’ll dance with Jōji-san. ...
Please, for mercy’s sake come with me! ...
Good boy, good boy, Jōji-san is a really good boy! ”
So in the end it was settled we would go, and now a long consultation began again over “What shall I wear. ”
“Just a moment, Jōji-san, which is good? ”
From four or five days before going out she would make a great fuss, pull out everything she had, and try each one on. “Ah, that will do,”
I would answer at random, tiring of it in the end, and she would say,
“Do you think so?
Isn’t this odd? ”
and go round and round in front of the mirror:
“It’s strange, somehow. I don’t like this,”
and at once throw it off, kick it into wrinkles with her foot like waste paper, and try the next.
But this kimono no, that kimono no, and it would come to
“Jōji-san, have a new one made! ”
“To go dancing it has to be much more showy; a kimono like this won’t stand out.
Come on!
Have it made!
We’ll be going out now and then from now on, so we must have clothes. ”
By that time my monthly income could no longer keep up with her luxury.

Originally I was quite particular about money; in my bachelor days I had fixed my monthly pocket-money and saved even a little of what remained, so when Naomi and I first set up house there was a fair surplus.

And though I was drowning in Naomi’s love I never neglected the company’s work; I was still a diligent, model employee, the directors’ confidence grew thicker, my salary rose, and adding the half-yearly bonus it came to four hundred yen a month on average.
So if we lived ordinarily the two of us should have been comfortable, and yet it was never enough.
To go into small points: first the monthly living expenses, even estimating inward, were over two hundred and fifty yen, sometimes three hundred.

Of this, rent thirty-five yen—it had been twenty, and risen fifteen in four years.—Then gas, electric light, water, fuel, Western laundry, and such miscellaneous costs deducted, of the remaining two hundred yen or so, two hundred thirty or forty, what was it spent on?
Most of it was food.

And no wonder: Naomi, who as a child had been satisfied with a single-dish beefsteak, had somehow grown luxurious in the mouth, and at every meal of the three would say “I want this,” “I want that,” luxuries unfitting her years.
Besides, she disliked the bother of buying materials and cooking herself, so she generally ordered from a nearby restaurant. “Aaah, I want something tasty,”
was sure to be Naomi’s phrase when she was bored.

And before she had liked only Western food, but lately not so: once in three meals she would say, impertinently, “I want to try the soup of such-and-such a house,” or “Let’s order sashimi from so-and-so. ”
At noon I was at the company, so Naomi ate alone, and on such occasions the luxury was even fiercer.
In the evening, coming back from the company, I often saw the lunch-house’s okamochi or the Western restaurant’s containers in a corner of the kitchen.
“Naomi-chan, you’ve ordered something again!
If you go on eating nothing but delivered food it costs a fortune.
First of all, a woman alone doing such a thing—think a little of waste. ” Even so Naomi was quite unconcerned:
“But I ordered because I was alone; it’s a bother to make side-dishes,”
and she would lie back on the sofa on purpose, sulking.
At this rate it was hopeless.
Side-dishes alone would have been one thing, but sometimes she even grudged cooking rice, and had even the rice brought from the lunch-house.

So at month’s end the totals of the bills brought from the fowl-shop, the beef-shop, the Japanese restaurant, the Western restaurant, the sushi-shop, the eel-shop, the cake-shop, the fruit-shop, rose to an amount that made one wonder she could have eaten so much.
Next after food came the Western laundry bills.
This was because Naomi would never wash even a pair of tabi herself, and sent all soiled things to the cleaner. And if I scolded, the second word was,
“I’m not a maid. ”
“If I do laundry and such, my fingers will get thick and I won’t be able to play the piano.
What did Jōji-san say about me?
You said I was your treasure, didn’t you?
Then what if these hands get thick? ”
That is what she said.
At first Naomi did the household work and labored in the kitchen, but that lasted only a year or half a year, I suppose.
So the laundry was still all right; what was worse was that the inside of the house grew more and more disorderly and unclean day by day.
Things taken off left off, things eaten left eaten: plates and bowls ravaged by eating, half-drunk teacups, soiled underclothes and yumoji, thrown about there whenever you went.

Dust had gathered, of course on the floor, but on chairs and table too; those Indian-chintz curtains we had taken such trouble over no longer kept a trace of former days, all sooted; the mood of the fairy-tale house that had been such a sunny “birdcage” had quite changed its flavor, and when you entered the room there was a smell peculiar to such places, thrusting at the nose. I was at a loss for this too, and said,
“Come, I’ll sweep; you go out in the garden,”
and tried sweeping and dusting; but the more I dusted the more dust came, and it was so scattered I could not even begin to put it in order.
This would not do, so two or three times I hired a maid, but every maid who came went home amazed, and none lasted five days.
First of all we had not meant that from the start, so even if a maid came there was nowhere for her to sleep.
On top of that we could no longer be unreservedly intimate, and even a little play between the two of us felt cramped.
When the hands increased, Naomi showed still more laziness, would not even turn a thing on its side, and drove the maid at every point.
And as usual, “Go to such-and-such a house and order this,” and being more convenient she listed still more luxuries.
In the end a maid was very uneconomical, and a hindrance to our “play” life; they were cowed, no doubt, but we too did not particularly want them to stay.

So, taking it that the monthly living cost that much, I wanted to save even ten or twenty yen a month from the remaining hundred to hundred and fifty; but Naomi’s spending was fierce, and there was no such surplus.
She always had one kimono made a month.
Even merino or meisen, buying lining and face, and not sewing it herself, paying a tailor’s fee, fifty or sixty yen would vanish.
And the finished article, if she did not like it, she would thrust into the back of the closet and never wear; if she liked it she would wear it to death until the knees gave.
So her cupboard was stuffed full of rags of old clothes.
Then she was luxurious about geta.

Zōri, koma-geta, ashida, hiyori-geta, ryōguri, geta for going out, everyday geta—these from seven or eight yen a pair down to two or three, bought about once in ten days, so accumulated it was not cheap.
“Wearing geta like this is unbearable; why not make it shoes? ”

I would say; once she had been glad to walk in shoes with hakama like a schoolgirl, but lately even going to lessons she went out mincing in everyday kimono, and she would treat me as a country fellow:
“I may not look it, but I’m an Edo child; however the rest of me is, I can’t be easy unless the footwear is proper. ”
Pocket-money too, concerts, streetcar fares, textbooks, magazines, novels, she would take three yen, five yen, not three days passing.

Besides that, English and music fees twenty-five yen, which had to be paid regularly every month; and to bear the above on an income of four hundred yen was not easy; far from saving, I came on the contrary to draw on savings, and what I had somewhat prepared in my bachelor days crumbled little by little.
And money, once you start touching it, goes truly fast; in these three or four years I had used up all my store, and now had not a sen.
Unluckily, as is usual with a man like me, I am bad at refusing debts, and so cannot be easy unless I pay accounts exactly; when the last day of the month came I suffered in a way I cannot say.
Even if I admonished, “If you spend like that we won’t get over the last day,”
“If we can’t get over it, we can have them wait. ”
she would say.
“—Living three or four years in one place, there’s no law we can’t put off the last day’s accounts; if we say we’ll surely pay at each half-year, anywhere will wait.
Jōji-san is small-hearted and has no flexibility, that’s why you’re no good. ”
In that tone, everything she wanted to buy was cash, and the monthly payments put off until the bonus came in.
And yet she too disliked making excuses for debt:
“I hate saying such things; isn’t that a man’s job? ”
and when month’s end came she would dart off somewhere.
So I may say I was offering my whole income for Naomi.

To keep her a little cleaner in her person, not to let her feel want or anything stingy, to let her grow at ease,—that of course was my true wish, so while I grumbled that it was hard, I allowed her luxury.

Then that much had to be cut from other sides; luckily my own social expenses cost nothing, but even so, when there was an occasional company meeting I would escape as far as I could even if it failed in duty.
Besides that I would cut my own pocket-money, clothing, lunch-box money, drastically.
On the government-line trains we took every day Naomi bought a second-class season, I put up with third.
Because cooking rice was a bother, and having delivered food would be terrible, I would sometimes cook the rice and make the side-dishes.
But when it came to that, Naomi did not like it.
“You needn’t work in the kitchen, being a man; it looks bad. ”
That is what she said.
“Jōji-san, instead of wearing the same clothes all year, why not get a little smarter?
Even if I look well, if Jōji-san is like that I still don’t like it.
Then we can’t walk together. ”
If I could not walk with her there was no pleasure, so I too had to have at least one so-called “smart” suit made.
And when I went out with her I had to ride second class on the train.
In short, not to wound her vanity, it would not do with her luxury alone.

In such circumstances I was hard put to make ends meet, and now lately Madame Shlemskaya took forty yen at a time, so if on top of that I bought her dance clothes we would be at a complete standstill.
But Naomi was not one to listen to that, and it being just month’s end I had cash in my pocket, so she would not be satisfied without my producing it.
“But you, if I put out this money now, you should see we’ll be short at once at month’s end. ”
“If we’re short, something will happen. ”
“Something will happen—what will happen?
There’s no way anything can happen. ”
“Then what did we learn dance for?—All right, then, from tomorrow I won’t go anywhere. ”
And she would fill those great eyes with dew, glare at me resentfully, and go stiffly silent.
“Naomi-chan, are you angry? ...
Eh, Naomi-chan, just a moment... turn this way. ”
That night, after I had got into bed, I said that, shaking the shoulder of her who had turned her back and was pretending to sleep.
“Come, Naomi-chan, turn this way, I said. ... ”
And I put a gentle hand on her and turned her over toward me, like turning a fish with the bone in; the unresisting, supple body, with eyes faintly half-closed, turned meekly toward me.
“What’s the matter?
Still angry? ”
“Eh, here... you needn’t be angry, I’ll manage somehow... ”
“Here, open your eyes, your eyes... ”
And as I said it I lifted the flesh of the eyelids whose lashes were trembling, and the plump eyeballs peeping out like shellfish-meat were, far from sleeping, looking straight at my face.
“I’ll buy it for you with that money, all right? ... ”
“But then won’t we be in trouble? ... ”
“I don’t mind being in trouble; I’ll manage somehow. ”
“Then how? ”
“I’ll tell them at home and have them send money, so it’s all right. ”
“Will they send it? ”
“Ah, they’ll send it, of course.
I’ve never once troubled them at home, and even Mother must understand that if two people keep a house all sorts of things cost. ... ”
“Is that so?
But isn’t it bad toward Mother? ”
Naomi’s tone sounded as if she were concerned, but in fact I could dimly read that in her belly there had long been the thought, “You ought to tell the country.
” My saying it was just what she wanted.
“Why, there’s nothing bad at all.
But as a matter of principle I disliked such things, so I didn’t. ”
“Then why did you change your principle? ”
“Because I felt sorry when I saw you cry just now. ”
“Is that so? ”
she said, her breast heaving as if a wave were coming in, a shy smile floating:
“Did I really cry? ”
“You said you wouldn’t go anywhere, with your eyes full of tears.
However long it is you’re still a spoiled child, a big baby... ”
“My Papa!
Dear Papa! ”

Naomi suddenly clung to my neck, and stamped the vermilion seal of her lips, like a busy post-office stamper, on my forehead, my nose, my eyelids, behind my earlobes, every part of my face, without a hair’s breadth of space.

It made me feel a pleasure as if countless petals, like camellia flowers, solidly heavy and dewy-soft, were falling, and in the scent of those petals I felt a dreamy state as if my neck were quite buried.
“What’s the matter, Naomi-chan, you’re quite like a madwoman. ”
“Ah, I am mad. ...
Tonight I’m so fond of Jōji-san I could go mad. ...
Or am I a nuisance? ”
“A nuisance?
How could you be; I’m glad too, glad enough to go mad; for you I don’t care what sacrifice I make. ...
Oh, what’s the matter?
Crying again? ”
“Thank you, Papa, I’m grateful to Papa, so the tears come of themselves. ...
You understand?
Mustn’t I cry?
If I mustn’t, wipe them for me. ”

Naomi took paper from her bosom and, without wiping herself, put it in my hand; her pupils stayed fixed on me, and before I wiped, she overflowed still more tears in a stream to the edge of her lashes.
Ah, what moist, beautiful eyes.

I thought, cannot these beautiful beads of tears be crystallized just as they are, and kept; I first wiped her cheeks, and wiped around the eye-sockets so as not to touch those round, piled beads of tears; and every time the skin slackened or was pulled, the beads were kneaded into various shapes, became like convex lenses, like concave lenses, and in the end crumbled and ran again, drawing threads of light over the cheeks I had taken such trouble to wipe.
Then I wiped those cheeks once more, stroked the still somewhat wet eyeballs, then with that paper held the nostrils of her who was still faintly sobbing, and said,
“Come, blow your nose. ”
And she went “cheen,” and had me blow her nose any number of times.
The next day Naomi took two hundred yen from me and went alone to Mitsukoshi, and I, in the noon rest at the company, wrote my first begging letter, addressed to my mother.

“... prices being high of late, a surprising difference from two or three years ago, and though we do not indulge in any particular luxury, pressed by monthly expenses, city life is by no means easy... ”
I remember writing so, and when I thought I had become so bold as to tell such a skillful lie to a parent, I felt a fear even of myself.
But my mother believed me, and besides had affection for Naomi as her son’s precious wife, as I could see from the reply that reached my hands two or three days later.
In the letter, more than I had told her, “Buy Naomi a kimono,” there was a money-order enclosed for a hundred yen extra.
The night of the Eldorado dance was a Saturday evening.
It was to be from half past seven in the afternoon; when I came back from the company around five, Naomi was already, with her post-bath skin still uncovered, busily making up her face.
“Ah, Jōji-san, it’s come! ”

she said the moment she saw my figure in the mirror, stretching one hand behind her; on the sofa she pointed to, the kimono and maru-obi we had had Mitsukoshi make in a great hurry were laid out long, the wrapping undone.

The kimono was a lined hiyoku with wadding at the mouth, of what they call kinsha-chirimen, I suppose: on a ground-color like blackish vermilion, flowers yellow and leaves green, a scattered all-over pattern; on the obi, two or three waves embroidered in silver thread wavered, and here and there old-fashioned boats like gozabune floated.
“How is it?
My choice is clever, isn’t it? ”
Naomi, dissolving powder in both hands, said, slapping hard right and left with those palms the well-fleshed shoulders and nape still steaming from the bath.
But honestly, on her thick-shouldered, large-hipped, breast-thrusting body, that water-soft fabric did not much suit.

In merino or meisen there is an exotic beauty, like a Eurasian girl; but strangely, when she wraps herself in such serious clothes she looks, on the contrary, vulgar, and the showier the pattern the more she has only a coarse feeling, like a woman of a chabuya around Yokohama.
I did not force an objection, because she was so proud by herself; but to ride a streetcar or appear in a dance hall with a woman in this poisonous dress made me feel my body shrink.
When Naomi had put on the clothes she said, unusually bringing out my suit, dusting it and putting an iron to it,
“Come, Jōji-san, you wear the navy lounge suit. ”
“I’d rather have brown than navy. ”
“You fool!
Jōji-san! ”
She glared once in that scolding tone of hers:
“A night party is settled as navy lounge suit or tuxedo.
And you don’t wear a soft collar, you put on a stiff one.
That’s etiquette, so remember it from now on. ”
“Oh, is that how it is. ”
“That’s how it is; you put on Western airs and don’t know that, what will you do.
This navy lounge suit is quite soiled, but with Western clothes if the wrinkles are stretched out sharp and the cut isn’t broken, that’s enough.
Come, I’ve made it proper, so wear this tonight.
And soon you’ll have to have a tuxedo made.
Otherwise I won’t dance with you. ”

Then the necktie should be navy or plain black, tied in a bow; the shoes should be patent leather, but if not, ordinary black low shoes; red leather is off the formal; socks too, silk is really best, but even if not, one should choose plain black.—Where she had heard it I don’t know, but Naomi gave such a lecture, putting her beak into not only her own dress but mine, one by one, and it took a good deal of time before we at last left the house.
We arrived after half past seven, so the dancing had already begun.

Going up the stairs hearing the noisy jazz band, at the entrance of the dance hall, the dining-room chairs cleared away, there was a notice: “Special Dance — Admission: Ladies Free, Gentlemen ¥3.00,” and a boy on watch taking the fee.
Of course, being a café, the “hall” was not so splendid; looking about, there were perhaps ten couples dancing, but even that many made a fairly noisy bustle.

On one side of the room tables and chairs were set in two rows; those who had bought tickets and entered occupied those seats, resting there now and then, the arrangement being, it seemed, to watch others dance.
Unknown men and women were talking in clumps, a group there, a group here.

And when Naomi came in they whispered something secretly among themselves, and with a strange look you see only in such a place, half hostile, half contemptuous, a fishy look, they gazed as if searching out her gaudy figure.
“Here, here, look at that woman come over there. ”
“Who’s that man with her! ”
I felt I was being so spoken of.
I clearly felt their gazes not only on Naomi but on me standing small behind her.
In my ears the orchestra music clanged, and before my eyes the dancing crowd... a crowd all far more skillful than I, making one great ring and going round and round.

At the same time I thought of myself as a small man of only five feet two, dark as a native, with irregular teeth, wearing a very unimpressive navy lounge suit made two years ago, so my face burned hot, a tremor ran through my body, and I could not help thinking, “I shouldn’t come to a place like this anymore. ”
“Standing here is no use. ...
Let’s go over there... toward the tables. ”
Naomi too, I suppose, felt a shrinking; she put her mouth to my ear and said so in a small voice.
“But I wonder, is it all right to cut through among these people dancing? ”
“It’s all right, surely... ”
“But if we bump into them it’s bad, isn’t it. ”
“Go so as not to bump... look, that person cut through there, didn’t they.
So it’s all right; let’s go and see. ”
I followed Naomi across the crowd in the open space, but my feet were trembling and the floor looked slippery, so it was a labor to get safely to the other side.
And I remember once almost falling with a clatter, and being glared at by Naomi with a “Tch,” and making a wry face.
“Ah, that one seems empty; let’s take that table. ”
Naomi, even so, was less abashed than I, and passed through, composed, among the staring, and sat at a certain table.

But though she had so looked forward to dancing, she did not at once say let’s dance; somehow for a little she seemed unsettled, taking a mirror from her handbag and secretly fixing her face, and saying, “Your necktie is crooked to the left,”
noting it to me in secret, watching the open space.
“Naomi-chan, Hamada-kun is here, isn’t he. ”
“Don’t say Naomi-chan; say san. ”
And Naomi made a difficult wry face again:
“Hama-san is here, and Ma-chan is here too. ”
“Where, which? ”
“Look, over there... ”
And hastily dropping her voice, “It’s rude to point,” she admonished me softly, then,
“Look, over there, dancing with that young lady in the pink Western dress, that’s Ma-chan. ” “Yah,”
Ma-chan said then, coming toward us, grinning over the shoulder of the woman he was with.

The pink Western dress was a tall, fat woman with long, sensual arms bared, a great deal of jet-black hair, more oppressive than abundant, cut short about the shoulders, frizzed loosely, with a ribbon headband; as for the face, red cheeks, large eyes, thick lips, and the outline of an urizane face with a long thin nose of the purely Japanese sort you might see in an ukiyo-e.
I am one who watches women’s faces quite closely, but I had never seen such a strange, discordant face.

This woman, I think, felt it the greatest misfortune that her face was too Japanese, and was taking desperate pains to make it as Western as she could; looking well, every bit of skin exposed was powdered as if bloomed with flour, and around the eyes a verdigris paint glittering like enamel was blended.
That bright red of the cheeks was undoubtedly rouge, and besides, the figure with that ribbon headband, I am sorry to say, however you thought of it could only be taken for a monster.
“Here, Naomi-chan... ”
I said it carelessly, and hastily corrected it to san, then,
“Is that woman a young lady even so? ”
“Yes, she is, though she looks just like a tart... ”
“Do you know that woman? ”
“I don’t know her, but I’ve often heard about her from Ma-chan.
Look, she has a ribbon wound on her head.
That young lady’s eyebrows are way up on her forehead, so to hide them she wears a headband and paints separate eyebrows lower down.
Look, those eyebrows are fake. ”
“But the features aren’t so bad, are they.
It’s because she’s daubed red and blue and such in a mess that it’s funny. ”
“In short, a fool. ”
Naomi seemed to be recovering her confidence, and delivered it in her usual conceited tone:
“Even the features, there’s nothing good.
Do you think a woman like that is a beauty, Jōji-san? ”
“Not a beauty, exactly, but the nose is high, the figure isn’t bad; if she made up ordinarily she’d be presentable. ”
“How disgusting!
Presentable, nothing!
Faces like that are common as dirt.
And besides, think: she takes all sorts of trouble trying to look Western, that’s all right, but she doesn’t look Western at all, so it’s a joke.
Quite a monkey. ”
“By the way, the woman dancing with Hamada-kun, isn’t she a woman I’ve seen somewhere? ”
“You would have seen her; that’s Haruno Kirako of the Imperial Theatre. ”
“Oh, does Hamada-kun know Kirako? ”
“Yes he does; he’s good at dance, so he makes friends with actresses everywhere. ”
Hamada, in a brownish lounge suit, chocolate box-shoes and spats, was dancing with a skillful step that stood out even in the crowd.
And what was quite outrageous—or perhaps there is such a way of dancing—he had his face stuck close against the woman’s.

Kirako, a small woman with slender, ivory-like fingers, who looked as if she would bend and break if you hugged her tight, was far more of a beauty than on the stage, and as her name suggested she wore a gorgeous, glittering costume, a maru-obi of satin or shuchin, I don’t know, with a dragon drawn in gold thread and deep green on a black ground.
Because the woman was shorter, Hamada had his head tilted sharply as if smelling her hair, his ear stuck against Kirako’s side-locks.
Kirako for her part had her forehead against the man’s cheek so hard that wrinkles gathered at the corners of her eyes.
The two faces, four eyeballs blinking, even if the bodies parted, the necks never left each other as they danced on.
“Jōji-san, do you know that way of dancing? ”
“I don’t know what it is, but it doesn’t look very nice. ”
“True, it’s really vulgar. ”
Naomi made a mouth as if spitting peh-peh:
“That’s called cheek dance, and they say you can’t do it in a serious place.
In America if you do that they tell you to leave.
Hama-san is all right, but he’s quite affected. ”
“But the woman is the woman, too. ”
“Of course; actresses are that sort anyway; it’s wrong to let actresses in here at all; if they do that, real ladies won’t come. ”
“Even the men—you were so particular, but there aren’t many in navy lounge suits, are there.
Hamada-kun is dressed like that too... ”
This was something I had noticed from the first.

Naomi, who likes to put on knowing airs, had picked up the so-called etiquette and forced a navy lounge suit on me; but when we came, only two or three were so dressed, there was not one tuxedo, and the rest were mostly in fancy-colored, studied suits.
“That’s so, but that’s Hama-san being wrong; navy is the formal. ”
“Even so... look at that Westerner, isn’t that homespun too.
So anything will do, I suppose. ”
“That’s not so; whatever people do, you yourself should come in formal dress.
Westerners come dressed like that because Japanese are bad.
And besides, a person like Hama-san who’s been on the floor a lot and is good at dancing is another matter; someone like Jōji-san looks bad if the clothes aren’t precise. ”
The current of dance in the open space stopped all at once, and hearty applause rose.
The orchestra had stopped, so they all, wanting to dance even a little longer, the keen ones whistling, stamping, were encored.
Then the music began again, the stopped current began to move round and round again.

After a spell it stopped again, another encore... two times, three times repeated, and at last however much they clapped they were not heard, and the men who had danced, following behind their partners like escorts, all came trailing back toward the tables.
Hamada and Ma-chan saw Kirako and the pink dress each to their tables, sat them in chairs, bowed politely before the women, and presently came together toward us.
“Well, good evening.
You’re quite late. ”
That was Hamada.
“What’s the matter, not dancing? ”
Ma-chan, in that rough tone of his, stood behind Naomi, looking her dazzling full dress up and down from above:
“If you’ve no promise, shall I dance with you next? ”
“I don’t want to, Ma-chan, you’re clumsy! ”
“Don’t talk rot; I don’t pay fees, but I can dance properly, that’s the wonder. ”
And spreading the holes of his great dumpling nose, making his lips a “he” character, he grinned eh-ra eh-ra:
“Because at bottom you’re so clever. ”
“Hm, don’t put on airs!
The figure of you dancing with that pink dress wasn’t a very pretty picture. ”
Amazingly, when Naomi turned to this man she at once used such violent language. “Yah, this one’s no good,”
Ma-chan said, shrinking his neck and scratching his head, glancing back at the pink at a far table:
“I don’t mean to take second in shamelessness, but I can’t match that woman, coming out here in that dress. ”
“What’s that, quite a monkey. ”
“Ahahaha, a monkey, well put, a monkey, no mistake. ”
“Well said, when you brought her yourself.—Really, Ma-chan, it looks bad, so give her a warning.
Trying to look Western, with that mug it’s impossible.
The features of the face, Nippon, Nippon, pure Nippon through and through. ”
“In short, a sad effort. ”
“Ahahaha, yes really, in short a monkey’s sad effort.
Even in Japanese clothes, a person who looks Western looks Western. ”
“In short, like you? ”
Naomi went “hm,” raising her nose, with a proud sneer:
“That’s right, I still look more like a Eurasian. ” “Kumagai-kun,”
Hamada, looking as if he were being careful of me, fidgeting, called Ma-chan by that name.
“Come to think of it, you haven’t met Kawai-san before, have you? ”
“Ah, I’ve seen the face any number of times, but—”
The Ma-chan called “Kumagai,” still standing behind the chair over Naomi’s back, threw a nasty glance at me.
“I’m Kumagai Masatarō.—I’ll introduce myself, please—”
“Real name Kumagai Masatarō, also known as Ma-chan.—”
Naomi looked up at Kumagai’s face from below:
“Ma-chan, while you’re at it, why not introduce yourself a little more? ”
“No, no good; if I say too much the rags come out.—Please hear the details from Naomi-san. ”
“Ara, how disgusting, what details do I know. ”
“Ahahaha. ”
I thought it unpleasant to be surrounded by this company, but Naomi had begun to romp in good humor, so I too, having no choice, laughed and said,
“Come, how about it.
Hamada-kun, Kumagai-kun, won’t you sit here? ”
“Jōji-san, my throat is dry, order something to drink.
Hama-san, what would you like?
Lemon squash? ”
“Eh, anything is fine for me, but... ”
“Ma-chan, you? ”
“If I’m being treated anyway, I’d like whisky and soda. ”
“Well I’m dashed; I hate drinkers, the mouth stinks! ”
“Stink or not, they say the stinking part is what you can’t throw away. ”
“That monkey? ”
“Ah, no good; if you say that I’ll apologize. ” “Ahahaha,”
Naomi, not caring who heard, rocking her body back and forth:
“Then Jōji-san, call the boy,—one whisky and soda, then three lemon squashes. ...
Ah, wait, wait!
I’ll stop the lemon squash; fruit cocktail is better. ”
“Fruit cocktail? ”
I wondered how Naomi knew such a drink I had never even heard of.
“If it’s cocktail isn’t it liquor? ”
“That’s a lie; Jōji-san doesn’t know,—come, Hama-chan, Ma-chan, listen, this person is this rustic. ”
When she said “this person” Naomi tapped my shoulder lightly with her forefinger:
“So really, even coming to dance, just the two of us with this person, it’s so vacant I can’t stand it.
He’s in a daze, so just now he slipped and almost fell. ” “The floor is slippery, you know,” Hamada said, as if defending me:
“At first everyone is vacant; as you get used to it you gradually get the hang, but... ”
“Then how about me?
Don’t I get the hang either? ”
“No, you’re different; Naomi-kun has nerve... well, a genius of social art. ”
“Hama-san isn’t not a genius either. ”
“Eh, me? ”
“That’s right, making friends with Haruno Kirako before one knows it!
Ma-chan, don’t you think so? ” “Unh, unh,”
Kumagai stuck out his lower lip and nodded, tossing his chin.
“Hamada, did you make a motion at Kirako? ”
“Don’t joke; would I do such a thing. ”
“But Hama-san is cute, making excuses all red.
There’s something honest somewhere.—Hama-san, won’t you bring Kirako here?
Come on!
Go and call her!
Introduce her to me. ”
“What, you mean to tease again?
If I fall under your poisonous tongue I can’t stand it. ”
“It’s all right, I won’t tease, so go and call her; it’s better if it’s lively. ”
“Then shall I call that monkey too. ” “Ah, that’s good, that’s good,” Naomi looked back at Kumagai:
“Ma-chan, go call the monkey too; let’s all be together. ”
“Unh, all right, but the dance has started; shall we dance once with you first. ”
“I don’t want Ma-chan, but it can’t be helped; shall I dance. ”
“Don’t say it, don’t say it, and you only just started learning. ”
“Then Jōji-san, I’ll go dance once, so watch.
Afterward I’ll dance with you. ”
I must have had a sad, odd expression, I think, but Naomi rose abruptly, linked arms with Kumagai, and went into the current of the crowd that had begun to move vigorously again.
“Yah, this time it’s number seven, foxtrot,—”
Hamada too, when it was just the two of us, seemed at a loss for a topic; he took a program from his pocket, looked, and lifted his rump furtively.
“Excuse me a moment; this number I have a promise with Kirako-san.—” “Please, don’t mind us,—”

I had to sit alone, staring blankly at the scene in the open space, with the whisky and soda the boy had brought after the three had vanished, and the so-called “fruit cocktail,” four glasses in front of me.
But originally I did not want to dance myself; I mainly wanted to see how much Naomi would stand out in a place like this, what sort of dancing she would do, so in the end this was easier.
And with a feeling as of being released, I followed with keen eyes Naomi’s figure appearing and disappearing among the waves of people.
“Hm, she dances quite well! ...
With that it doesn’t look bad... when you have her do a thing like that that child is clever after all. ... ”
On tiptoe in white tabi in pretty dance zōri, whirling her body round and round, the showy long sleeves fluttered and danced.
At every step the hem of the kimono in front leapt up like a butterfly.

The snow-white fingers pinching Kumagai’s shoulder with a hand like a geisha holding a plectrum; the gorgeous obi-cloth binding the torso heavily, solidly; the nape, the profile, the front, the back hairline, standing out in this crowd like a single flower-stem,—looking so, Japanese clothes are not to be thrown away, after all; and besides, perhaps because of women of eccentric design beginning with that pink dress, the gaudy taste I had privately worried about was by no means so vulgar.
“Ah, hot, hot!
How was it, Jōji-san, did you watch me dance? ”
When the dance was over she came back to the table and hurriedly drew the fruit-cocktail glass toward her.
“Yes, I watched; with that, you’d never think it was the first time. ”
“Really!
Then next, at the one-step, I’ll dance with Jōji-san, all right? ...
The one-step is easy. ”
“What happened to those fellows, Hamada-kun and Kumagai-kun? ”
“Eh, they’re coming now, dragging Kirako and the monkey.—You’d better order two more fruit cocktails. ”
“Come to think of it, the pink was dancing with a Westerner just now, wasn’t she. ” “Yes, that’s so, and isn’t it comic—”
Naomi, staring at the bottom of the glass, gulping, wetting her thirsty mouth:
“That Westerner isn’t a friend or anything; he came straight to the monkey and said please dance.
In short he’s making a fool of us; saying such a thing without an introduction, he must have mistaken her for a tart or something. ”
“Then she should have refused. ”
“That’s just it, isn’t it comic.
That monkey, because the other was a Westerner, couldn’t refuse and danced!
A real fool, a shameful sight! ”
“But you, you shouldn’t speak so cuttingly ill.
Listening from the side I get nervous. ”
“It’s all right; I have my own ideas.—Why, it’s better to say that much to a woman like that, otherwise we’ll be troubled too.
Even Ma-chan said it was a bother so he’d give her a warning. ”
“That’s all right if a man says it, but... ”
“Look!
Hama-chan has brought Kirako; when a lady comes you stand up from your chair at once.—” “Let me introduce you,—”
Hamada stopped in front of us two in a posture like a soldier’s “attention. ” “This is Miss Haruno Kirako.—”

In such a case I naturally take Naomi’s beauty as the standard: “Is this woman superior or inferior to Naomi”; and now Kirako, coming a step forward from behind Hamada, making a modest figure, a composed, confident smile at her mouth, was perhaps a year or two older than Naomi.
But in the lively, girlish point, perhaps because she is small, she was not at all different from Naomi, and in the luxury of her clothes she rather overwhelmed Naomi.
“How do you do... ”

she said in a modest manner, lowering clever, small, round, wide-open pupils, drawing her breast a little as she greeted; in that carriage, as one would expect of an actress, there was none of Naomi’s coarseness.
Naomi, in all she does, has gone beyond the lively and is too violent.
The way she speaks is snappish and lacks a woman’s gentleness, and at the least it becomes vulgar.

In short she is a wild beast; compared with this, Kirako’s way of speaking, of using the eyes, of twisting the neck, of raising the hands, all is refined, careful, nervous, with the feeling of a precious object polished to the extreme of artifice.
For instance when she sat at the table and took the cocktail glass, looking from palm to wrist, it is truly thin.
So thin and pliant it seems it could not bear even the weight of the quietly hanging sleeve.

In the fineness of the grain and the languorous gloss of color she is not inferior to Naomi, and I don’t know how many times I looked by turns at the four palms laid on the table; but the flavor of the two faces is very different.
If Naomi is Mary Pickford, a Yankee girl, this one is after all a beauty of Italy or France, of a faint coquetry held in the modest, a dim, bewitching beauty.
Of the same flower, Naomi blooms in the field, Kirako in a room.
That small nose in the tightly drawn round face, what a thin-fleshed, transparent nose!
Unless a master craftsman made a doll or something, even a baby’s nose can hardly be so delicate.
And last I noticed that the splendid set of teeth Naomi is always proud of, grains of pearl exactly the same, were growing like seeds in Kirako’s pretty mouth-cavity, like a split red melon.
At the same time I felt myself at a disadvantage, Naomi must have felt it too.
After Kirako joined the seats, Naomi, unlike her earlier arrogance, far from teasing, suddenly went quite silent, and the company turned cold.
But even so, she who is strong in sour grapes, because of the words she herself had said, “Call Kirako,” presently seemed to recover her usual tomboy mood, and began bit by bit:
“Hama-san, don’t sit silent, say something.—Kirako-san, from when did you become friends with Hama-san? ”
Kirako said, her clear pupils suddenly bright:
“Only the other day. ” “I,”
Naomi too, drawn into the other’s “watakushi” tone:
“I was watching just now, and you are quite skillful; have you practiced a great deal? ”
“No, I have been doing it, from before, but I don’t become skillful at all, being clumsy... ”
“Ara, that’s not so.
Hama-san, what do you think? ”
“She ought to be good; Kirako-san practiced properly at an actress-training school. ” “Well, saying such a thing,”
Kirako showed a manner as of blushing, and looked down.
“But you really are skillful; looking about, the best man is Hama-san, among the women Kirako-san... ”
“Well. ”
“What’s this, a dance criticism meeting? The best man is me, whatever you say.—”
There Kumagai broke in, bringing the pink dress.
This pink, according to Kumagai’s introduction, was the daughter of a businessman living toward Aoyama, named Inoue Kikuko.

Already twenty-five or six, past the marriageable age beginning to pass,—I heard this later: two or three years ago she had married somewhere, but because she was so fond of dance she had lately been divorced.—The dress, bared from shoulder to arm under such evening clothes on purpose, was no doubt selling a voluptuous beauty of flesh; but sitting face to face like this, rather than voluptuous it was the figure of a greasy older woman.
Of course this much flesh suits Western clothes better than a poor physique, but the trouble, whatever you say, is the features.

Features far from Western clothes, like a Kyoto-doll’s head on a Western doll,—and if they had been left as they were it would have been all right, but she had taken pains to bring the relation closer, putting extra work here and there, and spoiling the looks she had.
Looking, indeed, the real eyebrows were no doubt hidden under the headband, and what was drawn above the eyes was clearly fake.
Then the blue shading at the rims of the eyes, the rouge, the painted mole, the line of the lips, the line of the nose-ridge: almost every part of the face was unnaturally made.
“Ma-chan, do you dislike monkeys? ”
Naomi suddenly said such a thing. “Monkeys?—”
Kumagai said, holding in a burst of laughter:
“What’s this, asking a funny thing. ”
“I keep two monkeys at my house, so if Ma-chan likes them I thought I’d give you one.
How is it?
Doesn’t Ma-chan like monkeys? ”
“Ara, you keep monkeys? ”
Kikuko asked in earnest, so Naomi, getting still more above herself, her mischievous eyes glittering:
“Yes, we keep them; does Kikuko-san like monkeys? ” “I like all animals, dogs or cats—”
“And monkeys too? ”
“Yes, monkeys too. ”
The dialogue was so funny that Kumagai turned aside holding his belly, Hamada put a handkerchief to his mouth and snickered, Kirako too seemed to have caught it and was grinning.
But Kikuko, it seemed, was an unexpectedly good-natured woman, and did not notice she was being mocked.
“Hm, that woman is quite a fool; her blood doesn’t circulate well, does it. ”
Presently the eighth, the one-step, began, and when Kumagai and Kikuko had gone toward the floor, Naomi, not even holding back before Kirako, said in a dirty-mouthed tone:
“Kirako-san, didn’t you think so? ”
“Well, what is it... ”
“No, that person has a monkey-like feeling, doesn’t she, so I said monkey, monkey, on purpose. ”
“Well. ”
“Everyone laughing like that and she doesn’t notice—quite a fool. ”
Kirako, with a look half amazed, half contemptuous, stole a glance at Naomi’s face, and stuck to “well” throughout.
“Come, Jōji-san, the one-step.
I’ll dance with you; come. ”
After that, being so told by Naomi, I at last had the honor of dancing with her.
For me, though I say it is embarrassing, to try the usual practice in the field was of the moment, and especially with dear Naomi as partner, it was by no means not a pleasure.
Even if I was so clumsy as to become a laughingstock, that clumsiness would on the contrary set Naomi off, so I was rather satisfied.
And then I had an odd vanity.
That is, I wanted to be talked of: “That seems to be that woman’s husband.
” In other words, I wanted to boast greatly: “This woman is mine.
How’s that, take a look at my treasure.
” Thinking of that I felt brilliant and at the same time extremely gratified.
I felt as if the sacrifices and labors I had paid for her till today had been rewarded all at once.
From her manner from a while before, tonight she doesn’t want to dance with me, I had thought.
Until I get a little better she doesn’t like it.
If she doesn’t like it, I won’t force a dance until then either.
I had more or less given up, and then “I’ll dance with you” came, so that one voice, I cannot tell you how it pleased me.
So, excited like a fever patient, I remember as far as taking Naomi’s hand and starting the first one-step, but after that I was in a daze.

And the more I was in a daze, the more I could not hear the music or anything, my steps became a mess, my eyes flickered, my pulse grew violent; it was quite a different matter from doing it to gramophone records on the second floor of Yoshimura’s instrument shop; rowing out into this ocean of waves of people, I could not tell at all whether to go back or forward.
“Jōji-san, why are you trembling buru-buru; if you don’t get a grip it’s no good! ”
And on top of that Naomi was always scolding at my ear.
“Look, look, you slipped again!
Because you turn in such a hurry!
More quietly!
Quietly, I said! ”
But being so told I grew still more flushed.
Besides, that floor, especially for tonight’s dance, had been made very slippery, so if you were careless thinking of the practice-room, at once it came sliding.
“There, there!
Don’t raise your shoulders, I said!
Lower these shoulders more!
Lower! ”
And Naomi would twist free the hand I was gripping for all I was worth, and now and then press my shoulders down hard, cruelly.
“Tch, what are you doing gripping my hand so tight!
If you cling to me like that I’m cramped and can’t stand it! ...
There, there, the shoulders again! ”
At this rate it was nothing; it was as if I were dancing entirely to be shouted at by her; but even those nagging words hardly entered my ears.
“Jōji-san, I’ll stop now. ”
Presently Naomi got angry, and though people were still showering encores, she left me behind and went back to the seats at a clip.
“Ah, I’m amazed.
I still can’t dance with Jōji-san at all; practice a little at home. ”
Hamada and Kirako came, Kumagai came, Kikuko came, around the table it grew lively again, but I was quite soaked in the sorrow of disillusion, and only sat silent, the object of Naomi’s mockery.
“Ahahaha, if you talk like that, a timid person still less can dance.
Don’t say that; dance with him. ”
This, Kumagai’s words, stung me again.
“Dance with him”—what a way to put it.
What does he take me for?
This greenhorn!
“Why, he’s not as poor as Naomi-kun says; there are any number worse. ” Hamada said, and
“How about it, Kirako-san, this foxtrot, would you dance with Kawai-san? ”
“Yes, please... ”
Kirako nodded with an actress’s charm as usual. But I hastily waved my hands: “No, no good, no good,”
I said, comically flustered.
“No good, how can it be.
It’s because you’re so reserved, that’s why you’re no good.
Kirako-san. ”
“Yes... please, really. ”
“No, I can’t, I really can’t; when I’ve got good I’ll ask you. ”
“She says she’ll dance with you, so why not let her. ”
Naomi said, overlaying it as if it were an honor beyond me:
“Jōji-san is no good because he only wants to dance with me.—Come, the foxtrot has started, go; dance is better as a match with another school. ”
“Will you dance with me? ”
Then I heard that voice, and the one who came straight to Naomi’s side was the young foreigner who had been dancing with Kikuko just now, a slim figure, a womanish, affected face powdered.
Rounding his back, bending before Naomi, smiling niko-niko, perhaps paying compliments, he rattled something in a fast voice.
And only the pushy “please please” I understood.
Then Naomi too, with a troubled look, went red as if fire were coming out, and yet could not get angry, and grinned.
She wanted to refuse if she could, but how to express it most roundly, not a word of her English would come at a sudden moment.
The foreigner, seeing Naomi start to laugh, seemed to take it as goodwill, and with a manner of urging “Come,” demandingly required her answer.
When she said that and stood up reluctantly, her cheeks grew still more violently red, as if burning.
“Ahahaha, after all that fellow, putting on such airs, against a Westerner she’s spiritless. ”
Kumagai guffawed.
“Westerners are shameless, it’s a trouble.
Just now I was really at a loss. ”
That was Kikuko.
“Then shall I ask you once. ”
Kirako was waiting, so I was in a fix of having to say so whether I would or no.
Strictly speaking, it is not only today: in my eyes there is not a single woman besides Naomi.
