Of course, if I see a beauty I feel she is pretty.
But the prettier she is, the more I only want to look at her softly from afar, without even touching.
Madame Shlemskaya was an exception, but even that, the tranced feeling I experienced then was probably not ordinary desire.
Too ethereal, too hard to grasp a dreamy state to call “desire.
” And the other was a foreigner wholly apart from us, a dance teacher, so compared with Kirako, a Japanese, an Imperial Theatre actress, and wrapped besides in dazzling clothes, I felt easier.
Yet Kirako, unexpectedly, when I danced with her, was truly light.
The whole body was floating, like cotton, the softness of the hand a touch like the new buds of a tree.
And she grasped my breathing very well, and with a clumsy fellow like me as partner, matched her breath exactly, like a sensitive horse.
When it came to this, lightness itself had an inexpressible pleasure.
My heart suddenly floated and took courage, my feet naturally took lively steps, and as if riding a merry-go-round I went round and round, sliding smoothly, as far as I would.
“Pleasant, pleasant!
This is strange, it’s interesting! ”
I unbidden felt so.
“Well, you’re skillful; there’s nothing difficult about dancing at all. ”
Round and round!
In the midst of turning like a waterwheel, Kirako’s voice grazed my ear. ...
A gentle, faint, sweet voice, very like Kirako. ...
“No, that’s not so.
It’s because you’re skillful. ”
“No, really... ” After a while she said again,
“Tonight’s band is very fine, isn’t it. ”
“Yes. ”
“If the music isn’t good, even if you take the trouble to dance, somehow there’s no spirit. ”
When I noticed, Kirako’s lips were just under my temple.
This seemed to be this woman’s habit; as she had done with Hamada just now, her side-locks were touching my cheek.

The stroking feeling of the soft hair... and the faint whispers leaking now and then... for me, who had long been under the hooves of a restive horse like Naomi, it was the extreme of a “womanliness” I had never imagined.
Somehow as if the traces of wounds stabbed by thorns were being stroked by a kind hand...
“I thought I’d refuse quite a bit, but Westerners have no friends, so it would be a pity not to sympathize. ”
Presently when she came back to the table, Naomi was making excuses, looking a little drooped.
It was around half past eleven, I suppose, when the sixteenth, the waltz, ended.
After this there were still several extras.
Naomi said if it got late we’d go home by car, but I soothed her somehow and we walked to Shimbashi to catch the last train.
Kumagai and Hamada too, together with the women, came seeing us that far, trailing in a chain along Ginza-dōri.

Jazz-band still seemed to be ringing in everyone’s ears; if one of them began a melody, men and women at once joined the tune; but to me, who did not know the songs, their cleverness, their good memory, their youthful bright voices, were only something to envy. “La, la, lalala,”
Naomi walked taking the beat in a still higher tone.
“Hama-san, what do you like?
I like Caravan best. ”
“Oh, Caravan! ”
Kikuko said in a queer voice.
“Wonderful, that! ” “But I—” This time Kirako took it:
“Whispering is not bad either, I think. It’s very easy to dance,—”
“Madame Butterfly is good, I like that best. ”
And Hamada at once whistled “Madame Butterfly. ”
Parting from them at the ticket-gate, standing on the platform where the winter night-wind blew through, waiting for the train, Naomi and I did not talk much.
A feeling you might call the loneliness after pleasure ruled my breast.
Naomi, of course, had not felt such a thing, and she spoke to me:
“Tonight was interesting, wasn’t it; let’s go again soon. ”
But I only answered “unh” in my mouth, with a look of the fun gone.
What?
Is this what they call dance?
After deceiving my parents, quarreling as husband and wife, crying and laughing to the utmost, the ball I tasted was this foolish thing?
Aren’t they all a collection of vanity and flattery and conceit and affectation?—
But then what did I go out for?
To show Naomi off to them?—If so I too am a lump of vanity.
And how was the treasure I had boasted of to that extent!
“How is it, you, when you walked this woman about, did the world, as you ordered, gasp in surprise? ”
I could not help saying so to my own heart, in a self-mocking feeling.—
“You, you, ‘the blind man does not fear the snake,’ that’s you.
Indeed, for you this woman is the world’s number-one treasure.
But when you put that treasure on the bright stage, how was it?
A collection of vanity and conceit!
You put it well, but wasn’t the representative of that collection this woman?
Who do you think was the one putting on greatness by herself, speaking ill of others wildly, the most pinched-nose to look at from the side?
It wasn’t only Miss Kikuko who was mistaken by a Westerner for a tart, and couldn’t speak even simple English, and dealt with him floundering.
And this woman’s violent way of speaking, what a state.
Putting on airs as a lady, that talk is almost unbearable to hear, isn’t it; Miss Kikuko and Kirako have far more breeding. ”
—This unpleasant feeling, whether remorse or disappointment, an ugly feeling I cannot quite describe, stuck to my breast until we got home that night.
Even in the train I sat on purpose on the opposite side, and felt like looking once more, thoroughly, at this thing called Naomi in front of me.
What, after all, is it about this woman that I am so infatuated?
That nose?
Those eyes?
Counting so, strangely, the face that always has such charm for me seemed tonight truly dull, worthless.
Then at the bottom of my memory, the figure of Naomi when I first met this woman—Naomi of the Café Diamond days—floated dimly.
But compared with now, that time was far better.
Innocent, childish, shy, with a gloomy place, nothing like this coarse, impertinent woman.
I fell in love with the Naomi of those days, and the inertia of that has continued to today; but thinking of it, without my knowing, this woman has become a quite unbearable, ugly creature.

That figure sitting there, stiffly composed, as if to say “The clever woman is I,” that arrogant face as if to say “The beauty of the world is I,” “There is no woman so Western, so Western-looking as I.” And with that she cannot speak even the “e” of English, and does not even know the difference between passive voice and active voice: no one knows, but I know it well. ...
I secretly showered such abuse in my head.
She was leaning back a little, her face turned up, so from my seat the holes of that snub nose she most boasts of as Western-looking peeped black.
And to left and right of that cave there was the thick flesh of the nostrils.
Come to think of it, I am deeply familiar with these nostrils morning and evening.

Every night, when I hold this woman, I always peek into this cave from such an angle, and as I did only the other day I blow her nose, caress around the nostrils, and sometimes set my own nose and this nose interlocking like wedges; so this nose—this little lump of flesh attached in the middle of a woman’s face—is quite the same as a part of my own body, and I cannot think of it as another’s.
But looking with such a feeling, it became still more hateful and dirty.

Often, when one is hungry, one gobbles something bad in a daze; as the belly gradually fills, the moment one notices how bad what one has stuffed is, the chest suddenly turns, and one feels like vomiting,—well, a feeling resembling that, I suppose; tonight too, imagining going to bed as usual with this nose, face to face, I came to feel somehow clogged and exhausted, as if I wanted to say “I’ve had enough of this feast. ”
“This too is a parent’s punishment.
Trying to have a good time by deceiving your parents, nothing decent comes of it. ”
I thought in that way.
But readers, I should be sorry if you inferred from this that I had quite tired of Naomi.

No: I myself had no such memory till now, and for a time I even thought so; but when we got back to the Ōmori house and were just the two of us, that “full-belly” heart of the train gradually flew off somewhere, and again every part of Naomi, eyes, nose, hands, feet, came to be filled with enchantment, and each one of them became, for me, a supreme thing I could not taste to the end.
After that I always went dancing with Naomi, and each time her faults stuck in my nose, so on the way home I was sure to have an ugly feeling.
But it never lasted long, and my love and hate toward her changed any number of times in a single night, like a cat’s eyes.
The Ōmori house, which had been quiet, came to have Hamada, Kumagai, their friends, mainly men we had got to know at dances, going in and out more and more frequently.
They generally came of an evening, around the time I returned from the company, and then we would put on the gramophone and dance.
Naomi liked guests, there were no servants or old people to be careful of, and besides this atelier was just the thing for dance, so they would play forgetting the passage of time.
At first they were somewhat reserved, and said they would go when it was mealtime, but
“Look!
Why are you going!
Stay and eat! ”
Naomi would force them to stay, so in the end it became the custom, whenever they came, to order Western food from “Ōmori-tei” and treat them to supper.
It was one night in the damp rainy-season.

Hamada and Kumagai had come to play and talked past eleven, but outside it was a great blowing rain, rain beating za-za against the glass windows, so both said “Let’s go, let’s go,” and hesitated a while, when
“Well, what terrible weather; we can’t possibly go home in this, so stay tonight. ”
Naomi said suddenly.
“Come, isn’t it all right, staying.—Ma-chan of course is all right? ”
“Unh, I’m all right either way, but... if Hamada goes I’ll go too. ”
“Hama-san doesn’t mind either, Hama-san. ” And Naomi, peeking at my face:
“It’s all right, Hama-san, you needn’t be reserved at all; in winter we haven’t enough quilts, but now four or so we can manage somehow.
And tomorrow is Sunday, Jōji-san will be at home too, you can sleep as late as you like. ”
“How about it, won’t you stay; in this rain it’s really terrible. ”
I too, having no choice, urged them.
“Come, do that, and tomorrow let’s play at something again; yes, yes, from evening we can go to Kagetsuen. ” In the end the two stayed, but
“By the way, what shall we do about the mosquito-net? ” I said, and
“There’s only one mosquito-net, so we can all sleep together.
That’s more interesting, isn’t it. ”
Such a thing seemed very novel to Naomi; she said it laughing kya-kya, as if she had gone on a school excursion.
This was unexpected to me.

I had thought we would offer the mosquito-net to the two, and Naomi and I could pass the night on the atelier sofa, burning a mosquito-coil; I had not expected the four of us to sleep in a heap in one room.
But Naomi was in that mood, and showed no ugly face toward the two... and as usual while I was dithering she decided at a clip:
“Come, I’ll spread the quilts, so all three of you help,”
and leading, giving orders, she went up to the four-and-a-half-mat attic.
As for the order of the quilts, the mosquito-net being small, the four of us could not line our pillows in a row.
So three would be parallel, and one at right angles to them.
“Look, this will do, won’t it.
You three men line up there; I’ll sleep here alone. ”
Naomi said.
“Yah, it’s come to a terrible thing. ”
When the mosquito-net was hung, Kumagai said, looking through it.
“This is a pigsty no matter how you look at it; we’ll all get mixed up. ”
“Mixed up is all right; don’t be luxurious. ”
“Hm!
While we’re troubling someone else’s house. ”
“Of course; anyway tonight we won’t really be able to sleep. ”
“I’ll sleep, I’ll sleep snoring gu-gu. ”
Kumagai thudded, making the earth ring, and crawled in first, kimono and all.
“You may try to sleep but I won’t let you.—Hama-san, don’t let Ma-chan sleep; if he looks like sleeping, tickle him.—”
“Ah, it’s muggy, I can’t sleep like this at all.—”
On the right of Kumagai, who was lying back on the middle quilt with his knees up, Hamada in Western clothes, in trousers and undershirt only, had his thin body on his back, his belly dented in.
And as if quietly listening to the rain outside, one hand on his forehead, the sound of the other flapping a fan made it seem still more hot and oppressive.
“And besides, if a woman’s there I somehow feel I can’t sleep at ease. ”
“I’m a man, not a woman; Hama-san said he didn’t feel I was a woman, didn’t he. ”
In the dim place outside the mosquito-net, when she changed into a nightgown with a flash, Naomi’s white back was visible.
“That’s so, I did say it, but... ”
“... still, if you sleep beside me, you feel I’m a woman? ”
“Ah, well, that’s so. ”
“Then Ma-chan? ”
“I’m all right; I don’t count the likes of you as a woman. ”
“If not a woman, what am I? ”
“Unh, well, you’re a seal. ”
“Ahahahaha, which is better, a seal or a monkey? ”
“I’ll take neither, thanks. ”
Kumagai put on a sleepy voice on purpose.

I, lying on Kumagai’s left, was silently listening to the three chattering away, but I was privately worrying: when Naomi came in here she would have to turn her head either toward Hamada or toward me.
Because Naomi’s pillow had been thrown in an ambiguous position, belonging to neither.
When we spread the quilts just now, she had put it that way on purpose, I thought, so it could go either way later.
Then when Naomi had changed into a peach-colored crinkled gown, she presently came in and stood:
“Shall I put out the light? ”
she said.
“Ah, put it out for me... ”
Kumagai’s voice said so.
“Then I’ll put it out. ... ”
“Ah, that hurts! ”
Kumagai said, and at that instant Naomi jumped onto his chest, using the man’s body as a stepping-stone, and from inside the mosquito-net clicked the switch.

It had grown dark, but the tip of the street-lamp on the telegraph pole outside was reflected in the window-glass, so the room was mistily bright enough to tell one another’s faces and clothes; and the moment Naomi straddled Kumagai’s neck and jumped down onto her own quilt, the force of the nightgown’s hem flashing open teased my nose.
“Ma-chan, won’t you have a smoke? ”
Naomi did not at once try to sleep, but sat down on the pillow with her thighs open like a man, looking down at Kumagai from above.
“Come on!
Turn this way! ”
“Beast, you’re set on not letting me sleep. ”
“Ufufufu, come on!
Turn this way!
If you don’t I’ll bully you. ”
“Ah, that hurts!
Stop, stop, stop I said!
I’m a living thing, treat me a little politely; being used as a stepping-stone and kicked, even if I’m sturdy I can’t stand it. ”
“Ufufufu. ”
I was looking at the ceiling of the mosquito-net so I couldn’t tell clearly, but Naomi seemed to have pushed the man’s head with her toes: “Can’t be helped,”
Kumagai said, and presently turned over.
“Ma-chan, are you up? ”
Hamada’s voice said.
“Ah, I’m up; I’m being persecuted hard. ”
“Hama-san, you turn this way too, or I’ll persecute you. ”
Hamada too turned over in succession, and seemed to have gone on his stomach.
At the same time there was a sound of Kumagai rummaging a match from his sleeve, clatter.
And he struck the match, so a light came dimly over my eyelids.
“Jōji-san, why don’t you turn this way too?
What are you doing alone? ”
“U, unh... ”
“What’s the matter, sleepy? ”
“U, unh...
I was just starting to doze... ”
“Ufufufu, well put; aren’t you pretending to sleep on purpose?
Isn’t that so?
Aren’t you worried? ”
I had been hit on the mark, so though my eyes were shut I felt my face had gone quite red.
“I’m all right; we’re just making a noise like this, so you can sleep at ease. ...
Or if you’re really worried, why not look this way a little? You needn’t put on a thin front,—”
“You still want to be persecuted, don’t you. ”
That was Kumagai, lighting his cigarette, starting to smoke with a spat of the mouth.
“I don’t!
Persecuting a person like this is no use; I do it every day. ”
“Thanks for the feast. ”
What Hamada said I could not take as said from the heart, only as a kind of compliment toward me.
“Jōji-san,—but if you want to be persecuted I’ll do it. ”
“No, that’s plenty. ”
“If it’s plenty, turn toward me; it’s odd, one of you being left out of the company. ”
I turned round and laid my chin on the pillow.
And of Naomi’s feet, sitting with both shins braced in a character eight, one was at Hamada’s nose, one at mine.
And as for Kumagai, he had stuck his neck between that character eight, and was blowing a Shikishima at his ease.
“How is it, Jōji-san, this scene? ”
“What is unh. ”
“I’m amazed; a seal, no mistake. ”
“Yes, a seal; now the seal is resting on the ice.
The three sleeping in front are male seals too. ”

The pale-green mosquito-net hanging down over our heads like a low closed cloud... the white face in the hair undone long, black even at night... the breast, arms, plump calves showing here and there in the slovenly gown... this figure is one of the poses Naomi always tempts me with, and when I am shown such a figure I am made like a beast thrown bait.
I clearly felt, in the dimness, Naomi looking down at me steadily, with that inciting expression, smiling with spiteful eyes.
“‘Amazed’ is a lie.
You always say you can’t stand it when I put on a gown, but tonight because everyone’s here you’re putting up with it. Jōji-san, I hit it, didn’t I.”
“Don’t talk rot. ”
“Ufufufu, if you put on such airs, shall I make you surrender. ”
“Here, here, that’s not quite peaceful; such talk can wait till tomorrow night. ”
“Agreed! ”
Hamada too said, following Kumagai’s tail:
“Tonight I want everyone treated fairly. ”
“So I am treating fairly.
So there’ll be no grudges, this foot toward Hama-san, this one toward Jōji-san,—”
“Then what about me? ”
“Ma-chan is getting the most; you’re nearest me, sticking your neck out in a place like this. ”
“A great honor indeed. ”
“That’s right, you’re the most favored. ”
“But you, you’re not going to stay up all night like that, surely.
When we sleep, what happens? ”
“Well, what shall we do, which way shall I turn my head.
Shall I make it Hama-san, or Jōji-san. ”
“A head like that, whichever way you turn it, it’s no particular problem. ”
“No, that’s not so; Ma-chan is in the middle so it’s all right, but for me it’s a problem. ”
“Is that so?
Hama-san, then shall I make the head toward Hama-san. ”
“That’s just why it’s a problem; if the head is turned this way I worry, and if it’s turned toward Kawai-san I still somehow worry... ”
“And this woman’s sleeping figure is bad. ” Kumagai put in again:
“If you’re not careful, the one the feet are turned toward may get kicked in the night. ”
“How is it, Kawai-san, is the sleeping figure really bad? ”
“Yes, it’s bad; and not just ordinarily. ”
“Here, Hamada. ”
“Eh? ”
“He licked the soles when he was half-asleep, they say. ”
And Kumagai guffawed.
“Licking the feet is all right.
Jōji-san does it all the time; he says the feet are dearer than the face. ”
“That’s a kind of fetishism. ”
“But it’s so; Jōji-san, isn’t it?
You really like the feet better, don’t you? ”
Then Naomi, saying “It would be bad not to be fair,” turned her feet toward me, then toward Hamada, and every five minutes or so, any number of times, sprawled here and there on the quilts.
“Come, now Hama-san’s turn for the feet! ”
And she would whirl her body round and round like a spinner as she lay, and in the whirling raise both legs and kick the ceiling of the mosquito-net, or throw a pillow from that end to this.
The seal’s activity was so violent that the hem of the mosquito-net, already half off the quilts, flipped up pap-pap, and any number of mosquitoes flew in.
“This is no good, terrible mosquitoes,” Kumagai sat up with a heave and began mosquito-extermination.
Someone stepped on the mosquito-net and cut the hanging-cords and brought it down.
In the fallen thing Naomi thrashed still more.
Mending the cords and hanging the net again took a long time.
With such a fuss, it was around the time the east began to grow light that we at last felt somewhat settled.
The sound of rain, the noise of wind, Kumagai’s snore sleeping next to me... it stuck in my ears, and just as I thought I had dozed a little, my eyes would open.
This room is cramped even for two to sleep in, and the sweet scent and sweat-smell stuck to Naomi’s skin and clothes is shut in as if fermented.
Tonight two grown men have increased besides, so the human steam is still more unbearable, and inside the sealed walls there was a muggy heat as if there might be an earthquake, choking.
Now and then when Kumagai turned over, sweaty hands and knees touched one another, slimy.

Looking at Naomi, though the pillow was toward me, she had one foot on that pillow, one knee up, the instep of that foot thrust under my quilt, her head tilted toward Hamada, both arms spread wide, and even that tomboy, tired I suppose, was sleeping looking pleased.
“Naomi-chan... ”
I said in my mouth, watching everyone’s quiet sleeping breath, and stroked her foot under my quilt.

Ah this foot, this snow-white beautiful foot sleeping so peacefully, this is certainly mine; I put this foot in the bath every night from when she was a slip of a girl and washed it with soap; and this softness of skin—from her fifteenth year her body stretched and stretched, but this foot alone, as if it had not developed at all, is still small and dear.
Yes, this big toe is as it was then.
The shape of the little toe, the round of the heel, the swell of the puffed instep, all as it was then, isn’t it. ...
I could not help, unbidden, putting my lips softly to that instep.
After day broke I seemed to doze again, but presently I woke to a burst of laughter, and Naomi had thrust a kanjiyori into my nostril.
“What’s the matter?
Jōji-san, are you awake? ”
“Ah, what time is it. ”
“Half past ten already, but there’s no use getting up, so let’s stay in bed till the noon-gun. ”
The rain had stopped, the Sunday sky was blue and clear, but in the room the human steam still remained.
At that time, no one at the company should have known of my dissipated state.
When I was at home and when I was at the company, my life was sharply divided in two.
Of course even while I was at my desk Naomi’s figure was always flickering in my head, but it was not enough to hinder the work, still less for others to notice.
So I had believed that in my colleagues’ eyes I still looked a gentleman.

But one day—it was still before the rainy season had quite cleared, a sultry evening—an engineer named Namikawa, a colleague, was ordered abroad by the company, and a farewell party was held at Seiyōken in Tsukiji.

I had only attended as a matter of duty as usual, so when the meal was over, the dessert-course speeches finished, and everyone had trailed from the dining-room into the smoking-room and begun noisy talk over after-dinner liqueurs, I thought I might as well go home, and stood up, when “Here, Kawai-kun, sit down a bit,”
a man called S stopped me, grinning.
S, faintly flushed with drink, occupying one sofa with T and K and H, tried to force me into the middle of them.
“Come, you needn’t run away like that; are you going somewhere from here, in this rain.— ”
S said, looking up at my face as I stood belonging to neither side, and grinned again.
“No, it isn’t that, but... ”
“Then you’re going straight home? ”
That was H.
“Ah, sorry, but excuse me.
My place is Ōmori, and in weather like this the roads are bad; if I don’t go early there’ll be no rickshaw. ”
“Ahahaha, well put. ”
This time T said.
“Here, Kawai-kun, the seed is all out. ”
“What?... ”
What “seed” meant I could not make out from T’s words, and I asked again, a little flustered.
“I’m amazed, I thought you were only a gentleman... ”
Next K twisted his neck as if wildly impressed:
“When it comes to Kawai-kun dancing, the times have progressed, after all. ” “Here, Kawai-kun,”
S, being careful of those around, put his mouth to my ear.
“That wonderful beauty you’ve been walking about with, who is she?
Introduce her to us once. ”
“No, she isn’t a woman to introduce. ”
“But they say she’s an Imperial Theatre actress. ...
Eh, isn’t that so; there’s a rumor she’s a picture-actress, and a theory she’s a Eurasian; tell us the woman’s nest.
If you don’t we won’t let you go. ”
Not noticing I had a clearly unpleasant face and was stammering, S leaned his knees forward in a daze and asked, getting heated.
“Eh, you, can’t that woman be called except at a dance? ”
I might have said “Fool!
” a little more.

I had thought probably no one at the company had noticed yet; but lo, they had not only sniffed it out, and from the tone of S, who had a name as a rake, they did not believe we were a married couple, but thought of Naomi as a woman of the kind you can call anywhere.
“Fool!
Catching hold of a man’s wife and saying ‘Can she be called’!
Don’t say such impertinent things! ”
Against this unbearable insult I ought, of course, to have shouted so, changing color.
No: for a mere instant I certainly did change color with a flash.
“Here, Kawai, Kawai, tell us, really! ”
They counted on my good nature, shameless to the end; H said so, looking back at K:
“Eh, K, where did you say you heard it from.— ”
“I heard from a Keiō student. ”
“Hm, what? ”
“He’s a relative of mine, a dance maniac, always going in and out of dance places, so he knows that beauty. ”
“Here, what’s the name? ”
T stuck his neck in from the side.
“The name is... let me see... an odd name...
Naomi... wasn’t it Naomi. ”
“Naomi?...
Then she is a Eurasian after all. ”
And S, peeking at my face as if teasing:
“If she’s a Eurasian she isn’t an actress. ”
“She’s a great developer, they say, that woman.
She goes round ravaging Keiō students and such, they say. ”

I had a strange, convulsive thin smile floating, only my mouth twitching; but when K’s talk came this far, that thin smile suddenly froze, unmoving on my cheeks, and I felt my eyeballs sink back into the sockets.
“Hm, hm, that’s promising! ”
S said, quite delighted.
“That student relative of yours, was there something between him and that woman too? ”
“No, I don’t know about that, but among his friends there are two or three, they say. ”
“Stop, stop, Kawai will worry.—Look, look, he’s making a face like that. ”
When T said that, they all looked up at me at once and laughed.
“Why, worrying him a little doesn’t matter.
Trying to monopolize such a beauty in secret from us, the spirit is outrageous. ”
“Ahahahaha, how is it, Kawai-kun, even a gentleman may have a stylish worry now and then? ”
“Ahahahaha. ”
I was no longer in a state to get angry.
I could not hear at all who said what.
Only a burst of laughter clanged in both ears.
My sudden confusion was how to get through this place, whether to cry or laugh,—and that if I carelessly said something I would be still more mocked.
At any rate I flew out of the smoking-room, my head in the air, not knowing what was what.
And until I stood in the muddy street and was struck by the cold rain, my feet did not touch the earth.
Still feeling something chasing from behind, I fled on and on toward Ginza.
Coming out at the crossing one more to the left of Owari-chō, I walked from there toward Shimbashi. ...
Or rather, my feet only, unconsciously, unrelated to my head, moved in that direction.
In my eyes the street-lamps glittering on the rain-wet pavement were reflected.
Despite this weather, the street seemed quite full of people.
Ah, a geisha passing with an umbrella, a young girl passing in flannel, a streetcar running, a motorcar racing, ...
Naomi is a great developer.
She goes round ravaging students? ...
Can such a thing be?
It can, it certainly can; looking at Naomi’s manner of late, it would be strange not to think so.
In fact I myself had been privately concerned, but there were so many men friends around her that I had on the contrary been easy.
Naomi is a child, and lively.
“I’m a man,” as she herself says.
So she only likes gathering a crowd of men and making an innocent, lively, foolish racket.
Even if she had an ulterior motive, with so many eyes she could not hide it, surely she wouldn’t... and that “surely” I thought was the bad thing.
And yet surely... surely it isn’t fact, is it?
Naomi has become impertinent, but her character is a noble woman.
I know that well.
On the surface she may despise me, but she is grateful for the kindness of my bringing her up from fifteen.
I cannot doubt the words she often says with tears at bedtime, that she would never betray that.
That talk of K’s—perhaps the bad fellows at the company are teasing me?
Really, I wish it were so. ...
Who is that student relative of K’s?
Even among those the student knows, two or three have a relation?
Two or three? ...
Hamada?
Kumagai? ...
If anyone is suspicious these two are the most suspicious, but then why don’t the two quarrel?
Coming together, not separately, playing nicely with Naomi, what’s the idea?
A means to dull my eyes?
Is Naomi skillfully managing them, so they don’t know of each other?
No, more than anything, has Naomi fallen so far?
If she had a relation with the two, could she do such a shameless, brazen thing as that mixed sleeping the other night?
If so her behavior is worse than a prostitute. ...
Before I knew it I had crossed Shimbashi and walked, splashing mud, straight along the Shibaguchi road as far as Kanasugi-bashi.
The rain shut heaven and earth without a hair’s breadth of space, surrounding my body from front and back, left and right, raindrops falling from the umbrella wetting the shoulders of my raincoat.
Ah, the night of that mixed sleeping was rain like this too.
The night I first opened my heart to Naomi at the table of Café Diamond was spring, but rain like this too.
I thought such things.
Then tonight too, while I am walking here soaked like this, has someone come to the Ōmori house?
Is it mixed sleeping again?—Such a fear suddenly floated.
The lascivious scene of the atelier, Naomi in the middle, Hamada and Kumagai in ill-mannered postures, chattering jokes, came vividly before me.
“That’s it.
This is no time for me to dither. ”
Thinking so I hurried to Tamachi Station.
One minute, two, three... at last at the third minute a train came, but I had never experienced so long a three minutes.
Naomi, Naomi!
Why did I leave her behind tonight.
It’s because Naomi isn’t beside me, that’s the worst thing.—If I only saw Naomi’s face I felt this irritated heart would be somewhat saved.
I prayed that if I heard her open talk, saw her seemingly innocent pupils, the suspicion would clear.
But even so, if she should propose mixed sleeping again, what should I say?
From now on, toward her, toward Hamada and Kumagai who come near her, toward the miscellaneous others, what attitude should I take?
Should I, even if I offend her anger, boldly make the supervision strict?
If she meekly submits to me that would be well, but if she resists, what then?
No, that won’t happen.
If I say “Tonight I received a terrible insult from the company fellows.
So you too, so as not to be misunderstood by the world, be a little careful in your actions,” it is different from other cases, and for her own honor she will probably listen.
If she regards neither honor nor misunderstanding, then she is certainly suspicious.
K’s talk is fact.
If... ah, if such a thing...
I tried to be calm, settling my heart as much as I could, and imagined this last case.
If it became clear she had been deceiving me, could I forgive her?—Honestly, already I cannot live a day without her.
Half the sin of her fall is of course mine too, so if Naomi will only meekly repent her former faults and apologize, I do not want to blame her further, and have no qualification to blame.
But what I worry about is whether that stubborn woman, who especially toward me likes to grow still more stiff, even if I thrust evidence at her, would so easily bow her head to me.
Even if she bowed once, might she in fact not reform at all, look down on me as easy, and repeat the same fault two times, three times?
And in the end, from mutual stubbornness, come to part?—That was more fearful to me than anything.
To put it bluntly, more than her virtue itself, this was far more the source of headache.
Even in examining her, or supervising, I must decide beforehand my own belly in dealing with the occasion.
When she says “Then I’ll leave,” if I have the resolution to say “Leave as you please,” that would be well. ...
But I knew that on this point Naomi had the same weakness.
Because she can live in luxury to her heart’s content only living with me; once driven from here, besides that filthy house in Senzoku-chō, where has she a place to put herself.
Then, unless she becomes a real prostitute, no one will fuss over her.
However it was in the past, with the vanity of the present her, brought up to the full of self-will, she certainly cannot bear that.
Perhaps Hamada or Kumagai might take her in, but she must know that as students they cannot give her the luxury I have let her have.
Thinking so, it was a good thing I let her taste luxury.
Yes, come to think of it, that time in English-time when Naomi tore the notebook, when I got angry and said “Get out,” she surrendered, didn’t she.

If she had left then I don’t know how troubled I would have been, but she would be more troubled than I. She is she because of me; once she leaves my side, she will fall again to the bottom of society and become the underlayer of this world.
That must be quite fearful to her.
That fear cannot have changed from then.
She is already nineteen this year.
Having grown older, with a little more sense, she ought to feel it still more clearly.
If so, even if she says “I’ll leave” as a threat, she can hardly carry it out in earnest.
Whether I would be surprised by such a transparent threat or not, she must know that much. ...
By the time I reached Ōmori Station I had recovered some courage.
Whatever happened, Naomi and I would not have the fate of parting; that much, I felt, was surely certain.

When I came to the front of the house my hateful imagination was quite off: the atelier was pitch dark, there seemed to be not one guest, it was still, only a light burning in the four-and-a-half-mat attic. “Ah, she’s keeping house alone,—”
I stroked my breast with relief.
“This is well, truly fortunate,” I could not help feeling.
I opened the locked front door with a spare key, went in, and at once put on the atelier light.
Looking, the room was as usual scattered, but there was still no trace of a guest having come.
“Naomi-chan, I’m back, ...
I’ve come home... ”
Even so there was no answer; going up the stairs, Naomi had laid a bed alone in the four-and-a-half-mat room and was sleeping peacefully.

This is not unusual for her: if she is bored, day or night, not caring the time, she crawls into the quilts and reads a novel, and so falls sweetly asleep; so meeting that innocent sleeping face I was only the more reassured.
“This woman deceiving me?
Can such a thing be? ...
This woman, at this moment continuing peaceful breath before my eyes? ... ”
I sat secretly at the pillow-side so as not to wake her sleep, and for a while, holding my breath, watched that sleeping figure.
Once a fox changed into a beautiful princess and deceived a man, but while sleeping showed its true form and had the disguise stripped.—I recalled some such tale I had heard as a child.

Naomi, whose sleeping figure is bad, had stripped the wrapping-quilt completely, sandwiched the collar between her thighs, and on the breast bared as far as the breasts had one elbow up, the tip of that hand laid like a bent branch.
And the other hand stretched softly as far as around the knee where I sat.
The neck was turned toward the stretched hand, tilting as if about to slip from the pillow.
Just at the tip of that nose a book had fallen with the page open.
It was a novel called The Descendants of Cain by Arishima Takeo, who according to her criticism was “the greatest writer in the present literary world.
” My eyes were turned by turns upon the pure-white Western paper of that paper-bound book and the white of her breast.
Naomi’s skin-color, depending on the day, looks yellow or white, but when she is sleeping soundly or just up it was always very clear.
As if in sleep all the grease of the body had come out, she became clean.
Ordinarily “night” and “darkness” go together, but I always, thinking of “night,” cannot help associating the “white” of Naomi’s skin.
It is different from the “white” of broad day, without shade; it is a “white” wrapped, so to speak, in rags, in dirty, filthy, soiled quilts, and for that it drew me the more.
And looking thoroughly like this, her breast in the shadow of the lampshade came floating up vividly, as if at the bottom of deep-blue water.

That face, so sunny, so endlessly changing when she is awake, now has a mysterious expression, brows drawn melancholy as if given bitter medicine, like a person with the neck strangled; but I was very fond of this sleeping face of hers.
“When you sleep you become an expression like another person, as if seeing a fearful dream,” I often said.
“Then her death-face too must surely be beautiful,” I often thought.
Even if this woman were a fox, if the true form were such a bewitching thing, I would rather gladly wish to be enchanted.
I sat so in silence for about thirty minutes.
Her hand sticking out from the shade’s shadow toward the light, back down, palm up, was softly closed like a petal beginning to open, and at the wrist the quiet pulse beating was clearly known.
“When did you come back?... ”
The peaceful sleeping breath, suu, suu, suu, seemed a little disturbed, and presently she opened her eyes.
Still leaving that melancholy expression somewhere...
“Just now... a little before. ”
“Why didn’t you wake me? ”
“I called but you didn’t wake, so I left you quiet. ”
“Sitting there, what were you doing?—Looking at my sleeping face? ”
“Yes. ”
“Fu, what an odd person! ”
And she laughed innocently like a child, and laid the stretched hand on my knee.
“Tonight I was alone and it was dull.
I thought someone would come, but no one came to play. ...
Papa, won’t you sleep now? ”
“I don’t mind sleeping, but... ”
“Come on, sleep! ...
I napped, so I’ve been bitten by mosquitoes all over.
Look, like this! Scratch here a little!—”
As I was told, I scratched her arms and back for a while.
“Ah, thank you, it itches so I can’t stand it.—Sorry, but would you get the nightgown there?
And put it on me? ”
I brought the gown and scooped up her body lying in a great-character shape.
And while I undid her obi and changed her clothes, Naomi on purpose went limp, making her hands and feet floppy like a corpse.
“Hang the mosquito-net, then Papa sleep too, quickly.—”
There is no need to write at length the bedtime talk of the two of us that night.
When Naomi heard from me the talk at Seiyōken, she cursed dirty-mouthed, “Well, the impertinence!
What ignorant fellows!
” and laughed it off.
In short the world still does not understand the meaning of social dance.
If a man and woman only join hands and dance, people conjecture some bad relation between them, and at once raise such a rumor.
Newspapers with a grudge against the fashions of the new age write careless articles and slander, so the general person has decided that dance is an unsound thing.
So we must be prepared, anyway, to have that much said.—
“And I have never once been alone with a man besides Jōji-san.—Isn’t that so? ”
When we go dancing I am with her, when we play at home I am with her; even if I am out, guests are never one.
If one comes alone, if I say “Today I’m alone too,” they generally go home reserved.
Among her friends there is no such ill-mannered man.—Naomi said so, and
“However self-willed I am, I know the difference between good and bad.
If I wanted to deceive Jōji-san I could, but I would never do such a thing.
I’m really open and fair; there isn’t a single thing I’ve hidden from Jōji-san. ”
That is what she said.
“I know that too; it’s only that being told such a thing felt bad. ”
“If it felt bad, what will you do?
Say you’ll stop dancing? ”
“We needn’t stop, but we should be careful as far as we can not to be misunderstood. ”
“I’m associating carefully, as I just said. ”
“So I haven’t misunderstood. ”
“If only Jōji-san hasn’t misunderstood, I don’t fear whatever the world says.
Anyway I’m violent and foul-mouthed, so everyone hates me.—”

And she repeated in a sentimental, sweet tone that it was plenty if only I believed her and loved her, that because she is not like a woman she naturally makes men friends, that men are more refreshing and she likes that so she plays only with them, but she has not the least ugly feeling of color or love; and last, with stock phrases, “I have never forgotten the kindness of being brought up from fifteen,” “I think of Jōji-san as parent and as husband,” she shed tears copiously, had me wipe those tears, and rained kisses in rapid succession.
But talking so long, the names of Hamada and Kumagai alone, whether on purpose or by chance, she strangely did not say.
I too had wanted to say these two names and see the reaction appearing on her face, but in the end I missed saying them.

Of course I did not believe her words from one to ten, but if you doubt you can doubt anything, and there is no need to investigate even things past; if I watch and supervise from now on that will do... no, though I had meant at first to come out more stiffly, I was gradually made into such an ambiguous attitude.
And listening to the voice whispered mixed with the sound of sobbing, from among tears and kisses, while I hesitated whether it was a lie, it came to seem true after all.
After such a thing, I watched Naomi’s manner without seeming to, and she seemed little by little, to a degree not too unnatural, to be reforming her former attitude.
We still went dancing, but not so frequently as before; even going we did not dance too much, and cut it off at a moderate point.
Guests did not come annoyingly.
When I came back from the company she would be keeping house alone, quietly, reading a novel, knitting, listening quietly to the gramophone, planting flowers in the bed.
“Keeping house alone today too? ”
“Yes, alone; no one came to play. ”
“Then weren’t you lonely? ”
“If it’s settled from the start that I’m alone, there’s nothing lonely; I’m all right. ” And she said,
“I like it lively, but I don’t dislike loneliness either.
As a child I had no friends at all, and always played alone. ”
“Ah, come to think of it, you were like that.
In the Café Diamond days you didn’t talk much with the others, you were a little gloomy. ”
“Yes, that’s so; I seem a tomboy, but my true nature is gloomy.—Mustn’t I be gloomy? ”
“Being quiet is fine, but if you become gloomy that’s a trouble too. ”
“But isn’t it better than rampaging like the other day? ”
“I can’t tell you how much better. ” “I’ve become a good child, haven’t I.”
And she would suddenly fly at me, clasp my neck with both hands, and kiss so painfully, violently, my eyes would darken. Even if I invited from my side,
“How about it, we haven’t gone dancing for a while, shall we go tonight or so,”
she would give a half-hearted answer with a sunk look: “Either way—if Jōji-san wants to go,—” or often say,
“Rather let’s go to the pictures; tonight I don’t feel like dancing. ”
And that pure, happy life of four or five years ago came back between us.

Naomi and I, just the two of us with no outsider, went out to Asakusa almost every night, looked in at the picture-houses, and on the way back ate supper at some restaurant, talking of the dear past, “In those days it was like this,” “like that,” sinking into memory.

If I said, “You were so small I sat you on the rail of the Teikokukan and you held my shoulder looking at the picture,” Naomi would say, “When Jōji-san first came to the café you sat in a nasty sulk, staring at my face from far off, it was creepy. ”
“Come to think of it, Papa hasn’t put me in the bath lately; in those days you always washed my body, didn’t you. ”
“Ah yes, there was such a thing. ”
“Not ‘there was’; won’t you wash me anymore?
Now I’ve grown so big, do you dislike washing? ”
“Dislike?
How could I; I still want to wash you, but in fact I was holding back. ”
“Is that so?
Then wash me; I’ll be Baby again. ”
After such a conversation, luckily the hip-bath season was coming, so I again carried the Western bath that had been thrown in a corner of the storeroom into the atelier, and came to wash her body.
“Big Baby”—I had once said so, but the Naomi of now, four years of months having passed since then, lying that ample height in the tub, had already grown completely into a perfect “adult.
” The abundant hair that, undone, spread full as a rain-cloud; the round flesh with dimples at the joints here and there.
And those shoulders had gained still more thickness, breast and hips had still more elasticity, heaping in waves, and the graceful legs seemed still longer.
“Jōji-san, have I grown a little taller? ”
“Ah, you have indeed.
Lately you don’t seem much different from me. ”
“Presently I’ll be taller than Jōji-san.
The other day I weighed myself and I was fourteen kan two hundred. ”
“Amazing; even I am barely under sixteen kan. ”
“But Jōji-san is heavier than I?
For a shrimp. ”
“Of course I’m heavier; however much a shrimp, a man has a sturdy bone-structure. ”
“Then even now does Jōji-san have the courage to become a horse and let me ride?—When I first came you often did that, didn’t you.
Look, I’d straddle your back, make a towel into reins, saying hai-hai dō-dō, going round the room,—”
“Unh, in those days you were light; about twelve kan, I suppose. ”
“Now Jōji-san would be crushed. ”
“Crushed?
If you think it’s a lie, get on and see. ”
After joking, we played at horse again as in the old days.
“Come, I’ve become a horse. ”
And when I went on all fours, Naomi thudded onto my back with the weight of those fourteen kan two hundred, put the towel-reins in my mouth, and cried,
“Well, what a small tottering horse!
Firmer!
Hai-hai, dō-dō! ”
and, looking amused, squeezed my belly with her legs and yanked the reins.
I strained for all I was worth not to be crushed by her, and went round the room sweating.
And she would not stop that mischief until I collapsed.
“Jōji-san, this summer, after a long time, won’t we go to Kamakura? ”
When August came she said.
“I haven’t been since that time, so I want to go and see. ”
“Indeed, come to think of it, it was only that time. ”
“Yes, so this year let’s make it Kamakura; isn’t it our commemorative land. ”
How this word of Naomi’s pleased me.
As Naomi said, our honeymoon?—well, if you like, the place we went on our honeymoon was Kamakura.
There should be no land so commemorative for us as Kamakura.
After that we went somewhere every year to escape the heat, and had quite forgotten Kamakura; that Naomi should bring it up was a truly splendid idea.
“Let’s go, we must go! ”
I said, and agreed without a first or second thought.
Once the talk was settled, we soon got ten days’ leave from the company, locked the Ōmori house, and at the beginning of the month the two of us went to Kamakura.
For lodgings we rented a detached room of a gardener called Uesō, on the road from Hase-dōri toward the Imperial Villa.

At first I meant this time, it not being Kinparō surely, to stay at a somewhat smart inn; that we unexpectedly came to take lodgings was because Naomi brought the talk of this gardener’s detached room, saying “I heard a very convenient thing from Sugisaki-sensei.
” According to Naomi, an inn is uneconomical, and one has to be careful of the neighborhood, so if lodgings can be had that is best.
And luckily, a relative of the lady’s, a director of Tōyō Petroleum, had a rented room he had taken and was not using, and we could have it transferred to us, so wouldn’t that be better.

That director had rented it for three months, June, July, August, at five hundred yen, and stayed through July, but he had tired of Kamakura and would gladly let anyone who wanted it; if it was Sugisaki-sensei’s offices the rent didn’t matter, she said. ...
“Look, there’s no such good talk, so let’s do that.
Then it won’t cost money, so we can stay the whole month. ”
Naomi said.
“But you, I have the company, so I can’t play so long. ”
“But if it’s Kamakura you can commute by train every day, can’t you; come, won’t you? ”
“But without seeing whether that place suits you... ”
“Yes, I’ll go and see tomorrow even, and if it suits me may I settle it? ”
“You may settle it, but getting it for nothing feels bad, so we must arrange that somehow... ”
“I understand that.
Jōji-san is busy, so if it’s all right I’ll go to Sugisaki-sensei’s and ask her to take the money.
We’ll have to pay a hundred or a hundred and fifty yen, I suppose. ... ”
In this tone Naomi proceeded by herself, pap-pata, settled the rent at a hundred yen, and finished the money-dealings herself.
I was somewhat anxious, but when we went it was a better house than I had thought.

Though called a rented room, it was a one-story building independent of the main house, besides an eight-mat and a four-and-a-half-mat sitting-room there was an entry, a bathroom, and a kitchen, a separate entrance, you could go straight from the garden to the street, no need to meet the gardener’s family, so indeed it was as if the two of us had set up a new household here.
After a long time I sat on new, purely Japanese tatami, sat cross-legged before a long brazier, and stretched.
“Yah, this is good, the mood is very easy. ”
“A good house, isn’t it?
Which is better, Ōmori or this? ”
“This is far more settling; I feel I could stay as long as I liked. ”
“There, you see; that’s why I said we should make it here. ”
And Naomi was proud.
One day—perhaps three days or so after we came here—we had gone to bathe from noon, and after swimming about an hour, the two of us were lying on the sand, when
“Naomi-san! ”
someone called suddenly over our faces.
Looking, it was Kumagai.
He seemed just up from the sea, the wet bathing suit stuck close to his chest, and along those hairy shins seawater was dripping, drop by drop.
“Oh, Ma-chan, when did you come? ”
“I came today—I thought it was you for certain, and it was. ”
And Kumagai, raising a hand toward the sea,
“Hoi! ” called, and from the offing too
“Hoi! ”
someone answered.
“Who?
The one swimming there? ”
“Hamada—Hamada and Seki and Nakamura, four of us came today. ”
“Well, that’s quite lively; what inn are you staying at? ”
“Heh, nothing so prosperous.
It was so hot we couldn’t stand it, so we just came for the day. ”
Presently Hamada came up to where Naomi and he were talking.
“Well, it’s been a while!
We’ve quite neglected you,—how is it, Kawai-san, you haven’t appeared at dance at all lately. ”
“It isn’t that, exactly, but Naomi said she’d tired of it. ”
“Is that so, that’s outrageous.—When did you come here? ”
“Only two or three days ago; we’re renting a detached room of a gardener in Hase. ”
“That’s a really nice place; we rented it through Sugisaki-sensei’s offices, for the rest of the month. ”
“Quite chic. ”
Kumagai said.
“Then you’ll be here for a while? ” Hamada said, and
“But there’s dance in Kamakura too.
Tonight in fact there’s one at the Kaihin Hotel, and if I had a partner I’d like to go. ” “I don’t want to,”
Naomi said bluntly.
“Dance in this heat is forbidden; when it gets cooler again we’ll go out. ”
“That’s so too; dance isn’t a summer thing. ” And Hamada, fidgeting in an odd way:
“Here, what shall we do, Ma-chan—shall we go swim once more? ”
“Not me, I’m tired, let’s go home.
If we go now and rest a bit, it’ll be dark when we get back to Tokyo. ”
“Go now, where? ”
Naomi asked Hamada.
“Is there something interesting? ”
“Why, Seki’s uncle has a villa in Ōgigayatsu.
Today we were all dragged there, he says he’ll treat us, but it’s cramped so we’re thinking of running away without eating. ”
“Is that so?
So cramped? ”
“Cramped isn’t the word; a maid comes out and puts three fingers on the floor, it’s a letdown.
With that even if we’re treated the rice won’t go down the throat.—Eh, Hamada, let’s go home, go home and eat something in Tokyo. ”
And saying so Kumagai did not at once try to stand, but sat down heavily on the beach with his legs stretched, grabbing sand and throwing it on his knees.
“Then how about it, won’t you eat supper with us. You’ve come all this way,—”
Naomi, Hamada, and Kumagai all went silent for a spell, so I felt it would be awkward if I didn’t say so.
That evening we had a lively dinner for the first time in quite a while.
Hamada and Kumagai came, followed by Seki and Nakamura, and the six of us—hosts and guests—sat around a low table in the eight-mat detached room, talking until about ten o’clock.

At first I had disliked the idea of these fellows invading our new lodging, but when I actually met them like this from time to time, I could not help finding their energetic, refreshingly unreserved, boyish natures rather pleasant.
Naomi’s manner was also perfect; she showed an affability that put no one off, without becoming vulgar.
The way she added to the fun and looked after everyone was entirely ideal.
“Tonight was really enjoyable.
It’s not so bad to see those fellows once in a while. ”
Naomi and I had seen them off to the station for the last train and were now walking hand in hand along the summer night road, talking.
The stars were beautiful, and the wind blowing from the sea was cool.
“Oh?
You found it that much fun? ”
Naomi’s tone suggested she was glad my mood was good. After thinking for a moment she said,
“Those fellows aren’t really so bad if you get to know them. ”
“Yes, they’re not bad people at all. ”
“But I wonder if they won’t come bursting in again soon.
Seki said his uncle has a villa here, so from now on he’ll be bringing everyone along pretty often, didn’t he? ”
“Well, even so, I doubt they’ll keep descending on us like that... ”
“It’s all right once in a while, but if they come too often it’ll be a nuisance.
If they show up again, we shouldn’t treat them too kindly.
Don’t give them dinner or anything—just let them go home after a short visit. ”
“But we can’t exactly throw them out... ”
“Of course we can.
I’ll tell them straight out they’re in the way and send them packing. —You think that’s wrong? ”
“Hmm.
Then Kumagai will tease you again. ”
“Let him tease me.
We came all the way to Kamakura, and they’re the ones who come and bother us. —”
We had reached a dark spot beneath the pine trees.
As she spoke, Naomi suddenly stopped.
“Jōji. ”
The sweet, faint, pleading tone of her voice told me everything.
Without a word I took her body into my arms.
I tasted her lips—violent and strong, like swallowing a mouthful of seawater in one gulp—and...
After that, our ten days of holiday passed in the blink of an eye, but we remained as happy as ever.
Just as we had originally planned, I commuted to the office from Kamakura every day.
The group that had said they would “come often” only stopped by once, about a week later, and after that we hardly saw them at all.
Then, toward the end of the month, some urgent research came up and I began returning home late.
Normally I would be back by seven and could have dinner with Naomi, but now I would stay at the office until nine and not reach home until after eleven.
This was supposed to continue for five or six days.
It was on the fourth night of that stretch.
That evening, although I had expected to be kept until nine, the work finished early and I left the office around eight.
As usual I took the train from Ōimachi to Yokohama, changed trains, and reached Kamakura while it was still before ten.

For the past several nights—though in truth it had only been three or four—I had been coming home late, so I was more impatient than usual to get back to the house, see Naomi’s face, relax, and eat dinner at leisure.
From the station I took a rickshaw along the road beside the Imperial Villa.
After working all day in the sweltering summer heat and then being jolted home by train, the night air of the coast felt indescribably soft and refreshing against the skin.

It was not only that night, but this evening in particular a sudden evening shower had passed just at dusk, so from the damp blades of grass and the dew dripping from the pine branches rose a quiet vapor carrying a secret, moist fragrance.

Here and there puddles still shone even in the darkness, but the sandy road had dried enough that it no longer raised dust, and the running feet of the rickshaw man fell lightly, softly, as though treading on velvet.
From behind a hedge somewhere came the sound of a gramophone; occasionally one or two figures in white summer kimonos wandered about.
It truly felt as though we had come to a summer resort.
I dismissed the rickshaw at the gate and walked through the garden toward the veranda of the detached room.

I had expected that as soon as Naomi heard my footsteps she would immediately slide open the shoji and come out, but although the light inside was blazing brightly, there was no sign of her presence and the place was deathly still.
“Naomi dear... ”
I called two or three times, but there was no answer.
I stepped up onto the veranda, opened the shoji, and found the room completely empty.
Bathing suits, towels, and summer kimonos were hanging everywhere—on the walls, the sliding doors, the alcove—and the tea things, ashtrays, and cushions had been left scattered about.
The usual disorder reigned, yet there was a profound, eerie emptiness.
It was not the quiet of a room someone had only just left; with the special intuition of a lover I sensed that she had been gone for a long time.
“She’s gone somewhere...
Probably two or three hours ago... ”
Still, I looked in the toilet, checked the bathroom, and, to be absolutely sure, went down to the kitchen entrance and switched on the light.
What met my eyes were a one-liter bottle of Masamune that someone had evidently drunk heavily from and the remains of a Western-style meal.
That was right—there had been a great many cigarette butts in the ashtray as well.
There was no doubt that the whole gang had descended on the place...
“Landlady, Naomi doesn’t seem to be here.
Has she gone out somewhere? ”
I ran to the main house and asked the wife of the proprietor, Uesō. “Oh, you mean the young lady? —”
The landlady always referred to Naomi as “the young lady.
” Although we were husband and wife, we wanted the world to think of us merely as cohabiting or engaged, and if she were not called that, Naomi would become cross.
“The young lady came back once in the evening, had dinner, and then went out again with everyone. ”
“Everyone? ”
“Well... um... ”
The landlady hesitated a moment, then continued,
“Master Kumagai and the others—all of them together... ”
I found it strange that the landlady not only knew Kumagai’s name but even called him “Master Kumagai,” yet I had no time to inquire about that now.
“When you say she came back once in the evening, does that mean she was with them during the day as well? ”
“She went swimming alone after noon, and then came back with Master Kumagai... ”
“Just the two of them? ”

In fact, at that point I was not yet particularly alarmed, but the landlady’s words seemed increasingly difficult for her to utter, and the look of distress on her face grew stronger and stronger, gradually filling me with unease.
Though I hated the thought of letting this woman see my feelings, my voice could not help becoming urgent.
“So you’re saying it wasn’t a large group? ”
“Yes, at that time it was just the two of them.
They said there was dancing at the hotel during the day and went out... ”
“And then? ”
“Then in the evening they all came back together. ”
“Did they all have dinner here? ”
“Yes...
It was quite lively... ”
So saying, the landlady studied my expression and gave an awkward smile.
“About what time did they go out again after dinner? ”
“Let me see...
I believe it was around eight o’clock... ”
“Then it’s already been two hours. ”
The words slipped out before I could stop them.
“I wonder if they’re at the hotel.
Haven’t you heard anything, landlady? ”
“I don’t know the details, but perhaps they went to the villa... ”
Now that she mentioned it, I remembered that Seki’s uncle’s villa was in Ōgigaoka.
“Ah, so they went to the villa.
In that case I’ll go and fetch her.
Do you happen to know where it is? ”
“It’s right nearby, on the beach at Hase... ”
“Hase?
I was sure I had heard it was in Ōgigaoka...
What I mean is, I don’t know whether they came here tonight or not, but I’m talking about the villa belonging to the uncle of a man named Seki, a friend of Naomi’s... ”
At my words, a faint look of surprise flashed across the landlady’s face.
“Is it a different villa, then...? ”
“Whose villa is the one on the Hase beach? ”
“Well... it belongs to a relative of the Kumagai family... ”
“Of Kumagai...? ”
I suddenly turned deathly pale.
“Go straight down the Hase road from the station, turn left, and continue past the beach hotel.
The road naturally leads to the shore.
The Ōkubo villa at the corner where it ends is the one belonging to Master Kumagai’s relatives—that was what the landlady told me.
It was completely new to me.
Neither Naomi nor Kumagai had ever breathed a word of it.
“Does Naomi go to that villa often? ”
“Well...
I’m not sure... ”
Even so, I did not miss the landlady’s nervous, evasive manner.
“But of course tonight is not the first time, is it? ”
My breathing had grown rapid of its own accord; I could not stop my voice from trembling.
Perhaps frightened by my intensity, the landlady’s face also went white.
“Don’t worry, I won’t cause you any trouble.
Just tell me plainly.
What about last night?
Did she go out last night too? ”
“Yes...
It seems she went out last night as well... ”
“And the night before that? ”
“Yes. ”
“She went out then too? ”
“Yes. ”
“And the night before that? ”
“Yes, that night as well... ”
“Ever since I started coming home late, she’s gone out every single night? ”
“Yes...
I don’t remember every single night clearly, but... ”
“And what time does she usually come back? ”
“Usually... a little before eleven... ”
So from the very beginning the two of them had been deceiving me!
That was why Naomi had wanted to come to Kamakura!
My head began to spin like a whirlwind, and my memory at tremendous speed projected every single word and action of Naomi’s over the past days onto the bottom of my mind.
In an instant the entire mechanism surrounding me was laid bare with astonishing clarity.

There were lies upon lies—twofold, threefold—carefully arranged conspiracies of a kind my simple mind could never have imagined, and so complicated that I could not guess how many people were involved in the plot.

I felt as though I had been hurled from a flat, safe surface into a deep pit, and from the bottom of the hole I was watching Naomi, Kumagai, Hamada, Seki, and countless other shadows passing high above, laughing noisily, with envious eyes.
“Landlady, I’m going out now.
If she comes back before I do, please don’t tell her I’ve returned.
I have something in mind. ”
With that I dashed out the front door.
I came out in front of the beach hotel and followed the road I had been told, keeping as much as possible to the shadows.
It was a quiet street lined on both sides with large villas; at night there were few passersby and it was conveniently dark.
Beneath the light of a gate lamp I took out my watch.
It had only just turned ten.
I wanted to catch them in the act—whether Naomi was alone with Kumagai in the Ōkubo villa or whether the whole usual crowd was carousing there.
If possible I would secretly gather evidence without their noticing, then later test what barefaced lies they would tell me.
I would corner them so they could not escape and give them a thorough thrashing.
With these thoughts I quickened my pace.
I found the house at once.
For a while I walked back and forth in front of it, observing its appearance.
Inside the handsome stone gate was a thick grove of planted trees; a gravel path wound through them toward a deeply recessed entrance.

The aged lettering on the plaque reading “Ōkubo Villa,” the moss-covered stone wall enclosing the spacious garden—everything gave the impression not so much of a summer villa as of an old, long-established residence.
The more I thought about it, the more astonishing it seemed that Kumagai should have relatives who owned such a grand estate here.
I slipped inside the gate, taking care not to let my feet crunch on the gravel.

Because the trees were so dense, I could not make out the main house clearly from the street, but when I drew closer I saw something strange: both the front and rear entrances, the upstairs and downstairs—every room visible from outside was utterly silent, the doors closed and the lights out.
“Hmm.
Maybe Kumagai’s room is around back. ”
Thinking this, I crept along the side of the main building toward the rear, muffling my footsteps.
Sure enough, a light was on in one upstairs room and at the kitchen entrance below it.
It took only a single glance to know that the upstairs room was Kumagai’s.
On the veranda his familiar flat mandolin was leaning against the railing, and inside the room a Tuscan fedora I definitely recognized hung on a pillar.
Yet although the shoji stood wide open, not a single voice could be heard; it was obvious no one was there at present.
—Come to think of it, the shoji at the kitchen entrance was also wide open, as though someone had just gone out.
My attention was drawn along the faint light spilling from the kitchen onto the ground, and I discovered an old back gate only a few yards away.

It had no doors, only two ancient wooden posts; through the gap between them I could see the waves breaking on Yuigahama as sharp white lines in the darkness, and a strong smell of the sea came rushing toward me.
“They must have gone out this way. ”
The moment I stepped through the back gate onto the beach, I heard, almost simultaneously, Naomi’s unmistakable voice very close by.
It had probably not reached me earlier because of the wind.
“Wait!
Sand’s gotten into my shoes and I can’t walk.
Won’t somebody get it out for me?...
Ma-chan, take my shoes off! ”
“No way.
I’m not your slave. ”
“If you say that, I won’t pet you anymore...
Hamada’s so kind, though...
Thank you, thank you.
Hamada’s the only one for me—I like Hamada best. ”
“Damn it!
Don’t take advantage of me just because I’m nice. ”
“Ah-ha-ha-ha-ha!
Stop it, Hamada!
Don’t tickle the soles of my feet like that! ”
“I’m not tickling.
There’s sand stuck all over them, so I’m brushing it off. ”
“If you lick it while you’re at it, you’ll become Papa. ”
That was Seki.
Immediately afterward came a burst of laughter from four or five men.
Just where I stood, the sand dune sloped gently downward, and there was a reed-mat tea stall.
The voices were coming from inside that little hut.
The distance between me and the stall was no more than five yards.
Still wearing the dark alpaca suit I had worn to the office, I turned up my collar, buttoned the jacket all the way so my collar and shirt would not stand out, and hid my straw hat under my arm.
Bending low, almost crawling, I darted quickly into the shadow of the well beside the rear of the hut. At that very moment they said,
“All right, that’s enough. Let’s go over that way now,”
and Naomi, taking the lead, came trooping out with the rest.
They did not notice me.
From in front of the stall they headed down toward the water’s edge.
Hamada, Kumagai, Seki, and Nakamura—four men in loose summer kimonos.
In their midst was Naomi; I could see she was wearing a black mantle and high-heeled shoes.
Since she had not brought a mantle or such shoes with her to the Kamakura house, they must have been borrowed from someone.
The wind kept threatening to blow the hem of the mantle open; she seemed to be wrapping it tightly around her body with both hands from inside.
Each time she took a step, her large buttocks moved round and full beneath the cloth.
She walked with the unsteady gait of a drunkard, deliberately staggering so that her shoulders bumped against the men on either side of her.
Until then I had remained perfectly still, holding my breath.
When they had moved about half a block away and the white kimonos were only faintly visible in the distance, I finally stood up and began to follow them stealthily.
At first it seemed they were walking straight along the shore toward Katase, but midway they gradually turned left, crossed the sand hill, and headed toward the town.
Once their figures had disappeared behind the dune, I suddenly broke into a full run up the slope.
I knew that the path they had taken led into a dark villa district thick with pine trees—perfect cover for hiding.
If I stayed among those trees I could get much closer without fear of being discovered.
The moment I came down the other side, their cheerful singing struck my ears.
No wonder—they were only five or six steps ahead, marching in chorus and keeping time.
Just before the battle, mother, I am thinking most of you......
It was the song Naomi always sang.
Kumagai walked in front, waving his hands as though conducting.
Naomi continued to stagger from side to side, bumping her shoulders against the others.
The men she bumped into also swayed from one side to the other as though rowing a boat.
“Heave-ho!
Heave-ho!...
Heave-ho!
Heave-ho! ”
“Hey!
What are you doing?
If you push that hard I’ll crash into the wall! ”
There was a rattling sound as though someone had struck a fence with a stick.
Naomi shrieked with laughter.
“Now let’s do ‘Honey, Wah, Wiki, Wiki’! ”
“All right!
That’s the Hawaiian butt-shaking dance.
Everybody shake your ass while you sing! ”
Honey, wah, wiki, wiki!
Sweet brown maiden said to me......
And all at once they began shaking their buttocks.
“Ah-ha-ha-ha!
Seki’s the best at shaking his ass. ”
“Of course I am.
I’ve studied it quite seriously, you know. ”
“Where? ”
“At the Peace Exhibition in Ueno.
You know, the International Pavilion where the natives were dancing?
I went there for ten days straight. ”
“You’re an idiot. ”
“You should have gone on display in the International Pavilion yourself.
With your face they’d have mistaken you for one of the natives for sure. ”
“Hey, Ma-chan, what time is it now? ”
That was Hamada.
Since he did not drink, he seemed the most sober.
“Hmm, what time could it be?
Anybody got a watch? ” “Yeah, I do—”
Nakamura struck a match.
“Wow, it’s already twenty past ten. ”
“It’s fine.
Papa won’t be back before eleven-thirty.
Why don’t we walk all the way around the Hase main street before going home?
I want to stroll through the lively parts dressed like this. ”
“Agreed, agreed! ”
Seki shouted in a loud voice.
“But with this wind, what on earth do I look like? ”
“Like a lady general, no matter how you look at it. ”
“If I’m the lady general, then you’re all my troops. ”
“Aren’t we the four white-wave men? ”
“Then I’m Benten Kozō. ”
“Behold!
Lady General Kawai Naomi... ”
Kumagai spoke in the exaggerated tones of a movie narrator.
“...cloaked in a black mantle under cover of darkness... ”
“Ufu-fu-fu, stop it!
Don’t use that vulgar voice! ”
“...leading four scoundrels from the shore of Yuigahama... ”
“Stop it, Ma-chan!
If you don’t stop I’ll—! ”
Naomi slapped Kumagai’s cheek with her open hand.
That vulgar voice is my natural voice.
It’s one of the great regrets of my life that I never became a naniwa-bushi singer. ”
“But Mary Pickford never became a lady general. ”
“Then who?
Priscilla Dean? ”
“Yeah, that’s it—Priscilla Dean. ” “La la la la—”
Just as Hamada began singing the dance music again and started dancing, I saw him about to turn around while doing a step.
I quickly hid behind a tree, but at the same moment Hamada cried, “Hey! ”
“Who’s that—?
Isn’t that Mr. Kawai? ”
Everyone suddenly fell silent, stopped walking, and turned to peer through the darkness in my direction.
I thought, “Damn,” but it was too late.
“Papa?
Is that you, Papa?
What are you doing over there?
Come and join us. ”
Naomi came striding straight up to me, flung her mantle open, and threw her arms around my shoulders.
Beneath the mantle she was wearing not a single stitch of clothing.
“What the hell are you doing!
You’ve humiliated me!
You whore!
Slut!
Bitch! ”
“Oh-ho-ho-ho. ”
Her laughter reeked of liquor.
Until that moment I had never once seen her drink alcohol.
It was only after two full days and nights of questioning that I was finally able to drag the truth out of Naomi’s stubborn mouth and learn how she had been deceiving me.
Just as I had suspected, the reason she had wanted to come to Kamakura was so that she could play with Kumagai.
The story about having relatives in Ōgigaoka was a complete lie; the villa in Hase that belonged to the Ōkubo family was actually Kumagai’s uncle’s house.
And that was not all.
Even the detached room I was now renting had been arranged through Kumagai.
The nurseryman who owned the property did regular work for the Ōkubos, so Kumagai had pressured him, made some sort of deal, and had the previous tenant moved out so that we could move in.
Needless to say, this had all been planned between Naomi and Kumagai.
The tale about Miss Sugizaki’s introduction and the director of Oriental Petroleum had been nothing but one of Naomi’s wild fabrications.
No wonder she had taken charge of everything so briskly.

According to the nurseryman’s wife, when Naomi first came to inspect the place she had arrived together with Kumagai’s “young master,” behaved exactly as though she were a member of his family, and had already been introduced in that light.
The owners had therefore felt they had no choice but to turn away their previous guest and open the room for us.
“Madam, I’m terribly sorry to involve you in such an awkward matter, but would you please tell me everything you know?
I promise I will never mention your name.
I have no intention of going to Kumagai to confront him.
I only want to know the facts. ”
The next day I stayed home from the office for the first time in years.
I kept Naomi under strict surveillance, ordering her not to set foot outside the room, gathered up all her clothes, shoes, and purse, and carried them over to the main house.
There, in one of the rooms, I questioned the wife.
“So the two of them have been coming and going the whole time I was away? ”
“Yes, almost every day.
Sometimes the young master would come here, sometimes the young lady would go over there... ”
“Who exactly is staying at the Ōkubo villa? ”
“The family has gone back to their main residence this year.
They come occasionally, but it’s almost always just the young master, Mr. Kumagai, by himself. ”
“And what about Kumagai’s friends?
Did those fellows come often too? ”
“Yes, quite frequently. ”
“Would Kumagai bring them, or did they come on their own? ”
“Well... ”
Here the wife looked extremely uncomfortable.
(I only realized the significance of this later.)
Sometimes they came alone, sometimes with the young master.
It varied... ”
“Besides Kumagai, did any of the others ever come by themselves? ”
“I believe Mr. Hamada and some of the others did come alone at times... ”
“And on those occasions, would she take them out somewhere? ”
“No, they usually just talked inside. ”
This was the one thing I found completely incomprehensible.
If Naomi and Kumagai were involved with each other, why would she drag in people who would only get in the way?
Why would one of them visit and then sit talking with her?
If they were all after Naomi, why didn’t any fights break out?
The night before, the four men had been joking around together in perfect harmony.
The more I thought about it, the less sense it made, until I even began to doubt whether Naomi and Kumagai were actually involved at all.
On this point, however, Naomi refused to talk easily.
She stubbornly insisted that she had no deep scheme; she had simply wanted to make noise with a large group of friends.
When I asked why she had gone to such treacherous lengths to deceive me, she answered:
“Because Papa always suspects those people and worries about pointless things. ”
“Then why did you say there was a villa belonging to relatives of Seki?
What’s the difference between Seki and Kumagai? ”
At that, Naomi was suddenly at a loss for words.
She dropped her gaze, bit her lip, and glared up at me through her lashes with eyes that seemed ready to bore holes in my face.
“But Ma-chan was the one you suspected most...
I thought it would be a little safer to keep it as Seki for now. ”
“Stop calling him Ma-chan!
His name is Kumagai! ”
I had been holding myself back, but at that moment I finally exploded.
The sound of her calling him “Ma-chan” made my skin crawl.
“Look here!
You’ve been involved with Kumagai, haven’t you?
Tell me the truth! ”
“I haven’t been involved with anyone.
If you suspect me so much, do you have any proof? ”
“I don’t need proof.
I know. ”
“How?
How could you possibly know? ”
Naomi’s attitude was frighteningly calm.
A hateful little smirk even played about her lips.
“What about the way you behaved last night?
After carrying on like that, do you still expect me to believe you’re innocent? ”
“They all forced me to drink until I was drunk and then made me look like that.
I only walked around outside for a while. ”
“All right.
So you’re claiming to be completely innocent? ”
“Yes, I am. ”
“You swear to that? ”
“Yes, I swear. ”
“Fine.
Don’t forget that one word.
Because I no longer believe a single thing you say. ”
After that I stopped speaking to her altogether.

Fearing she might send a message to Kumagai, I confiscated all her writing paper, envelopes, ink, pencils, fountain pen, postage stamps—everything—and left it with the nurseryman’s wife along with her luggage.
So that she could not go out while I was away, I left her with nothing but a single red crêpe de Chine gown.
On the morning of the third day I pretended to leave for the office and departed Kamakura, but I spent the entire train ride thinking about how I might obtain proof.
In the end I decided to go first to the house in Ōmori, which had been empty for nearly a month.
If she really was involved with Kumagai, it could not have begun only that summer.
If I searched Naomi’s belongings at Ōmori, perhaps I would find letters or something.
Because I left later than usual that day, it was already around ten o’clock when I reached the house in Ōmori.
I climbed the front porch, opened the door with my key, crossed the atelier, and climbed the stairs to the attic to examine her room.
The moment I opened the door and stepped inside, I let out an involuntary “Ah!
” and stood frozen, unable to utter another word.
There, lying alone on the floor, was Hamada.
When he saw me enter, Hamada’s face suddenly flushed crimson.
He sat up.
For a while the two of us simply stared at each other, each trying to read the other’s mind.
“Hamada... what are you doing in a place like this? ”
Hamada moved his mouth as though about to speak, but in the end he remained silent, hanging his head before me as if begging for mercy.
“Well?
Hamada... since when have you been here? ”
“I just arrived... just a moment ago. ”
This time he spoke clearly, as though he had resolved that there was no longer any way to escape.
“But the house was locked.
How did you get in? ”
“Through the back door... ”
“The back door should have been locked too... ”
“Yes...
I have a key. ”
Hamada’s voice was so faint it was barely audible.
“A key?
How did you get one? ”
“Naomi gave it to me...
Now that I’ve said that, I imagine you can more or less guess why I’m here... ”
Hamada quietly raised his face and looked straight into my stunned eyes with a steady, almost dazzled gaze.
