In that expression there was an honest, boyish dignity that appeared only when he was cornered; he was no longer the delinquent youth I had known.
“Mr.
Kawai, I can imagine why you have come here so suddenly today.
I have been deceiving you.
Whatever punishment you choose to give me, I am prepared to accept it.
It may sound strange to say this now, but I have been wanting for a long time to confess my sin to you before you discovered me like this... ”
As he spoke, Hamada’s eyes filled with tears that began to spill down his cheeks.
Everything was completely outside my expectations.
I remained silent, blinking rapidly as I watched the scene before me.
Even if I accepted his confession at face value, there were still countless things I could not understand.
“Mr.
Kawai, won’t you please forgive me...? ”
“But Hamada, I still don’t understand.
You received a key from Naomi—what exactly were you doing here? ”
“I was...
I had arranged to meet Naomi here today. ”
“What?
You had arranged to meet Naomi here? ”
“Yes... and not only today.
We have met here many times before... ”
As I pressed him further, he told me that since we had moved to Kamakura the two of them had met secretly in this house three times.
Naomi would leave after I had gone to the office, taking a train one or two departures later, and come to Ōmori.
She usually arrived around ten in the morning and left by eleven-thirty, so she would be back in Kamakura by one o’clock at the latest.
The people at the inn never suspected she had gone all the way to Ōmori in that interval.
That morning, too, they had arranged to meet at ten, so when he heard someone coming up the stairs he had assumed it was Naomi.
Faced with this astonishing confession, the first thing that filled my breast was simply a feeling of utter bewilderment.
My mouth hung open and would not close.
It was beyond words; that was exactly how I felt.
Let me note here that I was thirty-two at the time and Naomi was nineteen.
That a girl of nineteen could deceive me so boldly, so cunningly!
Even now—yes, even at this moment—I could hardly believe that Naomi was such a terrifying creature.
“Since when exactly have you and Naomi been in that kind of relationship? ”
Setting aside the question of whether or not to forgive Hamada, I burned with the desire to dig up every last detail of the truth.
“It began quite a while ago.
Probably before you even knew me... ”
“Wasn’t there a time I first met you?
Last autumn, I think.
I came home from the office and found you and Naomi talking together by the flowerbed? ”
“Yes, that was it.
It’s been almost exactly a year now... ”
“So it started around then? ”
“No, even earlier than that.
I began taking piano lessons at Miss Sugizaki’s in March of last year, and that’s where I first met Naomi.
Not long afterward—about three months later—”
“Where did you meet at that time? ”
“Here, at your house in Ōmori.
Naomi said she had no lessons in the mornings, that she was lonely by herself, and asked me to come and keep her company.
At first I came with that intention. ”
“Hmm.
So it was Naomi who invited you to come and play? ”
“Yes, that’s right.
And I had no idea at all that there was someone like you.
Since my own home is in the country, she told me she was staying with relatives in Ōmori and that you were her cousin.
I only learned the truth when you first came to the El Dorado dance.
But by then...
I was already unable to do anything about it. ”
“Wasn’t the reason Naomi wanted to go to Kamakura this summer the result of discussions with you? ”
“No, that wasn’t me.
The one who urged Naomi to go to Kamakura was Kumagai. ”
Hamada spoke these words with sudden force.
“Mr.
Kawai, you are not the only one who was deceived!
I was deceived too! ”
So Naomi is also involved with Kumagai? ”
“Yes.
Right now the man who has the most control over Naomi is Kumagai.
I had vaguely sensed for some time that Naomi liked him.
But even though she was involved with me, I never dreamed she was also involved with Kumagai.
Naomi kept saying that she simply liked to make innocent noise with her male friends and that there was nothing more to it, so I thought, well, perhaps that’s true... ”
“Ah,” I sighed.
“That’s one of Naomi’s tricks.
I believed it because she told me the same thing...
So when did you discover that she was involved with Kumagai? ”
“It was the night we all slept together here when it rained.
That night I realized...
I truly felt sorry for you that night.
The brazen way the two of them behaved made it clear they were not merely friends.
The more jealous I became, the more I could understand how you must have felt. ”
“So when you say you realized it that night, you mean you only inferred it from their behavior? ”
“No, it wasn’t only that.
There was concrete proof.
Early the next morning, while you were still asleep, I couldn’t sleep myself.
I watched them kissing while I pretended to be dozing. ”
“Does Naomi know that you saw them? ”
“Yes, she knows.
I spoke to her about it afterward and told her she absolutely had to break with Kumagai.
I said I refused to be toyed with.
Now that things had come to this, I wanted to marry her... ”
“Marry her...? ”
“Yes.
I intended to confess everything to you and ask you to give Naomi to me as my wife.
Naomi said that since you were a reasonable man, if we told you how painful it was for us you would surely consent.
I don’t know whether it’s true, but according to Naomi you had only taken her in to give her an education.
Although you lived together, there had never been any promise that you would become husband and wife.
Besides, there was such a big difference in age that even if you did marry it was doubtful whether you could be happy... ”
“She said that?
Naomi said those things? ”
“Yes, she did.
She promised me again and again that she would speak to you soon and arrange for us to marry, and that I should wait just a little longer.
She also said she would break with Kumagai.
But it was all lies.
From the very beginning Naomi had never had the slightest intention of marrying me. ”
“Then has she made the same sort of promise to Kumagai? ”
“I don’t know about that.
I doubt it.
Naomi is the sort who quickly grows tired of things, and Kumagai isn’t serious either.
That fellow is far more cunning than I am... ”
Strange as it may seem, from the very first I had felt no hatred toward Hamada.
Listening to him talk like this, I was overcome instead by a sense of shared suffering—of one sick man pitying another.
And the more I felt that, the more I came to hate Kumagai.
I felt strongly that Kumagai was the common enemy of us both.
“Hamada, at any rate we can’t talk properly here.
Let’s go somewhere and have a meal while we talk.
There are still so many things I want to ask you. ”
I led him out of the house.
Since a Western-style restaurant would have been awkward, I took him to Matsuasa, a Japanese restaurant on the Ōmori shore.
“So you stayed home from the office today as well, Mr. Kawai? ”
Hamada’s tone was no longer agitated; he spoke with the relieved, open manner of someone who has set down a heavy burden.
As we walked he asked me this in a friendly way.
“Yes.
I stayed home yesterday too.
The office has been unusually busy lately, so I really shouldn’t be absent, but ever since the day before yesterday my mind has been in such turmoil that I simply can’t concentrate on work... ”
“Does Naomi know that you’re coming to Ōmori today? ”
“I stayed in all day yesterday, but this morning I told her I was going to the office.
Knowing her, she may have suspected something, but I doubt she thinks I’ve come to Ōmori.
I thought that if I searched her room I might find love letters or something, so I decided to stop by on the spur of the moment. ”
“I see.
I thought you had come to catch me.
If that’s the case, won’t Naomi come here afterward? ”
“No, it’s all right.
While I was away I took away all her clothes and her purse so she can’t step outside.
Dressed like that she can’t even go as far as the gate. ”
“What is she wearing? ”
“You remember that pink crêpe de Chine gown, don’t you? ”
“Ah, that one. ”
“She has only that one garment on, with nothing but a thin sash.
She’s quite safe.
It’s like a wild beast locked in a cage. ”
“Still, what would have happened if Naomi had walked in while we were there?
There would have been a real uproar. ”
“By the way, when exactly did Naomi arrange to meet you here today? ”
“It was the day before yesterday—the night you caught us.
I was sulking that night, so perhaps she was trying to humor me when she told me to come to Ōmori the day after tomorrow.
Of course I’m at fault too.
The proper thing would have been either to break with Naomi or to quarrel with Kumagai, but I couldn’t do either.
Even though I knew how spineless I was being, I was too weak and kept drifting along with them.
So although I say I was deceived by Naomi, in the end it was because I was a fool. ”
I felt as though he were talking about me.
When we were shown into a room at Matsuasa and sat facing each other, I began, strangely enough, to find the young man almost endearing.
“Well, Hamada, I feel much better now that you’ve told me the truth so honestly.
At any rate, shall we have a drink? ”
So saying, I offered him a cup.
“Then you’ll forgive me, Mr. Kawai? ”
“There’s no question of forgiving or not forgiving.
You were deceived by Naomi and had no idea about the relationship between her and me, so you’re not to blame at all.
I don’t hold anything against you anymore. ”
“Thank you.
If you say that, I can feel at ease. ”
Yet Hamada still seemed uncomfortable.
Even when I urged him to drink, he would not touch the cup.
He kept his eyes downcast, speaking haltingly and with reserve.
“Then, if you’ll pardon my asking, are you and Miss Naomi not actually related in any way? ”
After a pause, Hamada seemed to have gathered his resolve and asked this with a faint sigh.
“No, we’re not related at all.
I was born in Utsunomiya, but she’s a true-born Edo child—her family still lives in Tokyo.
She wanted to go to school, but family circumstances prevented it.
I felt sorry for her and took her in when she was fifteen. ”
“And now you’re married? ”
“Yes, that’s right.
We obtained permission from both sets of parents and followed all the proper procedures.
However, she was only sixteen at the time, far too young to be treated as a proper ‘wife,’ and I thought she herself would dislike it.
So we agreed to live together as friends for the time being. ”
“I see.
That was the source of the misunderstanding.
From the way Miss Naomi behaved, she didn’t seem like a wife at all, and she never said she was, so we were completely taken in. ”
“Naomi is at fault, but I bear responsibility too.
I’ve never liked the conventional idea of a ‘married couple,’ and I made it my principle to live as unlike a married couple as possible.
That turned out to be a terrible mistake, so from now on I intend to change.
Really, I’ve learned my lesson. ”
“That would be best.
And Mr. Kawai—this may sound strange coming from me after what I’ve done—but you should be careful with Kumagai.
He’s a bad sort.
I’m not saying this out of personal resentment.
Whether it’s Kumagai, Seki, or Nakamura, they’re all bad characters.
Miss Naomi herself isn’t such a bad person.
It’s those fellows who have corrupted her... ”
As Hamada spoke in a voice filled with emotion, tears once again glistened in his eyes.
So this young man had been in love with Naomi with such earnestness.
The thought made me feel both grateful and ashamed.
Had I not told him that she and I were already fully husband and wife, he would probably have offered to take her from me.
No—in fact, even now, if I were to give her up, he would immediately say he would take her in.
The passionate, almost touching fervor that overflowed from between his brows left no doubt of his resolve.
“Hamada, I’ll follow your advice and settle things one way or another within the next two or three days.
If Naomi truly breaks with Kumagai, all the better.
If not, I couldn’t bear to stay with her another day, so... ”
“But please—please don’t abandon Miss Naomi,” Hamada interrupted me urgently.
“If you were to cast her aside, she would surely fall into ruin.
None of this is her fault... ”
“Thank you.
Truly, thank you!
I can’t tell you how much your kindness means to me.
After all, I’ve looked after her since she was fifteen.
No matter what the world may say, I have no intention of abandoning her.
It’s just that she’s so stubborn—I’m only worried about finding a way to make her cleanly break with those bad friends of hers. ”
“Miss Naomi can be terribly obstinate.
Once she flies into a rage over some trivial thing, there’s no going back, so please handle that part carefully.
I know it’s presumptuous of me to say so... ”
I repeated “thank you, thank you” to Hamada countless times.
Had there been no difference in age or social position between us, and had we been closer friends from the start, I might well have taken his hand and wept with him in each other’s arms.
My feelings had at least reached that pitch.
“Please, Hamada, from now on you must come visit us whenever you like.
There’s no need to hold back,” I said as we parted.
“Yes... but I may not be able to come for a while,” Hamada replied, fidgeting slightly and looking down as though he disliked meeting my eyes.
“Why not? ”
“For a while... until I can forget about Miss Naomi... ”
With that, hiding his tears, he put on his hat, said “goodbye,” and walked off from the front of Matsuasa toward Shinagawa without taking the train, trudging along on foot.
After that I went to the office, but of course I could not concentrate on any work.
I wondered what Naomi was doing right about now.
I had left her with nothing but a single nightgown, so she could hardly have gone anywhere.
Yet even as I told myself this, I could not stop worrying.
The truth was that one astonishing revelation had followed another, and the more I realized how thoroughly I had been deceived, the more abnormally sharp and morbid my nerves became.
I began imagining and speculating about every possible scenario, until Naomi herself seemed to possess some supernatural, unfathomable power far beyond my comprehension.
I could never feel at ease, never know what she might be doing at any given moment.
I can’t stay here like this—there’s no telling what might have happened while I’ve been away.
With that thought, I left the office hastily and hurried back to Kamakura.
“Hello, I’m back,” I said the moment I saw the maid standing at the gate.
“Is she in?
Inside the house? ”
“Yes, she appears to be. ”
Relieved, I asked, “Has anyone come to visit? ”
“No, no one. ”
“How is she?
What’s her mood like? ”
I nodded toward the detached room and gave the maid a meaningful look.
Only then did I notice that the sliding doors of the room where Naomi should have been were tightly closed.
The interior behind the glass looked dim and utterly still, as though no one were there.
“Well... she’s been shut up in there all day today... ”
Hmm, so she really has stayed inside the whole day.
But why is it so strangely quiet?
What sort of expression is on her face?
Still somewhat agitated, I quietly stepped up onto the veranda and opened the sliding door of the detached room.
It was already a little past six in the evening.
In the dark corner of the room where the light did not reach, Naomi lay sprawled in an slovenly posture, fast asleep on her back.
She must have rolled this way and that to escape the mosquitoes.
She had wrapped my cravenette coat around her waist, but it only cleverly covered the lower part of her belly.

From the scarlet crepe gown, her pure white arms and legs protruded like the stalks of blanched cabbage, and at such moments they had the unfortunate effect of strangely, seductively stirring my heart.
Without a word I switched on the electric light, quickly changed into a Japanese robe by myself, and deliberately rattled the doors of the closet.
Whether she heard it or not, Naomi’s peaceful breathing continued.
“Hey, aren’t you going to wake up?
It’s already night... ”
For about thirty minutes I had been leaning at my desk pretending to write letters even though I had nothing to do.
Finally losing patience, I called out to her.
It was only after I had shouted two or three times that she gave this reluctant, sleepy reply.
“Hey!
Wake up! ”
She said nothing more and showed no sign of getting up.
“Hey!
What are you doing?
Hey, I said! ”
I stood up and roughly shook her around the hips with my foot.
“Aaah... ”
With that, Naomi first stretched her two supple arms straight up, clenched her small red fists tightly, and, stifling a half-yawn, slowly raised herself.
She glanced at my face for a moment, then immediately turned aside and began furiously scratching the mosquito bites on the tops of her feet, her shins, her back, and elsewhere.
Whether from sleeping too long or from having cried in secret, her eyes were bloodshot, her hair was wildly disheveled like a monster’s, and it hung down over both shoulders.
“Come on, change your clothes.
Don’t stay like that. ”
I went to the main house, fetched the bundle of her clothes, and tossed it in front of her.
Without saying a word, she sullenly put them on.
Then the dinner trays were brought in, and throughout the entire meal neither of us spoke a single word to the other.
During that long, oppressive staring contest, I thought of nothing but how I could make her confess, and whether there was any way to get this stubborn woman to apologize meekly.
Hamada’s warning—that Naomi was obstinate, and that once a quarrel started over some trivial matter it could never be undone—remained in my mind, of course.
He had probably learned that from experience, and I too had had many such occasions.
Above all, I must not anger her; I had to begin the conversation skillfully so that she would not become contrary, so that it would not turn into a fight, and yet so that I would not appear weak.
To interrogate her like a judge would be the most dangerous approach.
“You did such-and-such with Kumagai, didn’t you?
” “And with Hamada too, didn’t you?
” If I pressed her head-on like that, she was not the sort of woman who would meekly say, “Yes, that’s right.
” She would certainly resist.
She would stubbornly insist she knew nothing about it.
Then I would grow impatient and lose my temper.
If that happened, it would be all over.
So arguing back and forth was out of the question.
I decided to abandon any idea of forcing a confession and instead tell her myself what had happened today.
No matter how stubborn she was, she could hardly claim ignorance then.
All right, that’s what I’ll do, I thought, and began:
“Today, around ten in the morning, I stopped by Omori and ran into Hamada. ”
“Hmm. ”
Naomi seemed genuinely startled; she avoided my gaze and answered through her nose.
“Then, as we were talking, it got to be lunchtime, so I invited Hamada to Matsuasa and we ate together—”
From then on Naomi said nothing.
I watched her expression carefully and continued speaking as gently and without sarcasm as I could.
Until I had finished, she kept her head down and listened.
She showed no sign of being flustered; only the color of her cheeks grew slightly pale.
“Because Hamada told me everything, I now know it all without needing to ask you.
So there’s no point in being stubborn.
If you were wrong, just say you were wrong. ...
Well?
Were you in the wrong?
Do you admit it? ”
Naomi did not answer for a long time, and I began to fear the argumentative situation I had dreaded was about to arise.
But I spoke as tenderly as possible.
“Well, Naomi dear?
If you’ll just admit you were wrong, I won’t reproach you for anything that’s already happened.
I’m not asking you to get down on your hands and knees and apologize.
Just promise me there won’t be any more mistakes like this in the future.
All right?
You understand, don’t you?
You’ll say you were wrong, won’t you? ”
At that, Naomi, fortunately, gave a small nod with her chin.
“So you understand?
From now on you won’t go out playing with Kumagai or any of the others, right? ”
“Mm. ”
“You promise?
You’ll keep your word? ”
“Mm. ”
With these “mm”s we somehow reached a compromise that allowed both of us to save face.
That night, Naomi and I chatted in bed as though nothing had happened.
Yet to be perfectly honest, I could not shake the darkness from the bottom of my heart.
This woman is no longer pure.
The thought not only clouded my chest but halved the value of Naomi, who had once been my treasure.
For her value had lain largely in the fact that I myself had raised her, shaped her into such a woman, and alone knew every inch of her body.
In other words, Naomi was to me like a fruit I had cultivated with my own hands.
I had lavished care and labor on that fruit until it ripened into its present splendor.
To taste it was therefore my rightful reward as its cultivator; no one else had any claim to it.
Yet somehow, without my knowing, a stranger had peeled its skin and sunk his teeth into it.
And once soiled, no matter how she begged forgiveness, the damage could never be undone.
Upon the sacred ground of “her skin,” the muddy footprints of two thieves were now stamped forever.
The more I thought about it, the more unbearable the resentment became.
It was not Naomi herself I hated, but the event itself.
“Jōji, forgive me... please. ”
When Naomi saw me crying in silence, she spoke in a tone completely unlike her daytime manner.
Yet I could only nod through my tears.
Though my mouth said, “Yes, I forgive you,” the bitter knowledge that it could never be undone refused to leave me.
Our disastrous summer in Kamakura ended in this wretched way, and before long we returned to our house in Ōmori.
But as I have said, a knot had formed in my heart, and it showed itself in one way or another.
After that, the two of us could no longer get along smoothly.
On the surface we appeared reconciled, yet I had not truly opened my heart to Naomi again.
Even at the office, I remained tormented by thoughts of Kumagai.

So anxious was I about what she might be doing while I was away that I would pretend to leave in the morning only to slip back through the rear entrance, or follow her at a distance on the days she said she was going to her English or music lessons.
Sometimes I would steal glances at letters addressed to her and examine their contents.
The more I behaved like a secret detective, the more Naomi seemed to sneer at my persistence in her heart.
Though we no longer quarreled openly, she began to show a strangely spiteful attitude.
“Hey, Naomi! ”
One evening I shook her body as she lay pretending to sleep with an especially cold expression on her face.
(I should note that by then I had begun to call her simply “Naomi. ”)
“Why are you lying there pretending to be asleep?
Do you hate me that much? ”
“I’m not pretending.
I’m just closing my eyes because I want to sleep. ”
“Then open them.
It’s rude to keep your eyes shut when someone is trying to talk to you. ”
At that, Naomi reluctantly lifted her eyelids a fraction.
The narrow eyes peering at me from beneath her lashes only made her expression seem colder and more cruel.
“Well?
Do you hate me?
If you do, just say so. ”
“Why are you asking me that? ”
“I can more or less tell from the way you’ve been acting.
Lately we may not fight, but in our hearts we’re constantly at each other’s throats.
Are we still husband and wife? ”
“I’m not at your throat.
You’re the one who is. ”
“I think it’s mutual.
Your attitude gives me no peace, so I can’t help looking at you with suspicion... ”
“Hmph. ”
Naomi cut me off with a scornful laugh through her nose.
“Then let me ask you this: is there anything suspicious about the way I behave?
If there is, show me the evidence. ”
“Well, I don’t exactly have evidence, but... ”
“If you have no evidence and still suspect me, isn’t that unreasonable?
You refuse to trust me, you deny me the freedom and rights a wife should have, and then you expect us to act like a married couple?
That’s impossible.
Tell me, Jōji, do you think I don’t know?
I know perfectly well that you read my letters behind my back and follow me around like a detective. ”
“I admit I was wrong.
But because of what happened before, my nerves have become oversensitive.
You have to understand that. ”
“Then what exactly do you want me to do?
Didn’t we promise never to speak of the past again? ”
“I want you to open your heart to me completely so that my nerves can truly be at ease.
I want you to love me. ”
“But for that to happen, you have to trust me first... ”
“All right, I will.
From now on I’ll trust you completely. ”
Here I must confess the wretchedness of a man.
During the day I could hold out, but at night I always surrendered to her.
Or rather, the beast inside me was conquered by her.
The truth was that I still could not bring myself to trust her, yet my animal nature forced me to capitulate blindly, to throw everything away and compromise.
In short, Naomi was no longer a precious treasure or a revered idol to me; she had become nothing more than a whore.
There was no longer any purity of lovers, nor any affection between husband and wife.
All of that had vanished like a dream from the past!
If so, why did I remain obsessed with this unfaithful, soiled woman?
Because I was dragged along by nothing but the physical charm of her body.
This was Naomi’s fall, but at the same time it was my own.
For I had cast aside a man’s honor, fastidiousness, and pure feeling; I had thrown away my past pride and bowed before a whore without feeling the slightest shame.
At times I even worshipped the very form of that contemptible whore as though she were a goddess.
Naomi understood this weakness of mine with merciless clarity.
She had begun to realize that her flesh held an irresistible fascination for men, that once night fell she could defeat any man.
With that awareness, she became strangely cold and unfriendly during the day.
She made it plain that she was merely selling her “womanhood” to the one man who happened to be there, that beyond that she had no interest in him and no connection to him.
She would sit in sullen silence like a stranger on the roadside, and even when I spoke to her she would barely answer.
She replied only when absolutely necessary, with a curt “yes” or “no.
” To me, her behavior could only be seen as a passive form of resistance, an attempt to show the utmost contempt for me.
“Jōji, no matter how cold I am, you have no right to be angry.
Aren’t you simply taking from me what you can get?
And aren’t you satisfied with that?
” When I stood before her I felt as though I were being glared at with exactly those eyes.
And those eyes seemed at times to say quite openly:
“Hmph.
What a disgusting creature.
He’s like a dog, so pathetically greedy.
I’m only putting up with him because I have no choice. ”
Yet such a state could not last forever.
Each of us was probing the other’s heart, continuing a shadowy, underhanded struggle, both secretly prepared for the moment when it would finally explode.
Then one night I said, in a gentler tone than usual:
“Listen, Naomi. ”
“Listen, Naomi, let’s stop this pointless stubbornness.
I don’t know how you feel, but I can’t bear this cold life we’ve been living lately... ”
“Then what do you intend to do about it? ”
“Let’s try once more to become real husband and wife.
The trouble is that both of us have been acting out of spite.
We’ve stopped making any real effort to bring back the happiness we once had. ”
“Even if we make an effort, feelings don’t mend so easily. ”
“That may be true, but I believe there is a way for us to become happy again.
It all depends on whether you’ll agree... ”
“What way? ”
“Won’t you have a child for me?
Won’t you become a mother?
If we have even one child, I’m sure we can become true husband and wife and find real happiness.
Please, won’t you listen to my request? ”
“No.
I won’t. ”
Naomi answered instantly and decisively.
“You told me never to have a child.
You said you wanted me to stay young and girlish forever.
You said the worst thing that could happen between husband and wife was for them to have a child, didn’t you? ”
“There was a time when I thought that way, but... ”
“Then you no longer want to love me the way you used to?
You’re saying it doesn’t matter how old or how ugly I become?
No, that’s it—you simply don’t love me anymore. ”
“You’re misunderstanding me.
I loved you as a friend, but from now on I will love you as my true wife... ”
“And you think the old happiness will come back that way? ”
“It may not be the same as before, but it will be real happiness... ”
“No, no.
That’s not enough for me. ”
With that she shook her head violently before I could finish speaking.
“I want the happiness we had before.
If I can’t have that, I don’t want anything.
That was the promise I came to you under. ”
If Naomi absolutely refused to have a child, I had one more plan available to me.
It was to close up the “Fairy-Tale House” in Ōmori and establish a more serious, conventional household.

In the first place, I had been seduced by the fine-sounding name of the simple life and had chosen to live in this strange, thoroughly impractical painter’s studio, but there was no denying that this house itself had made our life dissolute.
When a young married couple lived in a place like this without even a maid, it was inevitable that each would grow selfish, the simple life would cease to be simple, and laxity would follow.
Therefore, in order to keep watch over Naomi while I was away, I would hire one parlor maid and one cook.
We would move into a purely Japanese-style house suitable for a middle-class gentleman—not one of those so-called “cultural residences”—large enough for a master and mistress and two maids.
I would sell off all the Western furniture we had been using and replace everything with Japanese-style furnishings.
I would also buy Naomi a piano of her own.
That way, for her music lessons I could ask Miss Sugizaki to come to the house, and for English I could have Miss Harrison come to us; naturally this would reduce the number of times Naomi went out.
The plan required a considerable sum of money, but I wrote home about it and resolved not to tell Naomi until everything was arranged.
Alone, I busied myself with house-hunting and estimating the cost of new furniture.
From home came a money order for fifteen hundred yen with a note saying they would send that much for the time being.
I had also asked them to help find maids, and my mother wrote: “There is a very suitable girl for parlor maid—Sentarō’s daughter, who used to work for us.
Her name is O-hana and she is fifteen this year, so you already know her character and can trust her.
I am also looking for a cook, and I will send her up to Tokyo as soon as you decide on a new house. ”
Naomi seemed to have vaguely sensed that I was secretly plotting something, but at first she remained eerily calm, as if to say, “Let’s just see what he does.
” Then, two or three days after the letter from my mother arrived, one night she suddenly said in a coaxing yet strangely mocking, feline voice:
“Say, Jōji, I want some Western clothes.
Won’t you have some made for me? ”
“Western clothes? ”
I was taken aback for a moment and stared at her face so hard I might have bored a hole through it.
“Aha,” I thought, “so she found out about the money order and is testing me. ”
“Come on, it doesn’t have to be Western clothes—Japanese ones are fine too.
I’d like a nice going-out kimono for winter. ”
“I’m not buying you anything like that for the time being. ”
“Why not? ”
“You already have more kimonos than you can wear. ”
“Even if I have plenty, I’m tired of them.
I want something new. ”
“I will no longer permit such extravagance. ”
“Oh?
Then what are you going to use all that money for? ”
So it had come at last! Feigning ignorance, I answered:
“Money?
What money are you talking about? ”
“Jōji, I saw that registered letter that was under the bookcase.
Since you read other people’s letters whenever you feel like it, I thought it was all right for me to do the same—”
This was completely unexpected.
I had assumed Naomi was only guessing that a money order had arrived because of the registered letter; I had never imagined she had actually found and read the letter I had hidden under the bookcase.
But she must have searched everywhere to sniff out my secret.
If she had read it, then she now knew not only the amount of the money order but also my plans to move and to hire maids.
“With all that money, I should think you could at least buy me one kimono. —Remember what you once told me?

‘For your sake I’d be willing to live in the tiniest, most cramped house and endure any inconvenience, and with that money I’d let you live in as much luxury as possible.’ Have you forgotten you said that?
You’re completely different now from the way you were then. ”
“My love for you hasn’t changed.
Only the way I show it has changed. ”
“Then why were you hiding the move from me?
Were you planning to do it by fiat, without consulting me at all? ”
“I intended to talk it over with you once I had found a suitable house, of course... ”
I softened my tone and tried to soothe her.
“Look, Naomi, to tell you the truth, I still want to give you a luxurious life.
Not just luxurious clothes, but a proper house as well.
I want to raise the whole standard of your daily life so that you become a more refined wife.
So there’s really nothing for you to complain about, is there? ”
“Oh, is that so?
Well, thank you ever so much... ”
“If you like, why don’t you come with me tomorrow to look at houses?
Any place with more rooms than this one that you happen to like will be fine. ”
“In that case I want a Western-style house.
I absolutely refuse to live in a Japanese house. ”
While I was still at a loss for an answer, Naomi, with an expression that said “Just as I thought,” spat out the words:
“And for the maids, I’ll ask the people in Asakusa.
I don’t want any country bumpkins from the sticks.
They’ll be maids I have to use. ”
As these quarrels multiplied, the low pressure between us grew steadily thicker.
There were days when we did not speak to each other at all.
The final explosion came two months after we had left Kamakura, in the first part of November, when I discovered irrefutable proof that Naomi was still involved with Kumagai.
There is no need to describe in detail the events leading up to that discovery.
While I had been preoccupied with preparations for the move, I had also, by intuition, come to regard Naomi with suspicion.
I had therefore never relaxed my detective-like vigilance.
As a result, one day I finally caught her and Kumagai on their way back from a brazen rendezvous at the Akebono-tei, a restaurant near our house in Ōmori.
That morning I had grown suspicious because Naomi was making herself up more gaudily than usual.
The moment I left the house I doubled back and hid behind the charcoal sacks in the storage shed at the rear entrance.
(This was why I had been absent from the office so often lately.) Sure enough, around nine o’clock—although it was not a day for her lessons—she came out dressed to the nines.
Instead of heading toward the station, however, she walked briskly in the opposite direction.

I let her get five or six yards ahead, then dashed back into the house, dragged out the cloak and hat I had used in my student days, threw them over my Western clothes, slipped on a pair of clogs with bare feet, and ran out after her.
From a distance I followed her until I saw her enter the Akebono-tei.
About ten minutes later Kumagai arrived.
I waited for them to come out.
They left separately.
This time Kumagai apparently stayed behind; Naomi appeared on the street first, around eleven o’clock.
I had been loitering near the Akebono-tei for nearly an hour and a half.
She walked straight home—the house was more than ten blocks away—without glancing left or right, exactly as she had come.
I gradually quickened my pace, so that the moment she opened the rear door and stepped inside, I followed her in less than five minutes later.
What I saw the instant I entered was Naomi’s eyes—fixed, filled with a kind of ghastly intensity.
She stood there as stiff as a pole, glaring at me sharply.
At her feet lay the hat, overcoat, shoes, and socks I had changed out of that morning, scattered exactly where I had left them.
She must have understood everything at a glance.
Her face, reflecting the bright light of the atelier on that clear autumn morning, was calmly pale, and upon it lay a profound stillness, as though she had resigned herself to everything.
“Get out! ”
I roared so loudly that my own ears rang.
After that single sentence I could say nothing more, and Naomi offered no reply.
The two of us stood like duelists who have drawn their blades and frozen in the chūdan stance, each watching for the slightest opening in the other.
At that moment I truly thought Naomi’s face was beautiful.
I learned that a woman’s face grows more beautiful the more a man hates her.
I understood perfectly the state of mind of Don José when he killed Carmen: the more he hated her, the more beautiful she became, and that was why he killed her.
There stood Naomi, the very incarnation of evil—staring fixedly, not a muscle in her face moving, her bloodless lips pressed tightly together.
Ah, that was the face of a whore, revealing her true nature without the slightest reserve.
“Get out! ”
The moment I shouted it a second time, driven by an indescribable mixture of hatred, terror, and beauty, I seized her by the shoulder and shoved her toward the door.
“Get out!
Now!
Get out, I said! ”
“Forgive me...
Jōji!
From now on I’ll never... ”
Naomi’s expression changed abruptly.
Her voice trembled with pleading, tears welled up in her eyes, and she dropped to her knees, gazing up at me imploringly.
“Jōji, I was wrong—please forgive me!
Forgive me, forgive me... ”
I had never expected her to beg for pardon so easily.
Startled by the unexpected turn, I grew even more furious.
I clenched both fists and struck her repeatedly.
“You beast!
You dog!
You monster!
I have no more use for you!
Get out, I said—get out! ”
Realizing at once that she had miscalculated, Naomi instantly changed her attitude.
She rose smoothly to her feet and said, in a tone exactly like her usual one:
“All right, I’ll go. ”
“Good.
Get out immediately! ”
“Yes, I’m going right now. —May I go upstairs and get some clothes to change into? ”
“You go straight back to your parents’ house and send someone for your things!
I’ll give you everything! ”
“But that would be inconvenient.
There are all sorts of things I need right away... ”
“Do as you like.
But be quick about it or I won’t allow it! ”
Taking her statement that she would move her belongings immediately as a kind of threat, I answered defiantly.

Naomi went upstairs, rummaged noisily through everything, packed an enormous load—baskets, cloth-wrapped bundles, more than she could possibly carry—and called a rickshaw herself to have it all loaded.
“Well then, goodbye.
Thank you for everything all this time. ”
Her parting words as she left were remarkably breezy.
Once her rickshaw had disappeared, I immediately took out my pocket watch, as if following some predetermined plan, and checked the time.
It was exactly 12:36 in the afternoon. .........
Ah, of course.
She had left the Akebono-tei at eleven, then we had that tremendous fight, and in the blink of an eye the situation had completely reversed.
The woman who had been standing here only moments ago was now gone.
All of that had taken merely one hour and thirty-six minutes. .........
People often unconsciously glance at a clock when they are watching a patient draw their final breath or when they experience a major earthquake.
The way I suddenly pulled out my watch was probably something like that.
November whatever, Taisho whatever year, 12:36 p.m.—at this exact moment on this day, I had finally parted from Naomi.
Our relationship might, from this moment onward, be over. .........
“First of all, what a relief!
The heavy burden has been lifted! ”
I had been utterly exhausted by the silent battle that had been going on for so long, so the moment I thought this, I collapsed limply into a chair and sat there in a daze.
My immediate feeling was one of liberation—“Thank God, I’m finally free”—a refreshing sense of release.
This was not only because I was mentally fatigued; my body itself was crying out for rest.
Naomi was like an extremely strong liquor.
I knew it was bad for me if I drank too much, yet every single day I was made to smell its rich aroma and shown a brimming cup, and in the end I could not help but drink.
As I drank, the poison gradually spread through every part of my body.
I felt sluggish, weary, my occiput grew heavy as if filled with lead.
If I stood up suddenly I would feel dizzy and almost fall backward.
I was constantly in a state like a hangover: my stomach felt sick, my memory deteriorated, I lost interest in everything, and I had no energy, like some kind of invalid.
Strange visions of Naomi would float through my head, sometimes rising like belches to make my chest heave.
Her scent, her sweat, her grease constantly filled my nostrils with a heavy, cloying smell.
So the disappearance of Naomi, who was “poison to the eyes,” felt like the rainy season sky suddenly clearing.
Yet, as I said, that was only an instantaneous feeling.
In truth, that refreshing sensation lasted no more than an hour.
No matter how robust my body might be, it could hardly have recovered from such exhaustion in a single hour.
But the moment I sat down in the chair and let out a sigh of relief, what rose in my chest was the memory of Naomi’s face during that fight—an extraordinarily terrifying expression.
It was the face she had worn at that one instant when she said, “The more a man hates me, the more beautiful I become.
” It was the face of a whore so hateful that I could have stabbed her to death and still not been satisfied.
That face had been burned permanently into my brain; no matter how I tried, I could not erase it.
For some reason, as time passed it appeared before my eyes with ever greater clarity.
I felt as though she were still staring fixedly at me, her pupils boring into mine.
And gradually that hatred transformed into a beauty of unfathomable depth.
When I thought about it, I realized I had never once seen her face overflow with such seductive, bewitching expression until today.
There was no doubt it was “the incarnation of evil,” and at the same time it was the form in which every ounce of beauty in her body and soul had been raised to its highest pitch.
Even in the middle of that fight I had been struck by that beauty without realizing it; I had even cried out in my heart, “How beautiful she is.
” So why had I not fallen to my knees at her feet then?
I was usually so weak-willed and spineless—how, no matter how furious I was, had I been able to hurl such abuse at that terrifying goddess and even raise my hand against her?
Where had such reckless courage come from?
Now it all seemed utterly mysterious to me, and a feeling almost like resentment toward my own recklessness and courage began to well up inside me.
“You fool.
You’ve done something terrible.
Do you really think that a little bit of misconduct can be traded for ‘that face’?
A beauty like that will never, ever appear in this world again. ”
I began to feel as though someone were saying this to me.
Yes, that’s right—I had done something truly trivial and stupid.
I had been so careful all this time not to anger her, and yet it had come to this.
It must have been the work of some evil spirit.
Such thoughts rose up in my mind from nowhere.
Only an hour earlier I had found her an unbearable burden and cursed her very existence.
Now I was cursing myself instead and regretting my rashness.
How could the woman I had hated so violently become so dear to me in such a short time?
This sudden reversal in my heart was something I could not explain even to myself; it was a mystery known only to the god of love.
Before I knew it I was on my feet, pacing back and forth across the room, wondering for a long time how I could ever cure this aching longing.
No matter how I thought about it, no cure presented itself.
All I could remember was how beautiful she had been.

Scenes from our five years of living together rose up one after another—ah, at that time she said this, she made that face, she looked at me with those eyes—and every single one of them became fuel for my regret.
What I could not forget above all were the nights when she was fifteen or sixteen and I used to put her in the Western-style bathtub and wash her body.
And the times I became a horse and let her ride on my back, crawling around the room going “Gee-up, whoa there.
” How could such silly things feel so unbearably nostalgic?
It was ridiculous, yet if she were to come back to me even once more, the first thing I would do would be to play those games again.
I would let her straddle my back once more and crawl around this room.
If only I could do that, I would be happier than I could say.
I daydreamed about it as though it were the greatest possible happiness.
No, it was not merely a daydream.
Overcome with longing, I unconsciously dropped to all fours on the floor and crawled around the room as if her weight were pressing down on my back even now.

Then—I am ashamed to write this—I went upstairs, pulled out some of her old clothes, piled several layers on my back, slipped her socks onto both my hands, and crawled around the room on all fours once more.
Readers who have been following this story from the beginning will probably remember that I kept an album entitled “Naomi’s Growth.
” It was a kind of diary in which, during the time I used to bathe her and wash her body, I had recorded in detail how her limbs developed day by day.
In other words, it was a notebook devoted exclusively to the process of Naomi transforming from a girl into a woman.
In various places I had pasted photographs I had taken of her many different expressions and every possible change in her posture at that time.

Recalling those pictures, I dragged the album, which had been lying covered in dust at the bottom of the bookcase, out into the open and turned the pages one by one, hoping they might at least serve as a keepsake.
Those photographs were absolutely not meant to be seen by anyone else, so I had developed and printed them myself.
Most likely the washing had not been thorough enough; now they were covered with freckle-like spots, and some had aged so badly that they looked like ancient, hazy images.
Yet that only increased their nostalgic power.
They felt like memories from ten or twenty years ago, like tracing a distant dream from childhood.
And there, captured almost without omission, were all the strange, light, luxurious, and comical costumes and styles she had loved to wear back then.
On one page was a photograph of her dressed as a man in a velvet suit.
Turning the page revealed her standing like a statue wrapped in thin cotton voile.
The next showed her in a glittering satin haori and kimono, a narrow obi tied high on her chest, with a ribbon half-collar.

Then came countless different expressions and poses imitating movie actresses—Mary Pickford’s smile, Gloria Swanson’s eyes, Pola Negri’s fierce glare, Bebe Daniels’s coquettish airs—furious, smiling, startled, entranced.
With each image her face and body moved differently, showing just how sensitive, skillful, and clever she was in such things.
“Oh, what have I done!
I really have let an extraordinary woman slip away. ”
My mind grew frantic.
In an agony of regret I stamped my feet and kept turning the pages.
Still more photographs appeared, taken with increasing intimacy and detail.

They showed close-ups of every part: the shape of her nose, her eyes, her lips, her fingers, the curve of her arms, her shoulders, her spine, her legs, her wrists, her ankles, her elbows, her knees, even the soles of her feet.
They were treated as reverently as if they were Greek sculptures or Buddhist statues from Nara.
At this point Naomi’s body had become pure art, and to my eyes it seemed more perfect than any statue from Nara.
Gazing at them intently, I even felt something like religious rapture.
Why on earth had I taken such precise photographs?
Had I somehow foreseen that they would one day become sad mementos?
My longing for Naomi accelerated.

The sun had already set; stars were beginning to twinkle outside the window and the air was growing chilly, yet I had not eaten since eleven that morning, had not lit a fire, and lacked even the energy to turn on the lights.
I wandered through the darkening house, going upstairs and downstairs, striking my own head while calling myself an idiot, shouting “Naomi!
Naomi!
” at the walls of the silent, tomb-like atelier, and finally pressing my forehead to the floor while repeating her name over and over.
I had to bring her back no matter what.
I would surrender to her unconditionally.
I would obey everything she said, everything she desired. .........
But what could she be doing right now?
She had been carrying so much luggage; she must have taken a car from Tokyo Station.
In that case, five or six hours must have passed since she reached the house in Asakusa.
Had she told her family honestly why she had been thrown out?
Or, true to her stubborn nature, had she spun some temporary lie, wrapped her sister and brother around her little finger, and was now holding court?
She had always hated being known as the daughter of a family that ran a low-class business in Senzoku-chō.
She treated her parents and siblings like ignorant savages and almost never went home.
What kind of emergency measures were being discussed right now among that mismatched clan?
Her sister and brother would surely tell her to go apologize.
“I’m not going to apologize, not ever.
Someone go get my things for me,” Naomi would say, remaining defiant to the end.

And then, looking as though she were not worried in the least, she would crack jokes, boast, rattle on in a mixture of English, show off her stylish clothes and possessions, and swagger about like a young lady from the nobility visiting a slum. .........
Still, no matter what Naomi said, the matter was serious enough that someone should have come at once.
If she herself refused to apologize, then her sister or brother ought to have come in her place.
Or perhaps none of Naomi’s family felt any real concern for her?
Just as she was cold toward them, they had never felt any responsibility toward her.
“We leave her entirely in your hands,” they had said when they entrusted the fifteen-year-old girl to me, washing their hands of her and leaving her to do as she pleased.
So perhaps they were doing the same thing now, letting her do whatever she wanted and ignoring the whole affair?
Even so, one would think they would at least come to collect her belongings.
I had told them, “Send someone as soon as she gets home and I’ll give you all her things,” yet no one had come.
Why?
She had taken a change of clothes and some daily necessities, but many of her finest outfits—second only to her life itself—were still here.
She could not possibly stay cooped up all day in that dingy house in Senzoku-chō.
She would surely go out every day in flashy clothes that would shock the neighbors.
In that case she would need her wardrobe even more; she could hardly endure without it. .........
Yet that night, no matter how long I waited, no messenger from Naomi arrived.
I had left the lights off until the house was completely dark.

Fearing it might be mistaken for an empty house, I hurriedly turned on every light in every room, checked that the nameplate by the gate had not fallen off, brought a chair to the entrance, and sat listening for footsteps outside for hours.
Eight o’clock became nine, ten, eleven.
A whole day had passed since morning, and still there was no word.
In the depths of despair, all sorts of wild speculations rose in my breast.
The fact that Naomi had not sent anyone might mean she was taking the matter lightly and assumed everything would be settled in a few days.
“It’ll be fine.
He’s crazy about me.
He can’t last a single day without me, so he’s bound to come begging.
” Perhaps she was playing a game of nerves.
She knew perfectly well that after living in luxury for so long she could never survive in that world.
And even if she went to another man, none would cherish her or indulge her whims the way I did.
Naomi understood all that perfectly.
While talking tough, she was secretly waiting for me to come for her.
Or perhaps tomorrow morning her sister or brother would finally come to mediate.
Their business kept them busy at night, so they might only be able to come during the day.
In any case, the fact that no messenger had come still left a thread of hope.
If there was still no word tomorrow, I would go to her myself.
At this point pride and appearances meant nothing.
After all, it was my pride that had caused this mess in the first place.

Even if her family laughed at me, even if she saw right through me, I would go, bow low, beg her sister and brother to put in a good word, and repeat “Please, I beg you for the rest of my life, come back to me” a million times.
Then she could save face and return with her head held high.
I barely slept that night.
The following day I waited until around six in the evening, but when there was still no word I could bear it no longer.
I dashed out of the house and hurried to Asakusa.
I wanted to see her as soon as possible; just seeing her face would be enough to calm me.
That was what “yearning” meant.
In my heart there was nothing but the single wish: to meet her, to see her.
It was probably around seven o’clock when I reached the house in Senzoku-chō, tucked away in a maze of alleys behind Hanayashiki.
Embarrassed, I quietly opened the lattice door and, standing in the dirt-floor entrance, said in a low voice,
“Excuse me.
I’ve come from Ōmori.
Is Naomi here? ”
“Oh, Mr. Kawai. ”
Her sister must have heard me, for she poked her head out from the next room. With a puzzled expression she said,
“Naomi-chan?
No, she hasn’t come here. ”
“That’s strange.
She should have.
She left yesterday saying she was coming here... ”
At first I suspected that my sister-in-law was hiding her at my wife’s request, so I tried every possible way to persuade her.
But as I listened further, it became clear that Naomi had not come here at all.
“That’s strange...
She was carrying a great many things with her.
She couldn’t possibly have gone anywhere else just as she was... ”
“Oh?
She had luggage with her? ”
“Yes—baskets, valises, furoshiki bundles—she took quite a lot.
The truth is, yesterday we had a silly little quarrel, and... ”
“So she herself said she was coming here? ”
“No, not her—I was the one who told her to go.
I said, ‘Go straight back to Asakusa this minute and send someone over.’ I thought that if one of you came, we could talk it over and clear things up. ”
“I see...
Well, in any case, she has not come to us.
If that’s how it is, she may turn up here before long. ”
“But look here, if she left last night, that changes things,” my brother-in-law put in, coming out as we were speaking.
“You’d better try looking somewhere else if you have any idea where she might be.
If she hasn’t come by now, I doubt she’ll come back here. ”
“Besides, Naomi hardly ever shows her face at home anymore.
Let me see, when was the last time...?
It must be two full months since we last saw her. ”
“Then I’m sorry to trouble you, but if she should happen to come, please let me know at once, no matter what she herself says. ”
“Yes, of course.
We have no intention of getting mixed up with that girl again, so if she comes we’ll inform you immediately. ”
I sat down on the raised threshold, sipping the coarse tea they had brought me, utterly at a loss.
Yet faced with a sister and brother-in-law who showed no particular concern even after hearing that their younger sister had run away, there was no point in pouring out my feelings here.
So I repeated my request: should she appear, they must notify me without delay—by telephone to my office during the day.
Lately, however, I had been absent from the office rather often; if I was not there, they should send a telegram at once to Omori.
I would come to fetch her myself, and until then they must on no account let her go anywhere.
I went on repeating these instructions at tedious length.
Still, something about these people’s careless manner made me doubt they could be relied upon, so as an extra precaution I gave them the telephone number of my office.
It also occurred to me that they might not even know the address of the house in Omori, so I wrote it out in detail before I left.
“Well, what am I to do now?
Where on earth has she gone? ”
I was on the verge of tears—perhaps I really was crying—as I emerged from the alley in Senzoku-chō.
With no particular destination in mind, I wandered aimlessly through the park, turning the matter over in my mind.
The fact that she had not returned to her parents’ house made the situation clearly far more serious than I had imagined.
“It must be Kumagai’s place.
She’s run off to him.
” Once the thought struck me, I remembered how, when she was leaving yesterday, she had said, “But that would be inconvenient—I need all sorts of things right away.
” It made perfect sense.
Of course—that was it.
She had taken so much luggage because she intended to go to Kumagai’s.
Or perhaps the two of them had arranged in advance what to do in such a case.
If that was true, this might prove very difficult indeed.
First of all, I had no idea where Kumagai lived.
Even if I could find out, it was hardly likely that he would be keeping her hidden in his parents’ house.
He might be a delinquent boy, but his parents appeared to be respectable people; they would never allow their son to do anything so improper.
Perhaps he too had run away from home and the pair of them were hiding somewhere together?
Or maybe they had stolen money from his parents and were out carousing?
If only I could know for certain, one way or the other.
Then I could go and speak firmly to Kumagai’s parents and ask them to intervene severely.
Even if the boy refused to listen to them, once their money ran out the two of them could not go on living together.
In the end he would return to his own home and Naomi would come back to me.
That, at least, was how it would surely finish.
But what about all the suffering I would have to endure in the meantime?
Would it be over in a month?
Two months?
Three?
Or might it drag on for half a year?
No—if it came to that, it would be disastrous.
While I was waiting, she might gradually lose any desire to return.
And who could say that a second or even a third man might not appear?
I could not afford to dawdle.
The longer we remained apart, the thinner the thread between us would become.
With every passing moment she was drifting farther away.
Damn it all!
I would not let her escape me!
I would drag her back no matter what!
When one is in trouble, one turns to the gods.
I had never been a religious man, yet at that moment the thought came to me and I went to pray at the Kannon temple.
With all my heart I prayed that Naomi’s whereabouts would be known to me as soon as possible, that she would come back to me tomorrow.
After that I have no clear memory of where I wandered.
I stopped at two or three bars, drank myself into a stupor, and it was past midnight when I finally returned to the house in Omori.
Even in my drunken state, thoughts of Naomi never left my head.
I could not fall asleep, and when the effects of the alcohol wore off I lay there brooding once more.
How could I discover where she was?
Had she really run off with Kumagai?
Before I could confront his parents I would have to be certain of the facts; yet short of hiring a private detective there seemed no way to confirm anything...
After turning the problem over uselessly in my mind for a long while, a name suddenly occurred to me: Hamada.
That was it—there was Hamada.
How could I have forgotten him?
That fellow would surely side with me.
When we parted at the Matsuasa I had taken down his address.
I should write to him first thing tomorrow.
But a letter would be too slow and agonizing—should I send a telegram?
That might seem a bit excessive.
Perhaps he had a telephone; I could ask him to call me.
No, there was no need to have him come.
It would be better to have him make inquiries about Kumagai.
At this moment the most urgent thing was to learn what Kumagai was doing.
Hamada had connections and could bring me a report at once.
Right now, the only person who could understand my distress and rescue me was that young man.
This too, perhaps, was “turning to the gods in time of trouble”...
The next morning I leapt out of bed at seven, ran to the public telephone nearby, and flipped through the directory.
Fortunately Hamada’s house was listed.
“Ah, is that the young master?
I’m afraid he is still asleep... ” When the maid answered, I insisted,
“I’m very sorry to trouble you, but it is an urgent matter.
Could you please call him to the phone? ”
After a while Hamada came to the receiver.
“Is this Mr. Kawai?
From Omori? ”
His voice was still thick with sleep.
“Yes, it’s me—Kawai from Omori.
I’m terribly sorry to have caused you so much trouble the other day, and now to telephone at such an hour is extremely rude, but the fact is—Naomi has run away, and—”
At the words “has run away,” my voice broke into a sob.
It was a bitterly cold morning, almost like winter.
I had rushed out wearing only a night kimono with a single padded robe thrown over it, and as I gripped the receiver my whole body would not stop trembling.
“Ah, Naomi-san...
So it really happened after all. ”
To my surprise, Hamada answered with perfect calm.
“Then you already knew? ”
“I met her last night. ”
“What?
You met Naomi?
You saw her last night? ”
This time a different kind of shudder ran through me; my whole body began to shake violently.
The trembling was so fierce that my front teeth struck the mouthpiece with a sharp click.
“Last night I went to the dance at the Eldorado, and Naomi-san was there.
I didn’t ask her any questions, but her manner seemed strange, so I guessed that something of the sort must have happened. ”
“Who was she with?
Wasn’t she with Kumagai? ”
“It wasn’t only Kumagai.
There were five or six men altogether, and some Westerners among them. ”
“Westerners...? ”
“Yes.
And she was wearing a very fine Western dress. ”
“But when she left the house she didn’t have any Western clothes with her... ”
“Nevertheless, she was wearing one.
And not just any dress—a magnificent evening gown. ”
I stood there stunned, as though fox-possessed, unable to think what I should ask next.
“Ah, hello?
Hello?
What’s the matter, Kawai-san...?
Hello...? ”
I had been silent for so long on the telephone that Hamada finally spoke up to urge me on.
“Ah, hello...?
Hello...? ”
“Is this Kawai-san...? ”
“What’s wrong...? ”
I don’t know what I should do... ”
“But there’s no point in just standing there thinking at the telephone, is there? ”
“I know there’s no point, but...
Hamada, I’m in real trouble.
I’m completely at a loss.
Ever since that woman disappeared, I’ve hardly been able to sleep at night.
I’m suffering terribly... ”
Here I poured all the pathos I could muster into my voice, hoping to win Hamada’s sympathy.
Hamada, at a time like this you’re the only person I can turn to, so I’m afraid I’m imposing on you, but...
I desperately want to know where Naomi is.
Is she with Kumagai, or has she gone to some other man?
I want to get to the bottom of it.
I know this is terribly selfish of me, but could I ask you to use your connections to look into it for me?
I thought that if you investigated rather than me, you might have all sorts of useful leads... ”
“Well, if I look into it, I imagine I could find out fairly quickly,” Hamada answered, sounding as if it were the simplest thing in the world.
“But Kawai-san, don’t you have any idea at all where she might be? ”
“I was absolutely certain she was with Kumagai.
Since it’s you, I’ll tell you the truth: Naomi had still been seeing Kumagai behind my back.
It all came out the other day, we had a terrible fight, and she ran out of the house... ”
“But from what you told me, there were Westerners and all sorts of other men, and she was wearing Western clothes, so now I have no idea what to think.
Still, if you could see Kumagai, I think you’d get a pretty clear picture of the situation... ”
“Right, all right, all right,” Hamada said, cutting short my plaintive rambling.
“I’ll look into it, then. ”
“I’d be very grateful if you could do it as quickly as possible...
If you could let me know the result today, even, it would be an enormous help... ”
“I see.
I should know something by the end of the day.
Where shall I reach you?
Are you still at the Ōimachi office these days? ”
“No, ever since this happened I’ve been taking time off from the company.
I keep thinking that Naomi might come back at any moment, so I’m trying not to leave the house empty.
This is terribly selfish of me, but speaking on the telephone isn’t very convenient...
If I could see you in person it would be much better.
Could you possibly come out to Ōmori once you’ve learned something? ”
“Certainly, that’s fine.
I’m free anyway. ”
“Oh, thank you!
If you’d do that for me, I’d be truly grateful! ”
Once that was settled, the thought of Hamada’s arrival became almost unbearable.
Still sounding frantic, I pressed him further.
“So, about what time do you think you’ll be able to come?
Could you know something by two or three at the latest? ”
“Well, I think I should, but I can’t say anything for certain until I’ve actually gone and asked.
I’ll do my best, but depending on how things go it might take two or three days... ”
“That can’t be helped.
Whether it’s tomorrow or the day after, I’ll stay shut up in the house and wait until you come. ”
“Understood.
I’ll give you the details when I see you.
Well then, goodbye. ”
“Ah, hello?
Hello? ”
Just as the call was about to end, I hurriedly called Hamada back.
“Hello?
Hello...?
Um... and one more thing...

This depends on the circumstances, so it may not matter, but if you should happen to meet Naomi directly and have a chance to speak with her, I’d like you to tell her this: I have no intention of blaming her.
I’ve come to understand that I myself bear a large part of the responsibility for her fall.
I will apologize to her a thousand times for my mistakes, and I will accept any conditions she sets.
Let’s wash away the entire past and have her come back to me.
If she doesn’t want that, then at least let her see me once... ”
After saying I would accept any conditions, what I really wanted to add, with complete honesty, was: “If she tells me to prostrate myself, I will gladly do so.
If she tells me to rub my forehead against the ground, I will rub my forehead against the ground.
I will apologize in any way she demands.
” But even I could not quite bring myself to say that much.
If you can, please tell her how deeply I still feel for her... ”
“I see.
If the opportunity arises, I’ll be sure to tell her that as well. ”
“And also... knowing her personality, even if she wants to come back she may be stubbornly refusing out of pride.
If that seems to be the case, please tell her how utterly crushed I am and, if necessary, bring her here by force.
That would be even better... ”
“Understood, understood.
I can’t promise that much, but I’ll do everything I can. ”
I had been so persistent that Hamada’s voice had begun to sound slightly fed up, yet from the public telephone I kept talking nonstop until the five-sen coin in my purse was gone.
I must have spoken three times in succession.
It was probably the first time in my life I had ever spoken with such desperate eloquence, my voice trembling and tearful, so shamelessly.
Yet once the call ended, far from feeling relieved, I was now unbearably impatient for Hamada to arrive.
He had said “probably by the end of the day,” but what if he didn’t come today?
What would I do then?
No—what would become of me?
At this moment I had no work, no purpose except to long desperately for Naomi.
I could do nothing.
I could neither sleep, nor eat, nor go outside; I could only remain shut up in the house, waiting helplessly for some stranger to run about on my behalf and bring me news.
There is no greater torment than having nothing to do, and on top of that I was dying with longing for Naomi.
To be writhing in that longing while entrusting my fate to another person and staring at the hands of the clock was, when I thought about it, unbearable.
Even a single minute felt astonishingly slow, stretching out into infinity.
Sixty such minutes made one hour, one hundred and twenty made two.
If I had to wait three hours, I would have to endure that unbearable, helpless “single minute” one hundred and eighty times while the second hand ticked around the dial.
And if it became four hours, five hours, half a day, a full day, two days, three days—then surely, I thought, the agony of waiting and the intensity of my longing would drive me mad.
Still, I had resigned myself to the fact that, no matter how quickly things went, Hamada would not arrive until evening.
Yet four hours after the call, around noon, the doorbell at the entrance rang violently, and I heard Hamada’s unexpectedly bright voice call out, “Hello!
” I leapt up without thinking, wild with joy, and hurried to open the door.
“Ah, hello.
I’ll open it right away—the key is in the lock,” I said, my voice trembling with excitement.
At the same time I thought, “I never imagined he’d come so soon.
Perhaps he found Naomi without any trouble, spoke with her, and brought her back with him.
” The mere possibility made fresh joy surge up inside me, and my heart pounded violently.
When I opened the door I glanced quickly around, expecting to see her standing behind him, but there was no one.
Hamada stood alone on the porch.
“Hello.
Sorry about earlier.
Well?
Did you find anything out? ”
I practically pounced on him with the question.
Hamada, strangely calm, looked at me with something like pity in his eyes and said firmly, shaking his head,
“Yes, I found out.
But Kawai-san, that woman is hopeless now.
You’d better give up. ”
“Wh-what do you mean by that? ”
“What I mean is, it’s completely beyond saving.
I’m saying this for your own good—forget all about Naomi. ”
“So you did meet her?
You spoke with her and realized there’s no hope? ”
“No, I didn’t meet Naomi.
I went to see Kumagai and got the whole story from him.
It was so awful I was genuinely shocked. ”
“But Hamada, where is Naomi?
That’s the first thing I want to know. ”
“She doesn’t have any fixed place.
She’s drifting from one house to another. ”
“She can’t possibly have that many places to stay. ”
“Naomi has any number of male friends you don’t know about.
On the day she first fought with you, she apparently went straight to Kumagai’s.
It would have been one thing if she’d phoned ahead and come quietly, but she arrived with all her luggage in a taxi, pulling right up to the front door.
The whole household was in an uproar asking who on earth she was, so they couldn’t very well say ‘Please come in.’ Even Kumagai was at a loss. ”
“Hmm.
And then? ”
“There was nothing else to do, so they hid her luggage in his room and the two of them went out.
They ended up at some dubious inn, and it turns out to be that ‘something-or-other Pavilion’ right near your house in Ōmori—the very place where you caught her that morning.
Can you believe the nerve? ”
“So she went back there that same day? ”
“Yes, that’s what they say.
Kumagai was bragging about it, mixing in all sorts of lascivious details.
It was unpleasant to listen to. ”
“So they spent the night there together? ”
“No, that’s not what happened.
They stayed until evening, then walked around Ginza together and parted at the corner of Owari-chō. ”
“But that’s strange.
Kumagai must be lying... ”
“No, listen.
When they parted, Kumagai felt a little sorry for her and asked, ‘Where are you staying tonight?’ She answered cheerfully, ‘I’ve got plenty of places to stay.
I’m going to Yokohama now,’ and walked off briskly toward Shimbashi without the slightest sign of depression. ”
“Who in Yokohama? ”
“That’s the strange part.
No matter how many acquaintances Naomi has, she couldn’t possibly have a place to stay in Yokohama.
Kumagai figured she must have gone back to Ōmori after all.
The next evening, however, she phoned him: ‘I’m waiting at El Dorado.

Come right away.’ When he went, there was Naomi in a dazzling evening gown, holding a peacock-feather fan, glittering with necklaces and bracelets, surrounded by Westerners and all sorts of other men, laughing and carrying on. ”
Listening to Hamada’s story was like opening a jack-in-the-box; one startling fact after another popped out.
It seemed Naomi had spent that first night with a Westerner.

The man’s name was William McConnell—the very same brazen, powdered, smirking fellow who, the first time I took Naomi to El Dorado, had come up without any introduction and forced her to dance with him.
What was even more astonishing—according to Kumagai’s observation—was that until the night she went to stay with him, Naomi had not been particularly close to this McConnell.
Of course, she had apparently been interested in him for some time.
He had the sort of face women like—clean-cut, rather like an actor.
Among the dance crowd he was known as “the lecherous Westerner,” and Naomi herself had once said, “That Westerner has a nice profile, doesn’t he?
He looks a bit like John Barry.
” (John Barry was the American actor John Barrymore, whom she knew from the movies.) So she had certainly had her eye on him.
She may even have flirted with him once or twice.
McConnell must have noticed and teased her about it.
In any case, she had gone to him with no deeper connection than that.
When she turned up, McConnell must have thought an amusing bird had flown into his cage.
“Won’t you stay at my house tonight?
” “Sure, I don’t mind.
” Something like that must have happened.
“No matter what, I find that hard to believe—going straight to a man she barely knows and spending the night with him... ”
“But Kawai-san, I think Naomi is quite capable of doing exactly that.
Even McConnell seemed a little surprised; he asked Kumagai last night, ‘Just who is this young lady, anyway?’”
“To take in a woman when you don’t even know where she’s from... ”
“Not only that—he bought her Western clothes, gave her bracelets and a necklace.
He’s really going all out.
And after just one night they were completely familiar with each other. Naomi calls him ‘Willie, Willie.’”
“So the clothes and jewelry were bought by him? ”
“Some of them, apparently.
Since he’s a Westerner, he may also have borrowed a friend’s dresses and altered them to fit her in an hour.
It seems she started by saying, ‘I’d like to try on Western clothes,’ acting spoiled, and the man ended up doing everything to please her.
The dress wasn’t off-the-rack; it fit her body perfectly.
The shoes were French heels with very high insteps, and the toes—probably new diamonds or something—were set with tiny jewels that sparkled.
Last night’s Naomi looked exactly like Cinderella from the fairy tale. ”
When Hamada told me this, the image of Naomi as Cinderella flashed before me and, before I knew it, my heart leapt with excitement.
Yet in the very next instant I was stunned by the sheer shamelessness of her behavior.
A miserable, wretched, mortifying feeling came over me, an indescribable disgust.

If it had been Kumagai it would have been bad enough, but to go to the house of some unknown Westerner, stay the night without hesitation, and have clothes made for her—could that really be the conduct of a woman who, only yesterday, had a husband?
Was the Naomi I had lived with for so many years actually such a filthy, whore-like creature?
Had I been blind to her true nature until this very moment, dreaming my foolish dream?
Ah, just as Hamada said, no matter how much I loved her, I would have to give her up.
I had been thoroughly humiliated; my manhood had been dragged through the mud...
“Hamada, I know I’m repeating myself, but I must ask once more: is everything you’ve told me the absolute truth?
Not only does Kumagai confirm it—you confirm it as well? ”
Seeing the tears welling up in my eyes, Hamada nodded with a pitying look.
“When you put it that way, I feel for you and it becomes hard to speak, but I was there myself last night, and I believe what Kumagai said is essentially true.
There are many more things I could tell you that would only make you realize how right I am, but please, for your own sake, don’t ask me to go any further.
Just trust me when I say I am not exaggerating the facts for amusement... ”
“Ah, thank you.
That’s enough.
I don’t need to hear any more... ”
For some reason, at that moment my voice caught in my throat and large tears began to spill down my cheeks.
Thinking “This won’t do,” I suddenly threw my arms around Hamada, buried my face in his shoulder, and burst out sobbing. In a wild voice I cried,
“Hamada!
I... have now completely and cleanly given that woman up! ”
“That’s only natural!
It’s perfectly natural that you should say so! ”
Hamada, as if caught up in my emotion, answered in a thick, hoarse voice as well.
“To tell you the truth, I came here today intending to tell you plainly that there is no longer any hope with Naomi.
Of course, knowing her, she may show up at your door again one of these days with a perfectly innocent face, but the truth is that no decent person will have anything to do with her anymore.
According to Kumagai, she has become nothing but a plaything for everyone, and she’s been given an utterly unspeakable nickname.
You have no idea how much shame you’ve been suffering without knowing it... ”

Hamada, who had once loved Naomi as passionately as I had, and who had been betrayed by her just as I had—this young man’s every word, filled with righteous indignation and spoken from the bottom of his heart for my sake, cut into me like a sharp scalpel slicing away rotten flesh.
Everyone was using her as a plaything; she had been given an unspeakable nickname.
This brutal revelation, rather than crushing me, strangely cleared my head.
It was as if a fever had broken; my shoulders suddenly felt lighter and even my tears stopped.
“How about it, Kawai?
Instead of staying shut up indoors like this, why don’t you come out for a walk to clear your head?
” urged Hamada.
For the past two days I had neither rinsed my mouth nor shaved, so I replied, “Just give me a moment,” then took up my razor, washed my face, and finally felt refreshed.
It was around half past two when Hamada and I stepped outside together.
“On a day like this, it’s better to walk in the suburbs,” Hamada suggested, and I agreed.
But when he said, “Shall we head this way?
” and started toward Ikegami, I suddenly felt a wave of revulsion and stopped in my tracks.
“Ah, that direction is no good.
That’s the unlucky quarter. ”
“Eh?
Why? ”
“The place from our earlier conversation—the Akebono-ro—is in that direction. ”
“Ah, that’s no good at all!
Then what shall we do?
Shall we go straight out to the coast and head toward Kawasaki? ”
“Yes, that sounds best.
That should be the safest route. ”
This time Hamada turned completely around and began walking toward the station, but on second thought that direction was not entirely free of danger either.
