If Naomi was still going to the Akebono-ro, there was no guarantee she might not come out with Kumagai around this very hour.
Nor was it impossible that she was shuttling back and forth between here and Yokohama with that foreigner.
In any case, I decided that any place where the suburban trains stopped was to be avoided. So I said, quite casually,
“I’m afraid I’ve put you to a great deal of trouble today. ”
Then I took the lead, turned down a side street, and headed for the level crossing that lay along the path through the fields.
“Not at all.
I’ve been expecting something like this to happen sooner or later. ”
“Hmm.
From your point of view I must have looked utterly ridiculous. ”
“But I was ridiculous myself once, so I have no right to laugh at you.
When my own fever cooled, I simply felt terribly sorry for you. ”
“Still, you’re young, so it’s all right.
But for a man of thirty-odd like me to make such a fool of himself—there’s nothing to be said for it.
And if you hadn’t told me, I might have gone on being a fool forever... ”
Once we reached the fields, the late-autumn sky stretched high and clear, as if to console me, but a strong wind whistled sharply, stinging the swollen rims of my eyes where I had been crying.
In the distance the forbidden suburban train went roaring along through the paddies.
“Hamada, have you had lunch?
” I asked after we had walked a while in silence.
“No, not yet, actually.
And you? ”
“Since the day before yesterday I’ve had nothing but liquor and almost no food.
Now I’m suddenly ravenous. ”
“That’s only natural.
You really shouldn’t treat your body so recklessly.
You’ll ruin your health. ”
“No, I’m fine.
Thanks to you I’ve come to my senses, so I won’t do anything foolish anymore.
Starting tomorrow I’m going to be a new man.
And I intend to go back to the office. ”
“That’s the best thing.
It will take your mind off things.
When I was jilted, I threw myself into music with all my might, trying to forget. ”
“It must be nice to have music at a time like that.
I have no such talent, so I suppose I’ll just have to plod away at my company work.
But anyway, aren’t you hungry?
Let’s eat something somewhere. ”
Chatting in this way, we strolled all the way to Rokugo.
Soon afterward we climbed the stairs of a beef restaurant in Kawasaki, sat down around a bubbling pot of sukiyaki, and began exchanging cups again just as we had done at Matsuasa.
“Here, have another. ”
“Oh, you’re pouring too fast.
My stomach’s empty, so it hits me hard. ”
“Come on, it’s all right.
Tonight is my farewell to bad luck, so raise a glass with me.
Starting tomorrow I’m giving up drink, but tonight let’s get thoroughly drunk and talk our hearts out. ”
“Ah, is that so?
Then here’s to your health. ”

By the time Hamada’s face had flushed bright red and the heads of the pimples covering his cheeks began to glisten like little bubbles rising in the boiling broth, I too was quite drunk and could no longer tell whether I was sad or happy.
“By the way, Hamada, there’s something I want to ask you. ”
I judged the moment right, edged my knees forward, and continued.
“What exactly is this terrible nickname they’ve given Naomi? ”
“No, I can’t tell you that.
It’s really too awful. ”
“Awful or not, what does it matter?
That woman is now a complete stranger to me, so there’s no need to hold back.
Come on, what do they call her?
Tell me.
Hearing it will actually make me feel cleaner. ”
“It may be that way for you, but for me it’s simply too painful to say.
Please forgive me.
Just imagine the worst possible nickname and you’ll probably be right.
I could tell you the story behind how she came to be called that, though. ”
“Then tell me the story. ”
“But Kawai... this is awkward. ”
Hamada scratched his head.
“It’s really quite dreadful.
If you hear it, I’m sure you’ll feel sick. ”
“It’s all right, it’s all right.
Tell me!
Right now I want to know that woman’s secrets purely out of curiosity. ”
“Very well, I’ll tell you a little of the secret.
When you were in Kamakura this past summer, how many men do you think Naomi had? ”
“Well, as far as I knew, only you and Kumagai... were there others? ”
“Kawai, you mustn’t be shocked.
Both Seki and Nakamura were involved as well. ”
Though I was drunk, I felt as if an electric current had shot through my body.
Without thinking I gulped down five or six cups in succession, then finally spoke.
“So all those fellows at the time were... every one of them? ”
“Yes, that’s right.
And do you know where they were meeting? ”
“At the villa in Okubo? ”
“No—in the detached room behind the nurseryman’s house that you were renting. ”
“Hmmm... ”
I fell into a heavy silence, as though the breath had been knocked out of me. At last I managed to groan,
“Hmmm...
I see.
I’m truly astonished. ”
“So at that time the person who must have been most troubled was the nurseryman’s wife.
Because she owed Kumagai a favor she couldn’t very well tell them to leave, yet her house had turned into a kind of den of iniquity with all sorts of men constantly coming and going.
It looked bad to the neighbors, and she was terrified that you might find out, so she was in a constant state of panic. ”
“I see.
Now that you mention it, I remember once when I asked the wife about Naomi she seemed terribly flustered and frightened.
So that was the reason.
My house in Omori was turned into your secret meeting place, the nurseryman’s detached room became a den of vice, and I knew nothing about any of it.
My goodness, what a sorry state of affairs. ”
“Ah, Kawai!
Let’s not talk about Omori!
If you mention that I’ll have to apologize. ”
“Ah ha ha ha!
No need.
It’s all in the past now, so it doesn’t matter.
But when I think how completely that devil Naomi deceived me, I almost find it exhilarating.
Her technique was so flawless that all I can do is gasp in admiration. ”
“It was exactly like being caught in a perfect sumo throw and slammed flat on your back. ”
“I agree completely.
Exactly as you say.
So all those men were being toyed with by Naomi and none of them knew about the others? ”
“No, they knew.
Sometimes two of them would even run into each other. ”
“And there was no fighting? ”
“They had formed a tacit alliance and were sharing Naomi among themselves.
That’s how the terrible nickname came about.
Behind her back they all called her by that name.
You were fortunate not to know it, but I found the whole thing utterly sordid.
I tried to find some way to rescue Naomi, but when I offered advice she would turn up her nose and treat me like a fool instead.
There was nothing I could do. ”
Hamada, apparently recalling those days, grew sentimental.
“You know, Kawai, when I met you at Matsuasa that time I didn’t tell you anything like this, did I? ”
“From what you said then, the one who had free run of Naomi was Kumagai... ”
“Yes, that’s what I said.
And it wasn’t a lie.
Naomi and Kumagai got along best; their coarse sides matched.
So Kumagai was the ringleader.
I thought he was the one teaching her all the bad things, which is why I spoke that way.
But I simply couldn’t bring myself to tell you any more than that.
At the time I was still hoping you would not abandon Naomi and would somehow guide her back to a decent life. ”
“Instead of guiding her, I was the one who got dragged along... ”
“Once a man gets caught by Naomi, that’s what happens to all of them. ”
“That woman has a strange demonic power. ”
“It really is demonic!
I felt it myself, which is why I realized I must never go near her again.
If I did, I would be the one in danger... ”
Naomi, Naomi—how many times the name was repeated between us I cannot say.
The two of us used that name as a relish for our drink.
We rolled its smooth syllables on our tongues like a food even more delicious than the beef, savored them, licked them with saliva, and brought them to our lips.
“But it’s all right.
It’s not such a bad thing to be deceived by a woman like that at least once in your life,” I said, filled with deep emotion.
“Exactly!
Thanks to her, at least I learned the taste of first love.
Even if it was only for a short while, she let me see a beautiful dream.
For that I must be grateful. ”
“But what will become of her in the end? ”
“She’ll just keep falling lower and lower, I suppose.
According to Kumagai, she can’t stay at McConnell’s place for long, so in a few days she’ll probably move on again.
He said she might even come back to him because he still has some of her luggage.
Does Naomi have no real home of her own? ”
“Her home is a cheap sake house in Asakusa.
I’ve never told anyone because I felt sorry for her. ”
“Ah, I see.
So blood will tell after all. ”
“According to Naomi, her family were once retainers of a banner lord and when she was born they lived in a splendid mansion in Shimo-nibancho.
She said her grandmother, who gave her the name ‘Naomi,’ was a modern woman of the Rokumeikan era who danced foreign dances.
How much of that is true I don’t know.
In any case, her home life was bad.
Now I understand that only too well. ”
“When I hear that, it becomes even more frightening.
So Naomi was born with a strain of lewdness in her blood and was destined to end up this way, even though you had taken her in... ”
The two of us talked on for about three hours.
It was past seven in the evening when we finally went outside, yet our conversation showed no sign of ending.
“Hamada, are you taking the suburban train home?
” I asked as we walked through the streets of Kawasaki.
“Well, walking from here would be quite a distance... ”
“That’s true, but I’m taking the Keihin line.
If that woman is in Yokohama, the suburban line feels dangerous. ”
“Then I’ll take the Keihin line too.
Still, the way Naomi is flitting about in all directions, we’re bound to run into her somewhere. ”
“If it comes to that, I won’t even be able to walk outside without being on my guard. ”
“She’s definitely going in and out of dance halls, so the Ginza area is the most dangerous zone. ”
“Omori isn’t entirely safe either.
There’s Yokohama, there’s Hanayashiki Garden, and of course the Akebono-ro...
I may end up closing the house and moving into lodgings for a while.
Until the scandal cools down I don’t want to see her face. ”
I accompanied Hamada on the Keihin electric train and parted from him at Omori.
While I was suffering the pains of unrequited love in that solitude, another sad event occurred.
My mother back in the country suddenly died of a cerebral hemorrhage.
The telegram announcing she was in critical condition arrived on the morning of the day after I had met Hamada.
I received it at the office, rushed straight to Ueno Station, and reached our house in the countryside at dusk.
By then my mother had already lost consciousness.
She did not seem to recognize me.
Two or three hours later she drew her last breath.
Having lost my father when I was very young and been raised solely by my mother, I was experiencing for the first time what is called “the grief of losing a parent.
” Moreover, the bond between my mother and me had been far closer than that of ordinary parent and child.
When I look back on the past, I cannot recall a single instance of having defied her or of her having scolded me.
This may be partly because I had always respected her, but far more because she was a woman of great consideration and overflowing affection.
It is common in this world for parents to worry or grow suspicious about a son once he grows up, leaves his hometown, and moves to the city; sometimes this leads to estrangement.
Yet even after I went to Tokyo, my mother continued to trust me, to understand my feelings, and to think always of my welfare.
She had only two daughters besides me, and letting her eldest son go must have left her feeling lonely and anxious, yet she never once complained.
She prayed constantly for my success in life.
Precisely because I was so far away from her, I felt the depth of her love more strongly than when I had lived under her roof.

Especially in the period just before and after my marriage to Naomi, and during all the selfish demands I made afterward, every time she kindly granted my wishes I could not help being moved to tears by her warmth.
To lose such a mother so suddenly and unexpectedly left me in a daze as I sat beside her remains.

The man who, only yesterday, had been utterly intoxicated by Naomi’s sensual charms, and the man who now knelt before the Buddha offering incense—these two “selves” seemed to have no connection at all.
Which was the real me: yesterday’s or today’s?
Even as I wept in grief, sorrow, and astonishment, a voice seemed to reach me from somewhere: “Your mother’s death at this moment is no accident.
She is warning you.
She has given you a lesson.
” At the same time another whisper came: “This is your punishment.
” Then, remembering my mother as she had been in life, I was overcome with remorse.
Fresh tears of regret would burst forth, and because I was ashamed to be seen crying so much, I would slip away to the wooded hill behind the house.
There, gazing down at the forest, the paths, and the fields filled with memories of my boyhood, I would weep uncontrollably.
It goes without saying that this great sorrow purified me, cleansing the filthy accumulations that had settled in my heart and body.
Had it not been for this grief, I might still be unable to forget that loathsome whore and still be writhing in the agony of lost love.
When I think of it that way, my mother’s death was not meaningless after all.
No—at the very least, I must not allow it to be meaningless.
At the time I resolved to leave the city air I had come to detest.
Success in life did not mean living frivolously and superficially in Tokyo.
A country bumpkin like me belonged in the country.
I would withdraw to my hometown, live close to its soil, watch over my mother’s grave, and become a farmer like my ancestors, dealing with the villagers.
Such thoughts even crossed my mind.
But my uncle, my sisters, and the other relatives all said, “That’s far too hasty.
It’s natural that you should feel discouraged right now, but a man shouldn’t throw away his entire future just because his mother has died.
Everyone feels despair when they lose a parent, yet with time the sorrow fades.
If you’re going to do that, you should think it over much more carefully.
Besides, it would be unfair to the company if you suddenly quit.
” I came close to blurting out, “Actually, there’s more to it—my wife has run away from me...
” but I was ashamed to say such a thing in front of everyone, and the house was in such confusion that I kept silent.

(I had already explained Naomi’s absence by saying she was ill.) After the seventh-day memorial service was over, I left all further matters in the hands of my uncle and his wife, who had been managing the family property as my agents, and, heeding everyone’s advice, returned to Tokyo for the time being.
Yet once I was back at the company, nothing felt worthwhile.
My standing among the staff was no longer what it had been.

The man once nicknamed “the gentleman” for his diligence, integrity, and upright conduct had now thoroughly disgraced himself because of Naomi; neither the executives nor my colleagues trusted me anymore.
Some even sneered that my mother’s death was merely an excuse for taking time off.
All of this made me increasingly disgusted.
On the night of the fourteenth-day memorial, when I returned home for one evening, I even let slip to my uncle, “I may quit the company before long.
” He replied only with a vague “Well, well,” and did not take it seriously.
So the next day I dragged myself back to the office.
The hours at work were bearable, but once evening came I had no idea how to pass the time.
The reason was that I still could not decide whether to move back to the country or remain in Tokyo.
Consequently I had neither returned to my old lodging house nor properly settled in the deserted house in Ōmori; I was simply sleeping there alone.
After the office closed, I still hated the thought of encountering Naomi, so I avoided lively districts and took the Keihin train straight back to Ōmori.
I would eat a perfunctory supper of simple prepared dishes, soba, or udon at a neighborhood shop, and after that there was nothing to do.
With no other choice I would go up to the bedroom, pull the quilt over my head, but I rarely fell asleep easily.
I would lie awake for two or three hours.
The bedroom was the familiar room in the attic.
Her belongings were still there, and the smell of five years of disorder, dissipation, and wildness had soaked into the walls and pillars.
That smell was, in short, the odor of her skin.
Because she was slovenly, she would roll up soiled garments without washing them and stuff them away; now they had filled the poorly ventilated room.
Unable to bear it, I later tried sleeping on the sofa in the atelier, but there too I found it just as hard to fall asleep.
Three weeks after my mother’s death, in early December, I finally made up my mind to resign.
It was arranged that I would leave the company at the end of the year.
Since I had decided this on my own without consulting anyone beforehand, my family in the country still knew nothing about it.
With only one month left to endure, I felt somewhat calmer.
I now had a little mental leeway and began to read or take walks in my spare time.
Even so, I never went near any dangerous areas.
One evening, feeling particularly bored, I walked as far as Shinagawa.
To kill time I decided to see a Matsunosuke film and stepped into a moving-picture house, only to find a Lloyd comedy playing.
When young American actresses appeared on the screen, all sorts of memories came flooding back and I could not stand it.
“I must never watch a Western film again,” I told myself at that moment.

Then, one Sunday morning in mid-December, I was lying upstairs (by then the atelier had grown cold, so I had moved back to the attic) when I heard a rustling sound downstairs and sensed someone’s presence.
Strange, I thought—the front door should be locked.
While I was wondering about it, familiar footsteps came climbing boldly up the stairs.
Before I had time to feel a chill in my chest, a bright voice called out,
“Hello! ”
The door flew open and Naomi stood before me.
“Hello!
” she said again, staring at me with a blank expression.
“What have you come for?
” I asked, remaining in bed.
I spoke quietly and coldly, astonished in my heart that she could have the nerve to show up at all.
“Me?
I’ve come for my things. ”
“You may take your things, but where did you get in? ”
“Through the front door.
I still had my key. ”
“Then leave the key when you go. ”
“All right, I will. ”
I turned my back on her and said nothing more.
For a while she bustled about near my pillow, tying up a furoshiki bundle.
Then I heard the sharp sound of a sash being untied.
When I looked, she had gone to a corner of the room—well within my line of sight—turned her back to me, and begun changing her clothes.

I had noticed her outfit the moment she entered: it was an unfamiliar meisen silk garment, clearly one she wore every day, for the collar was soiled, the knees were baggy, and the whole thing was rumpled.
After undoing her sash she slipped off the dingy meisen and stood in nothing but a dirty merinsu under-robe.

She then took out a long under-robe of gold-threaded crepe she had just unpacked, draped it lightly over her shoulders, and, wriggling inside it, let the merinsu slide smoothly to the floor like a shed skin.

Over that she put on one of her favorite garments, a turtle-shell-patterned Ōshima kimono, wrapped a red-and-white checkered date-maki sash tightly around her waist until her torso was sharply cinched, and finally turned toward me, squatted down, and began changing her socks.
Nothing tempted me more powerfully than the sight of her bare feet.
I tried not to look in that direction, yet I could not keep from glancing at them now and then.
She was of course fully aware of this and deliberately flexed her feet like fins, occasionally stealing glances at my eyes to see how I was reacting.
Once she had finished putting on her socks, she quickly gathered up the clothes she had discarded.
“Good-bye,” she said, dragging the furoshiki bundle toward the door.
“Hey, don’t forget to leave the key,” I called out for the first time.
“Oh, right,” she answered, taking the key from her handbag.
“I’ll leave it here, then.
But I can’t carry everything in one trip, so I may have to come again. ”
“You don’t need to come.
I’ll send everything to the Asakusa house. ”
“I’d be in trouble if you sent it to Asakusa.
There are reasons... ”
“Then where should I send it? ”
“I haven’t decided yet where I’m staying... ”
“If you don’t come for it by the end of the month, I’ll send it to Asakusa anyway.
I can’t keep your things here forever. ”
“All right.
I’ll come for them soon. ”
“And one more thing: send a servant with a cart so you can take everything in one go.
Don’t come yourself. ”
“I see.
I’ll do that. ”
With that she left.
I thought the matter was settled, but two or three evenings later, around nine o’clock, while I was reading the evening paper in the atelier, I heard the front door rattle.
Someone was inserting a key into the lock.
“Who is it? ”
“It’s me. ”
The moment she spoke, the door flew open with a bang, and a large, black, bear-like shape burst into the room from the darkness outside.
But in an instant the black thing was thrown off, revealing a young Western woman I had never seen before.
She wore a pale aqua French crêpe de Chine dress that left her fox-white shoulders and arms exposed.
Around her plump neck sparkled a crystal necklace that glittered like a rainbow.
Beneath a black velvet hat pulled low over her eyes, the tips of an eerily white nose and chin were visible, giving her an almost mystical air, while her lips stood out in a vivid, fresh vermilion.
“Good evening. ”
At the sound of her voice, as the Western woman removed her hat, I thought, “Wait, who is this woman—?
” Then, as I stared intently at her face, I gradually realized it was Naomi.
It may sound strange, but in truth her appearance had changed so completely that it was almost unrecognizable.
No, even if her figure had altered, I should never have failed to recognize her; what deceived my eyes above all was her face.
By what sorcery had it been transformed?
The color of her skin, the expression in her eyes, even the very contours had all changed.
Had I not heard her voice, even after she removed her hat I might still have believed she was some unknown Westerner.
Next was the terrifying whiteness of her skin, as I have already mentioned.
Every part of her rich, full body that showed beyond the dress was as white as the flesh of an apple.
Naomi had never been particularly dark for a Japanese woman, yet she could not possibly have been this white.
When I looked at her arms, which were bare almost to the shoulders, I simply could not believe they belonged to a Japanese.

Once, when the Bandman Opera Company performed at the Imperial Theatre, I had been captivated by the whiteness of a young Western actress’s arms; Naomi’s arms were exactly like hers—indeed, they seemed even whiter.

Then Naomi, letting her soft aqua dress and necklace sway gently, came clicking across the floor on the toes of her high-heeled patent-leather shoes adorned with new diamond ornaments. —Ah, these must be the Cinderella slippers Hamada spoke of the other day, I thought at that moment.
With one hand on her hip, elbow thrust out, she twisted her torso in an oddly coquettish pose full of self-satisfaction and suddenly drew close to my dumbfounded face without the slightest reserve.
“Jōji, I’ve come to collect my things. ”
“You didn’t have to come yourself.
I told you to send someone. ”
“But I didn’t have anyone I could ask. ”
Even as she spoke, Naomi could not keep still for a moment.

Though her face wore a serious, almost severe expression, she kept shifting her weight—standing with her feet pressed tightly together, then stepping forward with one foot, then tapping the floorboards sharply with her heel.
Each time she changed the position of her hands, squared her shoulders, tensed every muscle in her body like a taut wire, and set every part of herself in nervous motion.
My own optic nerves were forced to follow suit, straining so that I could not help but take in every single gesture, every movement of her limbs, every inch of her body without missing a thing.
When I looked closely at her face, it was no wonder she seemed transformed.
She had cut the hair at her forehead short, to about two or three inches, trimmed the ends neatly, and let it hang down like a fringe over her brow in the manner of Chinese girls.

The rest of her hair was gathered into a single mass, flattened into a smooth, round shape that covered the crown of her head and reached just above her earlobes, resembling the cap worn by the god Daikoku.
This was a hairstyle I had never seen on her before, and it was surely what made the shape of her face look like an entirely different person.
Looking still more carefully, I noticed that the shape of her eyebrows was also different from usual.
Her natural brows were thick, sharply defined, and rather heavy, yet tonight they had been drawn into long, soft, hazy arcs, and the skin around those arcs had been carefully shaved to a bluish tint.
I could see at once that all this artifice had been applied, but what I could not fathom was the trick behind her eyes, her lips, and the color of her skin.
That her eyes looked so strikingly Western was partly due to the eyebrows, but there seemed to be some further device at work.
It must be the eyelids and the eyelashes—there was some secret there.
Yet I could not tell exactly what the trick was.

Her lips, too, had an unnaturally sharp cleft in the center of the upper one, exactly like the petal of a cherry blossom, and their vivid red possessed a fresh, living luster quite unlike ordinary lipstick.
As for the whiteness of her skin, no matter how long I stared I could detect no trace of powder; it looked like her natural complexion.
And it was not only her face—her shoulders, arms, and even the tips of her fingers were the same pure white.
If she had applied powder, she must have covered her entire body with it.
This inscrutable, mysterious girl—rather than say she was Naomi, it seemed as though Naomi’s soul, through some mysterious operation, had become a phantom possessing an ideal beauty.
I even began to feel that might be the case.
“Listen, it’s all right, isn’t it?
If I go upstairs to get my things—? ”
So spoke Naomi’s phantom, but when I heard her voice it was unmistakably the usual Naomi, and certainly no ghost.
“Yes, that’s fine... that’s fine, but... ”
I was clearly flustered and answered in a slightly shrill voice.
How did you open the front door? ”
“How?
With a key, of course. ”
“But I left the key here the other day, didn’t I? ”
“I have several keys.
It’s not just one. ”
At that moment her crimson lips suddenly curved into a smile, and she gave me a look that was both seductive and mocking.
“I might as well tell you now—I had a lot of duplicate keys made.
So it doesn’t matter if you take one away. ”
“But it matters to me.
I can’t have you coming here so often. ”
“Don’t worry.
Once I’ve taken all my things away, I won’t come even if you beg me to. ”
Then, spinning on her heel, she trotted briskly up the stairs—ton, ton, ton—and disappeared into the attic room.
How many minutes passed after that?
While I leaned back on the sofa in the atelier, waiting absently for her to come down from upstairs—whether it was less than five minutes, or half an hour, or even a full hour—I cannot say.
The passage of time during that interval remains unclear to me.
All I knew was that the image of Naomi as she had appeared that night lingered in my chest like the afterglow of some beautiful music, trailing a rapturous pleasure.
It was a soprano song, impossibly high, impossibly pure, as though it rang out from some sacred realm beyond this world.
At such a moment there was no longer any lust or love...
What I felt in my heart was an ethereal intoxication utterly removed from such things.

I thought about it again and again: the Naomi of tonight could not possibly coexist with that filthy whore Naomi, that Naomi who was no better than a prostitute to whom many men had given vile nicknames.
She had become an exalted object of yearning before whom a man like me could do nothing but kneel and worship.
If the tip of one of those pure white fingers were to touch me even slightly, far from rejoicing I would probably tremble with awe.
How can I make the reader understand this feeling?
Imagine a rustic father who goes up to Tokyo and by chance meets on the street the daughter who ran away from home when she was small.
But the daughter has become a splendid woman of the city; she does not recognize the dirty country peasant as her father.
The father realizes who she is, yet because their stations in life are now so different he cannot even approach her.
He is stunned—So this is what my daughter has become—and, overwhelmed with shame, he slinks away.
That father’s lonely yet reverent emotion.
Or picture a man who was jilted by his fiancée; five or ten years later he stands on the pier in Yokohama as a merchant ship docks and a crowd of returning travelers disembarks.
Unexpectedly he spots her among them.
So she has been abroad and has now returned, he thinks, yet he no longer has the courage to go near her.

He is still nothing but a poor student, unchanged from the old days, while she—there is no trace left of the unsophisticated girl she once was; she has become a chic, modern woman accustomed to Parisian life and New York luxury.
A thousand miles now lie between them.
That student’s feeling—his self-contempt at having been abandoned, and yet his joy at her unexpected success.
Even saying all this does not fully express it, but if I must offer an analogy, perhaps it is something like that.
In any case, the Naomi I had known until then had past stains that no amount of washing could remove; they had soaked into her very flesh.

But when I looked at tonight’s Naomi, those stains had been erased by skin as pure white as an angel’s, and what had once seemed revolting to remember now felt so sacred that even touching the tip of her finger would be sacrilege.
Is this a dream?
If not, where and from whom had Naomi learned such magic, such sorcery?
Only two or three days ago she had been wearing that shabby, dingy meisen kimono, and yet...
Ton, ton, ton—once again came the energetic sound of footsteps descending the stairs, and the toes of those new diamond-adorned shoes stopped right before my eyes.
“Jōji, I’ll come again in a few days,” she said.
Though she stood before me, she kept a distance of about three feet between our faces, and the hem of her dress, light as the wind, never once brushed against me.
“Tonight I only came to take two or three books.
I can’t very well carry a big load all at once, especially dressed like this. ”
At that moment my nose caught a faint scent I had smelled somewhere before.
Ah, that fragrance... a scent that called to mind distant lands across the sea and wondrous foreign flower gardens...
It was the same perfume that had once risen from the skin of the dance instructor, Countess Shlemskaya.
Naomi was wearing the same scent...
No matter what Naomi said, I could only nod and murmur, “Mm-hmm.

” Even after her figure had melted once more into the darkness of night, I remained there, chasing with sharpened senses the fragrance that still drifted through the room, growing fainter and fainter, as though pursuing a vision.

Readers, by now you will already have guessed from the events recounted up to the previous chapter that Naomi and I would soon be reconciled—that such a development was neither strange nor surprising, but the perfectly natural outcome.
And in fact the result turned out exactly as you predicted.
Yet getting to that point took far more trouble than I had expected, and I made a complete fool of myself in any number of ways and wasted a great deal of effort.
After that night, Naomi and I began speaking to each other again with easy familiarity.
The reason was simple: the very next evening, and every evening thereafter, she never failed to come by to collect some piece of luggage.
Each time she would go upstairs, pack a bundle, and come back down; but the bundles were always tiny things, hardly worth wrapping in a crepe-silk furoshiki.
“What have you come for tonight?
” I would ask.
“This?
Oh, it’s nothing.
Just a trifle. ”
She would answer vaguely, then say something like, “I’m terribly thirsty.
Won’t you give me a cup of tea?
” and sit down beside me.
We would chat for twenty or thirty minutes before she left.
One evening, as we sat facing each other across the table drinking black tea, I asked her:
“Are you living somewhere nearby? ”
“Why do you want to know? ”
“There’s no harm in asking, is there? ”
“Maybe not, but why? ...
What are you planning to do with the information? ”
“I’m not planning anything.
I’m simply curious. —Come on, where are you staying?
It’s all right to tell me. ”
“No, I won’t. ”
“Why not? ”
“I have no obligation to satisfy your curiosity, Jōji.
If you want to know so badly, why don’t you follow me?
Shadowing people is one of your specialties. ”
“I don’t feel like going quite that far, but I’m convinced you must be living somewhere in the neighborhood. ”
“Oh?
Why? ”
“Because you come here every single night to carry things away. ”
“That doesn’t prove I live nearby.
There are trams and taxis, you know. ”
“So you come all the way from somewhere far off on purpose? ”
“Well... who knows? ”
She dodged the question neatly and changed the subject with practiced skill.
“Is it so wrong to come every night? ”
“It’s not exactly wrong, but... even if I told you not to come, you’d barge in anyway, so there’s nothing I can do about it now... ”
“Exactly.
I’m stubborn.
If you tell me not to come, I’ll come even more. —Or are you afraid of having me around? ”
“Well...
I can’t say I’m not a little afraid... ”
At that she threw her head back, showing the pure white underside of her chin, opened her scarlet mouth wide, and burst into peals of laughter.
“But don’t worry.
I won’t do anything wicked.
I’d rather forget all about the past and be friends with you from now on, Jōji.
All right?
There’s nothing wrong with that, is there? ”
“That sounds rather odd to me. ”
“What’s odd about it?
Why should it be strange for two people who used to be married to become friends?
Isn’t that just old-fashioned, out-of-date thinking? —Honestly, I don’t think about the old days at all anymore.
Of course, if I really wanted to seduce you, I could do it right here and now without the slightest trouble, but I swear I won’t.
It would be cruel to undermine the resolution you’ve worked so hard to make... ”
“So out of pity you’re offering to be my friend? ”
“That’s not what I mean at all.
You should just pull yourself together so you don’t need anyone’s pity. ”
“The trouble is, I’m not sure I can.
I think I’m steady enough now, but if I start seeing you again I may gradually begin to waver. ”
“You’re such an idiot, Jōji. —So you don’t want to be friends? ”
“No, I suppose I don’t. ”
“If you won’t be friends, then I’ll seduce you.
I’ll trample all over your precious resolution and turn everything upside down. ”
Naomi said this with a strange, ambiguous smile—half joking, half serious—her eyes glinting.
“Which is better: staying friends and keeping things pure, or being seduced and suffering horribly again? —Tonight I’m blackmailing you, Jōji. ”
At that moment I wondered what on earth this woman was really thinking when she proposed we become “friends.
” Her nightly visits could not be motivated merely by a desire to tease me; she must have some further scheme in mind.
Perhaps she intended to become friends first, gradually soften me up, and then arrange things so that I would be the one to beg for a reunion rather than her surrendering.
If that was her true intention, she needn’t have bothered with such a roundabout strategy; I would have agreed at once.
For deep in my heart a feeling had already begun to smolder—a feeling that if I could become her husband again I would never say no.
“Listen, Naomi, being nothing but friends is pointless.
Why don’t we just go back to being husband and wife the way we were? ”
Depending on the moment, I might have been ready to say those words myself.
But the way Naomi was behaving that night made it clear that even if I opened my heart to her in earnest, she was unlikely to answer with a simple “All right. ”
“I’d rather not hear any of that.
If it’s not just friends, then no thank you. ”
Once she sensed what I was feeling, she would only grow bolder and mock me all the more.
I had no desire to see my sincere feelings treated so lightly.

Besides, if her real aim was not to become my wife again but to remain completely free, to toy with any number of men and simply add me to her collection, then I could hardly afford to speak carelessly.
The very fact that she refused even to tell me where she lived suggested she still had some man or other.
If I took her back as my wife under those conditions, I would only be inviting fresh misery.
So I thought quickly and answered with a smirk:
“All right, we can be friends.
I can’t very well refuse when I’m being threatened. ”
My own hidden motive was that if we remained friends I would gradually discover her true intentions.
If any sincerity still remained in her, I would then have the chance to reveal my own feelings and persuade her to become my wife again—perhaps even on more favorable terms than before.
“So you agree? ”
Naomi peered into my face with a ticklish, mischievous look.
“But remember, Jōji, just friends. ”
“Of course. ”
“We mustn’t think any indecent thoughts about each other. ”
“I understand. —If we did, I’d be in trouble. ”
“Hmm. ”
Naomi gave her usual little sniff of laughter through her nose.
After that exchange she began visiting even more frequently.
When I returned from the office in the evening she would come flying in like a swallow.
“Jōji! ”
“Won’t you treat me to dinner tonight?
Friends can do at least that much, can’t they? ”
She would make me take her out for Western food, eat her fill, and go home.
Or on a rainy night she would arrive late, knock on the bedroom door with a tap-tap-tap, and call out:
“Hello?
Are you already in bed? —If you are, you don’t have to get up.
I’ve come tonight intending to stay over. ”
Then she would march into the next room, make up the bed, and go to sleep.
Sometimes I would wake in the morning to find her already there, sound asleep and snoring peacefully.
And every other sentence out of her mouth was, “We’re friends, so it can’t be helped. ”
Around that time I came to feel that she was a born whore by nature.

What led me to that conclusion was this: although she was naturally amorous and thought nothing of showing her body to any number of men, she also knew perfectly well how to keep that same body strictly hidden in ordinary circumstances.
Even the smallest portion of it was never exposed to a man’s eyes without purpose.
To hide and conceal what she was perfectly willing to grant to anyone—this, to my mind, was the instinctive self-protective psychology of the whore.
For a whore’s skin is her most precious “merchandise,” her “goods.
” Depending on the situation she must guard it even more jealously than a chaste woman guards her own, or its market value will steadily decline.
Naomi understood this delicate balance perfectly.
In front of me, her former husband, she was more careful than ever to keep her body wrapped up.
Yet she was not always prim and proper.
Sometimes, while I was there, she would deliberately change her clothes; as she did so her under-kimono would slip from her shoulders with a rustle and she would cry “Oh!
” and cover her bare shoulders with both hands before fleeing into the next room.
Or she would return from the bath, begin undressing in front of the mirror, then suddenly pretend to notice me and say, “Oh, Jōji, you mustn’t stay there.
Go somewhere else,” and chase me away.

The occasional, seemingly accidental glimpses she gave me of her skin were only tiny fragments—perhaps the curve of her neck, an elbow, a shin, or a heel—yet I could not fail to notice that her body had become even glossier and more maddeningly beautiful than before.
Again and again I found myself compelled, in the world of imagination, to strip her of every stitch and gaze insatiably at her curves.
“Jōji, what are you staring at? ”
She asked me once while she was changing with her back turned toward me.
“I’m looking at your figure.
Somehow it seems even fresher and more youthful than before. ”
“Oh, how disgusting. —A gentleman shouldn’t look at a lady’s body. ”
“I’m not looking, but even through your clothes I can more or less tell.
You always had a prominent bottom, but lately it seems to have grown even rounder. ”
“Yes, it has.
My bottom keeps getting bigger.
But my legs are still slim; they don’t look like daikon radishes. ”
“No, your legs have been straight ever since you were a child.
When you stand they press tightly together.
Do they still do that? ”
“Yes, they do. ”
She stood up straight inside the circle of her kimono and said, “See?
They touch perfectly. ”
At that moment a sculpture by Rodin that I had seen in a photograph floated into my mind.
“Jōji, do you want to see my body? ”
“Would you show it to me if I did? ”
“That wouldn’t do at all.
We’re friends, aren’t we? —Now go away until I’ve finished changing. ”
She slammed the door behind me with a sharp bang.
In this way Naomi constantly worked to inflame my desire.
She would lure me right up to the brink, then set up an impenetrable barrier beyond which I could not advance a single step.
Between Naomi and me there stood a wall of glass.
No matter how close we seemed, an uncrossable gulf always remained.
If I tried to reach out carelessly I would only collide with that wall; no matter how I writhed I could never touch her skin.
Sometimes Naomi would appear to lift the barrier for a moment, and I would think, “Oh, is it all right now?
” But the moment I approached, it would slam shut again.
“Jōji, you’ve been such a good boy.
I’ll give you one little kiss. ”
She often said such things half in jest.
Knowing I was being teased, I would still lean forward when she offered her lips.
Just as our mouths were about to meet, hers would dart away; from two or three inches away she would blow her breath onto my lips and say with a grin:
“That’s a friend’s kiss. ”
This peculiar form of greeting—the “friend’s kiss”—in which I had to content myself with breathing in her breath instead of tasting her lips—soon became a habit.
When she was about to leave she would purse her lips and say, “Well, goodbye.
I’ll come again,” and I would thrust my face forward, open my mouth like a man inhaling from a vaporizer, and wait.
She would blow a soft “haa” into my mouth; I would draw it deep into my lungs with my eyes closed, swallowing it as though it were something delicious.
Her breath was moist and warm, carrying a sweet floral fragrance that seemed impossible to have come from human lungs.

(Later I learned that she secretly dabbed perfume on her lips to bewilder me, but at the time I had no idea.) I often wondered whether, in a woman as bewitching as Naomi, even her internal organs were different from those of ordinary women, so that the air that passed through her body and lingered in her mouth acquired such a seductive scent.
My mind grew more and more confused, toyed with exactly as she pleased.
I no longer had the luxury of insisting on formal marriage or complaining about being manipulated.
To be honest, I should have known from the beginning that things would come to this.
If I had truly feared her seduction I should simply have refused to see her.
All my talk of wanting to discover her true intentions or to wait for a more advantageous moment had been nothing but self-deception.
While I kept saying I was afraid of seduction, the truth was that I had been secretly longing for it.
Yet no matter how long I waited she continued the same tiresome “friends” game and never took the next step.
This must be her strategy, I thought—to torment me until I could bear it no longer.
When she judged the moment ripe she would suddenly drop the mask of friendship and reach out with her devilish hand.
She was bound to make a move eventually; she was not the sort of woman who would leave things as they were.
So I decided to play along with her scheme as cleverly as I could.
When she said “beg,” I would beg; when she said “sit,” I would sit.
If I performed every trick exactly as ordered, sooner or later the prize would be mine.
Day after day I waited with twitching nostrils, but my expectations were never fulfilled.
Just when I thought she would finally drop the mask today, or that her devilish hand would strike tomorrow, at the very last instant she would slip away like a shadow.
At last I began to suffer in earnest.
I practically shouted with my whole body, “I’m waiting like this—seduce me, and do it quickly!
” I left every opening exposed, revealed every weakness, and finally began trying to seduce her myself.
But she would have none of it.
“What are you doing, Jōji!
That breaks our promise! ”
She would scold me with the stern eyes of a mother correcting a naughty child.
“I don’t care about promises anymore. I—”
“No, no!
We’re friends! ”
“Please, Naomi... don’t say that...
I beg you... ”
“Oh, you’re so tiresome!
I said no!...
Here, I’ll give you a kiss instead. ”
And once again she would breathe that soft “haa” over me.
“There.
Isn’t that enough?
You’ll just have to be satisfied with this.
It may even be more than friends should do, but I’m giving you special treatment because it’s you, Jōji. ”
Yet this “special” caress, far from calming my nerves, only stimulated them to an abnormal degree.
“Damn it!
Another failure today. ”
I grew more and more irritable.
The moment she flitted out like a breeze I would be unable to settle to anything.
Furious with myself, I would pace the room like a caged wild beast, smashing or tearing whatever came to hand.
I was truly tormented by these fits of madness—what might be called masculine hysteria.
Since she came every day, the attacks occurred with almost clockwork regularity—once a day.
What was worse, unlike ordinary hysteria, once an attack had passed I did not feel suddenly lighthearted.

On the contrary, as soon as my mood calmed I would recall, with even greater clarity and persistence than before, the smallest details of Naomi’s body: the foot that had peeped from beneath her kimono when she changed, the lips that had come within two or three inches when she breathed on me.
These images appeared far more vividly in memory than when I had actually seen them.

My imagination would travel along the lines of those lips and that foot, expanding further and further, until even the parts I had never actually seen began to emerge as though a photographic plate were being developed.
In the end a figure resembling a marble Venus would suddenly appear in the darkness at the bottom of my mind.
My brain had become a stage enclosed by a velvet curtain, upon which a single actress named “Naomi” appeared.
The stage lights pouring from every direction illuminated only her white body, floating in the darkness, wrapped in a brilliant circle of light.
The longer I stared, the brighter the glow on her skin became, sometimes seeming to burn my very eyebrows.
Every part was magnified with the vividness of a cinema close-up...
The illusion assaulted my senses with a realism indistinguishable from reality.
The only thing lacking was the ability to touch her; in every other respect the vision was more alive than the real thing.
If I stared too long I would finally feel a dizzying vertigo; all the blood in my body would rush to my face at once and my heart would begin to pound violently.
Then another hysterical fit would seize me.
I would kick over chairs, rip down curtains, and smash vases to pieces.
My delusions grew more violent day by day.
The moment I closed my eyes Naomi was there behind my dark eyelids.
I would often remember the sweet scent of her breath, open my mouth to the empty air, and inhale with a loud “haa.
” Whether I was walking along the street or shut up in my room, whenever I yearned for her lips I would suddenly tilt my head back and breathe in sharply again and again.
Everywhere I looked I saw Naomi’s scarlet lips; every particle of air in the world seemed to be her breath.
In short, Naomi had become an evil spirit filling the space between heaven and earth, surrounding me, tormenting me, listening to my groans, and laughing as she watched.
“You’ve been acting strangely lately, Jōji.
There’s something wrong with you. ”
Naomi said this one night when she came to visit.
“Of course there’s something wrong.
When you torment me this much... ”
“What do you mean, ‘hmm’? ”
“I intend to keep our promise very strictly. ”
“How long do you intend to keep it? ”
“Forever. ”
“Don’t be ridiculous.
If things go on like this I’ll really lose my mind. ”
“Then I’ll tell you a good remedy.
Just pour a bucket of cold tap water over your head. ”
“Look here, Naomi, honestly... ”
“There you go again!
It’s because you make that face that I feel like teasing you even more.
Don’t come so close.
Stay farther away.
And don’t you dare touch me with even a single finger. ”
“Then at least give me a friend’s kiss. ”
“I will if you behave yourself.
But you won’t go crazy again afterward, will you? ”
“I don’t care if I do.
I can’t worry about that anymore. ”

That night Naomi made me sit on the far side of the table with the warning “Don’t lay a single finger on me,” and while she watched my tormented face with obvious amusement, she kept up a stream of idle chatter until late.
When the clock struck twelve, she said again in that teasing tone:
“Jōji, I’m staying over tonight. ”
“Fine, stay.
Tomorrow’s Sunday and I’ll be home all day. ”
“But just so you know, even if I stay, it won’t be on your terms. ”
“No need to worry.
You’re not the kind of woman who does what I want anyway. ”
“You’re hoping it works out that way, aren’t you? ”
She gave a little snort of laughter, then said,
“All right, you go to bed first.
And don’t talk in your sleep. ”
She chased me upstairs, then slipped into the next room and clicked the lock shut with a loud snap.
Of course I couldn’t fall asleep; the room next door weighed on my mind.
When we lived as husband and wife there had never been anything so ridiculous.
She used to sleep right beside me.
The thought filled me with unbearable resentment.
On the other side of the thin wall Naomi was noisily—perhaps deliberately—thumping about, spreading the futon, pulling out the pillow, getting ready for bed.
Now she’s undoing her hair, I thought.
Now she’s taking off her clothes and putting on her nightgown.
Every movement was so clear I could see it with my eyes closed.
Then came the sound of the covers being flung back, followed by a heavy thud as her body collapsed onto the futon.
“You’re making quite a racket,” I said, half to myself and half so she would hear.
“Are you still awake?
Can’t sleep?
” Naomi answered at once from the other side of the wall.
“No, I don’t think I’ll be able to sleep at all.
I’ve got a lot on my mind. ”
“Hee hee hee.
I can guess what Jōji is thinking without being told. ”
“But it really is strange.
You’re right there on the other side of this wall, and there’s nothing I can do about it. ”
“There’s nothing strange about it at all.
Wasn’t it exactly like this a long time ago, when I first came to live with you?
We slept like this back then, didn’t we? ”
When she said that, I thought, Yes, that’s right, there was a time like that.
Back then we were both so innocent.
For a moment I felt a pang of nostalgia, but it did nothing to calm the lust that burned inside me now.
On the contrary, it only made me feel more keenly how tightly we were bound together by fate and how impossible it would be for me to ever leave her.
“You were so innocent back then,” I said.
“I’m still perfectly innocent.
You’re the one who’s corrupted. ”
“Say whatever you like.
I intend to chase after you no matter where you go. ”
“Hee hee hee. ”
“Hey! ”
I thumped the wall hard.
“Oh, what are you doing?
This isn’t some lonely house in the middle of nowhere.
Please keep it down. ”
“This wall is in the way.
I want to smash it to pieces. ”
“My, how noisy.
The mice are really acting up tonight. ”
“They certainly are.
This mouse is hysterical. ”
“I don’t like old-man mice. ”
“Don’t be stupid.
I’m not an old man.
I’ve only just turned thirty-two. ”
“I’m nineteen.
From nineteen, thirty-two looks like an old man.
I’ll give you some friendly advice: go find yourself another wife.
That might cure your hysteria. ”
No matter what I said, Naomi eventually answered only with that soft, mocking laugh. Before long she announced, “I’m going to sleep now,”
and began to snore loudly.
Soon she really did seem to be asleep.
The next morning when I woke up, Naomi was sitting beside my pillow in a loose, disheveled nightgown.
“What’s the matter, Jōji?
You were in quite a state last night. ”
“Yeah, lately I sometimes get like that.
Were you scared? ”
“It was funny.
I’d like to see it again. ”
“I’m fine now.
It’s completely gone this morning.
Ah, what a beautiful day. ”
“It is a beautiful day.
Why don’t you get up?
It’s already past ten.
I got up an hour ago and went to the baths. ”
Still lying down, I looked up at her fresh from the bath.
There is a true beauty in a woman’s “just-out-of-the-bath” appearance that is often best appreciated not immediately after she leaves the water but fifteen or twenty minutes later.
No matter how lovely a woman’s skin may be, right after a bath it is over-steamed and the fingertips turn pink and puffy.
Only after her body has cooled to the right temperature does it become translucent, like wax that has hardened.
Naomi had just come back from the baths and had been touched by the outside air, so she was at the most beautiful moment of her post-bath glow.
Her delicate, thin skin still held a trace of steam yet shone pure white, and around the collar of her robe, where her chest was hidden, there was a purplish shadow like watercolor pigment.
Her face glistened as though coated with a film of gelatin; only her eyebrows remained damp.
Above them the clear winter sky showed faintly blue through the window.
“Why on earth did you go to the baths first thing in the morning? ”
“None of your business.
Ah, I feel wonderful. ”
She patted both sides of her nose lightly with the palms of her hands, then suddenly thrust her face close to mine.
“Look!
Tell me honestly, is there any stubble? ”
“Yes, there is. ”
“I should have stopped at the barber’s and had them shave me. ”
“But you always said you hated shaving your face.
You told me Western women never shave their faces. ”
“These days it’s the fashion in America.
Look at my eyebrows.
All the American women shave them like this. ”
“I see.
So that’s why your face has looked different lately, even the shape of your eyebrows. ”
“Yes, that’s why.
It took you this long to notice?
You’re so behind the times. ”
Naomi seemed to be thinking of something else. Then she suddenly asked,
“Jōji, has your hysteria really gone away? ”
“Yes, it’s gone.
Why? ”
“If it has, I have a favor to ask.
It’s too much trouble to go all the way to the barber’s now.
Will you shave my face for me? ”
“You’re trying to bring on another attack, aren’t you? ”
“No, I’m perfectly serious.
Can’t you be a little kind?
Of course, if you have another fit and cut me, that would be terrible. ”
“I’ll lend you my safety razor.
You can do it yourself. ”
“That won’t work.
It’s not just my face; I need to shave all the way around my neck and the back of my shoulders. ”
“Why would you shave all the way back there? ”
“Because when I wear an evening gown my shoulders are completely exposed. ”
She deliberately slipped the robe off one shoulder just a little to show me.
“See?
I need to shave right down to here.
I can’t do that myself. ”
Then she quickly pulled the robe back up, but although I had been tricked by this maneuver many times before, it was still an irresistible temptation.
I knew perfectly well that Naomi didn’t really want her face shaved; she had gone to the trouble of taking a bath just to torment me.
Yet the idea of being allowed to shave her skin was a new and unprecedented challenge.
Today I would be able to get very close and study that skin to my heart’s content.
Of course I would also be allowed to touch it.
Just thinking about it, I had no courage to refuse her request.

While I busied myself boiling water on the gas ring, pouring it into the basin, and changing the blade in the Gillette razor, Naomi carried the desk over to the window, set up a small mirror on it, dropped her hips neatly between her spread legs, and wrapped a large white towel around her neck.
When I moved behind her, rubbed the bar of Colgate soap with water, and was about to begin, she spoke up.
“Jōji, I’ll let you shave me, but there’s one condition. ”
“A condition? ”
“Yes.
It’s not difficult. ”
“What is it? ”
“Don’t try to cheat by touching me all over while you pretend to shave.
You mustn’t let your fingers touch my skin at all. ” “But—”
“There’s no ‘but.’ You can shave without touching.
Use the brush for the soap and the Gillette razor.
Even a skilled barber doesn’t touch you. ”
“I can’t stand being compared to a barber. ”
“Stop being so arrogant.
You know you want to do it.
If you don’t want to, I won’t force you. ”
“I do want to.
Don’t say that.
I’ve already prepared everything. ”
Staring at the long, bare nape of her neck where the collar had been pulled down, I had no choice but to agree.
“You’ll follow the condition exactly? ”
“Yes. ”
“You absolutely must not touch me. ”
“I won’t. ”
“If you touch me even a little, I’ll stop immediately.
Keep your left hand on your knee the whole time. ”
I did as I was told.
Using only my right hand, I began shaving around her mouth.
She sat perfectly still, eyes fixed dreamily on the mirror, as though savoring the pleasant sensation of the razor gliding over her skin.
I could hear her slow, sleepy breathing; I could see the carotid artery pulsing beneath her chin.
I was now so close that my eyelashes could almost brush her face.
Outside the window the dry air was bright with morning light, so clear that I could count every pore.
Never before had I gazed so long, so closely, or in such bright light at the face of the woman I loved.
Seen from this distance her beauty had a colossal, overwhelming scale.
Those frighteningly long eyes, that splendid nose like a fine piece of architecture, the two bold lines running from nose to mouth, and beneath them the deep, rich crimson of her lips.
Was this mysterious substance called “Naomi’s face” really the source of all my torment?
The thought filled me with wonder.
Without thinking I picked up the brush and lathered the surface of that substance with furious energy.
No matter how violently I scrubbed, it remained calm and unresisting, moving only with soft resilience.
The razor in my hand crept down the smooth skin like a silver insect, moving from her neck toward her shoulders.
Her well-fleshed back, white as milk, broad and full, filled my field of vision.
Does she know how beautiful her back is, even though she can see only her face?
She herself probably has no idea.
I am the one who knows best.
I used to wash this back for her every day.
I would work up a lather just like this...
This is a historic site of my love.
My hands, my fingers, once played joyfully across this dazzling snow, treading freely and happily upon it.
There may still be traces left somewhere.
“Jōji, your hand is shaking.
Hold it steady... ”
Naomi’s voice suddenly broke in.
My head was ringing, my mouth was dry, and I could feel my whole body trembling.
I realized with a start that I was losing my mind.
I fought desperately to control myself; my face flushed hot, then cold.
But Naomi’s mischief was not over.
When she had finished with her shoulders, she rolled up her sleeves, raised her elbows high, and said,
“Now the armpits. ”
“The armpits? ”
“Yes.
When you wear Western clothes you have to shave under your arms.
It would be rude to show them like this. ”
“You’re being cruel! ”
“Why is it cruel?
You’re so strange.
I’m getting cold from the bath, so please hurry. ”
At that instant I flung the razor aside and threw myself at her elbow—no, I sank my teeth into it.
As though she had been expecting exactly that, Naomi immediately jerked her elbow back, knocking me away, but my fingers had apparently brushed her somewhere; they slid on the soap.
Before I could recover she shoved me violently toward the wall and cried sharply,
“What do you think you’re doing! ”
Her face—perhaps because mine had gone deathly pale—was also, no longer in jest, completely white.
“Naomi!
Naomi!
Stop tormenting me!
I’ll do anything you say!
Anything! ”
I have no idea what I said.
I was babbling frantically, rapidly, as though in a fever.
Naomi simply stood there stiffly, staring down at me with a look of utter astonishment.
I threw myself at her feet and knelt.
“Why are you silent?
Say something!
If you won’t, then kill me! ”
“You’re insane! ”
“Is it wrong to be insane? ”
“Who would bother with a madman like you? ”
“Then treat me like a horse.
Ride on my back like you did before.
If that’s all you’ll allow, I’ll take even that! ”
I dropped to all fours on the floor.
For a moment Naomi seemed to think I really had gone mad.
Her face grew even paler, almost livid, and the eyes fixed on me held something close to terror.
But suddenly she assumed a fierce, bold, brazen expression, swung her leg over my back with a thud, and said in a voice like a man’s,
“There.
Is this what you wanted? ”
“Yes, that’s it. ”
“Will you do everything I say from now on? ”
“Yes. ”
“Will you give me as much money as I want? ”
“Yes. ”
“Will you let me do whatever I like without interfering? ”
“Yes. ”
“Will you stop calling me ‘Naomi’ and call me ‘Naomi-san’ instead? ”
“I will. ”
“Promise? ”
“I promise. ”
“All right, then.
Since you’re so pitiful, I’ll treat you like a human being instead of a horse. ”
And so Naomi and I became covered in soap.
At last we’re really husband and wife.
This time I won’t let you get away,” I said.
“Were you that troubled when I ran away? ”
“Yes, terribly.
For a while I thought you would never come back. ”
“Do you understand now how frightening I can be? ”
“I do.
I understand only too well. ”
“Then don’t forget what you just promised.
You’ll let me do anything I want.
And even though we’re husband and wife, I won’t tolerate a stuffy, conventional marriage.
If you do, I’ll run away again. ”
“So from now on it’s ‘Naomi-san’ and ‘Jōji-san,’ is it? ”
“Will you take me dancing sometimes? ”
“Yes. ”
“May I associate with all sorts of friends?
You won’t complain like before? ”
“No. ”
“Though I have broken off with Ma-chan, you know. ”
“You broke with Kumagai? ”
“Yes.
He’s the most unpleasant man.
From now on I intend to associate mostly with Westerners.
They’re much more interesting than Japanese. ”
“That fellow from Yokohama, McConnell? ”
“I have many Western friends.
McConnell isn’t anything suspicious. ”
“Hmm, I wonder... ”
“That’s exactly why it’s no good.
You always suspect me.
If I say something is so, you must believe me.
All right?
Now, do you believe me or not? ”
“I believe you! ”
“I still have more conditions.
What are you going to do now that you’ve quit the company, Jōji? ”
“I was thinking of retreating to the country if you left me, but now that things have come to this I won’t.
I’ll liquidate my property in the country and bring the cash here. ”
“How much will that be? ”
“Well, I should be able to bring twenty or thirty thousand yen. ”
“Is that all? ”
“That should be more than enough for just the two of us. ”
“Can we live luxuriously on that? ”
“We can’t live purely for pleasure.
You may play as much as you like, but I intend to open an office and work independently. ”
“You mustn’t pour all the money into your work.
You have to set aside a separate sum for my luxuries.
Understood? ”
“Yes, understood. ”
“Then you’ll set aside half?
If it’s three hundred thousand, half is one hundred and fifty thousand; if two hundred thousand, then one hundred thousand. ”
“You’re being very precise. ”
“Of course.
We’re setting the conditions at the beginning.
Well?
Do you agree?
Is it so unpleasant to have me as your wife even on these terms? ”
“No, it isn’t unpleasant at all. ”
“If it is, say so now.
There’s still time to change everything. ”
“It’s fine, I said.
I agree. ”
“There’s more.
We can’t stay in a house like this anymore.
I want you to move us into a much grander, more modern house. ”
“Of course. ”
“I want to live in a Western-style house in a neighborhood where Westerners live, with a beautiful bedroom and dining room, and employ a cook and a houseboy. ”
“Is there such a house in Tokyo? ”
“There isn’t in Tokyo, but there is in Yokohama.
There’s a furnished house for rent on the Bluff that’s empty right now.
I looked at it the other day. ”
Only then did I realize how deep her scheme had been.
From the very beginning Naomi had planned all this, laid her trap, and lured me in.
And so the story now moves forward three or four years.
After that we moved to Yokohama and rented the Western-style house in the Yamate district that Naomi had found earlier.
But as our taste for luxury gradually took deeper root, we soon decided the house was too cramped.
Before long we bought the house in Honmoku—complete with all its furniture—that a Swiss family had been living in, and moved in.
The great earthquake completely destroyed Yamate, but much of Honmoku was spared.
Our house suffered nothing worse than a few cracks in the walls and escaped virtually undamaged.
One never knows what will turn out to be a blessing.
And so we have continued to live in this house ever since.

As planned, I resigned from the company in Ōimachi, settled my family’s property in the countryside, and together with two or three former classmates from school I established a limited partnership whose purpose was the manufacture and sale of electrical machinery.
Although I am the largest investor, my friends handle the actual operations, so I do not need to go to the office every day.
For some reason, however, Naomi does not like me to stay at home all day, and therefore—reluctantly—I make a point of going in at least once a day.
I leave Yokohama around eleven in the morning, spend an hour or two at the office in Kyōbashi, and usually return home by four in the afternoon.
I used to be extremely diligent and rose early, but these days I do not get up until half past nine or ten.
As soon as I am awake I slip on my nightclothes, steal on tiptoe to the door of Naomi’s bedroom, and knock softly.
But Naomi is even more of a late riser than I am, so at that hour she is still half asleep.
Sometimes she answers with a faint “Mmm,” and sometimes she remains unaware that I am there.
If she answers, I enter the room and greet her; if not, I turn away from the door and head straight to the office.
In this way, without our noticing, my wife and I have come to sleep in separate rooms.
The idea was originally Naomi’s.
A woman’s boudoir is sacred, she declared, and not even a husband may enter it at will.
She took the larger room for herself and assigned the smaller one next to it to me.
Although the rooms are adjacent, they are not directly connected.
Between them lies a bathroom and toilet reserved for the couple; in other words, the two rooms are separated by that distance, and to go from one to the other one must pass through it.
Every morning Naomi stays in bed until after eleven, drifting between sleep and wakefulness, smoking cigarettes and reading the newspaper.
She smokes Dimitrino’s slim cigarettes, reads the Miyako Shimbun, and looks at magazines such as Classic and Vogue.
Or rather, she does not so much read them as gaze intently, page by page, at the photographs—mainly pictures of dress designs and the latest fashions.
Her room faces east and south, with the sea of Honmoku lying just below the veranda, so it grows bright very early.
Her bed stands in the center of a room large enough to hold twenty tatami mats if it were Japanese-style.
It is no ordinary cheap bedstead.
It is a grand canopied bed with white gauze curtains hanging from it that had been put up for sale by a certain Tokyo embassy.
Ever since she acquired it, Naomi seems to find sleeping even more pleasant, and she has become even more reluctant to leave her bed.
Before washing her face she drinks black tea and milk in bed.
While she does so, the maid prepares her bath.
When she gets up she goes straight to the bathroom, and after bathing she lies down again for a while to receive a massage.
Then she does her hair, polishes her nails, and spends a long time working on her face with dozens of creams, lotions, and implements—far more than the proverbial “seven tools.
” After much indecision about what to wear, she usually appears in the dining room around half past one.
Once lunch is over she has almost nothing to do until evening.
In the evening she is either invited out, gives a party herself, or goes dancing at a hotel; she is never without some engagement.
So at that hour she applies her makeup once more and changes her clothes.
On nights when there is a ball she takes particular trouble: she goes to the bathroom, has the maid help her, and covers her entire body with powder.
Naomi’s friends kept changing.
Hamada and Kumagai stopped coming to the house altogether, and for a while it seemed that the man called McConnell had become her favorite, but before long he was replaced by a man named Dugan.
After Dugan came a friend called Eustace.
This Eustace was even more unpleasant than McConnell; he was extremely skilled at flattering Naomi.
Once, in a fit of rage, I struck him at a dance.
It caused a terrible commotion.
Naomi took Eustace’s side, called me a “madman,” and hurled abuse at me.
I grew even more furious and chased after Eustace.
Everyone grabbed me and shouted “George!
George!
” at the top of their voices.
(My name is Jōji, but Westerners think of it as George and so call me “George, George.
”) As a result Eustace stopped coming to our house, but at the same time Naomi presented me with a new set of conditions, and I was forced to submit to them.
Of course, after Eustace came a second and a third Eustace.
Yet today I have become astonishingly docile—even I find it strange.
It seems that once a person has had a truly terrifying experience, it becomes a fixed idea that remains in the mind forever.
I still cannot forget the dreadful moment when Naomi ran away from me.
The words she spoke then—“Now do you understand how frightening I can be?
”—still cling to my ears.
I had always known how fickle and self-willed she was; if those faults were taken away, her value would disappear.
The more I think of her as a fickle, willful creature, the more adorable she becomes and the deeper I fall into her trap.
I therefore understand that becoming angry only ensures my own defeat.
Once self-confidence is lost, all is lost.
At present I cannot begin to match her even in English.
She must have improved naturally through constant practice.

When I hear her rattling away fluently at a party, scattering charm among ladies and gentlemen, her pronunciation—which was already excellent—sounds so convincingly foreign that I often cannot catch what she is saying.
And from time to time she calls me “George” in the Western manner.
With this I bring to a close the record of our married life.
Those who find it ridiculous may laugh.
Those who find it instructive may take it as a warning.
As for me, I am in love with Naomi, so it does not matter what anyone thinks of me.
Naomi is twenty-three this year.
I am thirty-six.
